REST

THE NOONDAY - At rest amid the flush of golden corn, When rest is short and sweet; t At rest from toil begun at early morn By willing hands and feet. Above, the sky, in all its wide expanse,'" ' • " Laughs with its deepest blue, And stray winds waking upward from their trance, Scarce stir a stalk or two. How sweet such rest is to each working one! That mother sitting there Suckles a tender babe but late begun This life so strange and fair. And he, the father, looking down can feel • A new strength in his arm, And life and toil in softer tones reveal A deeper sacred charm. 0 weary ones that rise at labour's call! Toil on in hope and pain; A sure rest cometh when at evenfall Death stoops to reap his grain. ib—" Good Words" for December.

- "Con you tell me how the word saloon is spelt?" was asked of a Cockney. "Certainly," said the Londoner, with a look of triumph. "There's a hess, and a hay, and a hell, and two hoes, and a hen." A good lady who, on the death of her husband, mar- ried his brother, has a portrait of the former hanging in her dining-room. One day a visitor, remarking the I painting, asked, "Is that a member of your family ? " "Oh, that's my poor brother-id-law," was the ingenious reply. A gentleman, who was closely wrapped up in a fur coat, surmounted by a cap to match, took a seat in a railway carriage by the side of a lady. Ile made several attempts to draw her into conversation, but without avail. At last he exclaimed, "Madame, why are you so ungracious? Do you take me for a wolf in sheep's clothing?" "No; quite the reverse," answered the lady. A person named Danger kept a public-house on the Huntingdon road, near Cambridge. On being compelled to quit the house, which was not his own, he built an inn on the opposite side of the road, and caused to be painted beneath the sign, "Danger from over the way." His successor in the old house retorted by inscribing over his door, "There is no Danger here now. The English tell some large stories, and justly too, about their heavy ordnance. An American gentleman, who was listening in a London coffee-house to a descrip- tion of these monsters, said abruptly, " Pooh ! gentle- men, I won't deny that's a fair sized cannon; but you are a leetle mistaken in supposing it to be the largest in the world. It's not to .be named in the same minute with one of our Yankee cannon that I saw in Charleston last year. Supiter ! that was a cannon! Why, gentle.' men, it was so large that the sailors had to employ two yoke of oxen to draw in the ball." "The deuce they were P' exclaimed one of his hearers with a smile of triumph. "Pray can you tell me how they got the oxen out again ?" "Why, my dear sir," said the Yankee, "they unyoked 'em, and drove 'em through the vent 'ole !" At his death, the Lord of—, in Argyleshire, left a beautiful young widow—of course, inconsolable for her loss. After the burial and banquet, clansman and clans- woman, attended by the piper and the fiddler, convened for a dance in the castle hall, resolved to mitigate their grief with the Highland fling; when, unexpectedly, the widow herself came in, all weeds and tears, with the tip of her nose scarcely peeping from her crape cap, and she I seated herself carefully on a bench. The gentleman who was to lead down the dance thought he could not, in good breeding, ask any other lady than the mistress of the house to stand up with him—and, with a deep sigh, she consented. He then asked the disconsolate widow the name of the spring, i.e.,the tune, she would wish to have played. "0," said she, "let it be a light spring, for I have a heavy heart." Her aristocratic manner and rich elaborate toilet seemed somewhat/ out of place in the plebeian sur- roundings of the third-class railway carriage which she entered at a suburban station. Drawing her skirts about her, she retired as far as possible into a corner, and gazed persistently out of the window. On the op- posite side sat a neatly attired young man, with very white hands and an air generally suggestive of the clergy. He glanced at the fair vision in the corner from time to time in a reproachful manner. She looked fur- tively at him from beneath her lashes, and with a pretty puckering of her brow, seemed trying to recall where she had met him. That his face was familiar was evi- dent, and, finally deciding that he rightfully belonged to the army of captives that had laid their hearts at her feet at Scarborough last August, she concluded to end his misery by recognising him. He was well dressed and apparently well bred. So, turning with a little start of recognition, their eyes met, and she bowed stiffly. He seemed delighted, and changing his seat to her sale, he said, "You are very kind to remember me." "oh, no!" she replied, with an air of polite reserve. "I recall per- fectly the occasion on which we met." A few common- places followed, and, emboldened with his success, the gentleman said gravely, as he produced a card, "I hope .you will permit me to call upon you again." She glanced at the card, a wave of colour swept over her face, and the train stopping, she drew down her veil and bounced out of the carriage with the swiftness of a tennis ball. ' The address upon the card read—" IL Bullfinch, chiropo. I dist. Corns and bunions extracted without pain." GADOMOROUGH.--THE MITE AND THE PROFEWIR,— Whenever he listened to any eminent musician, Gains- borough was immediately possessed by the boyish illu- sion that he could himself reproduce the excellence of the performance if only he could purchase the instru- ment. In this way he bought Giardini's violin and Abel's viol-de-gamba. At another time he was fascinated by Fischer's hautboy and Crosdil's violoncello, and finally, having seen a lute in a picture by Vandyck, he 'cast about until he had discovered a German professor who owned such an instrument, when, according to his biographer, the following amusing scene took place. Bursting.in upon the professor, who was quietly smok- ing his pipe, the impetuous artist thus accosts him:— "I have come to buy your lute. Name your price and I will pay it." "I cannot sell my lute." "Not for a guinea or two perhaps; but you must Sell at some price, and so I tell you." "My lute is worth much money— ten guineas." "Indeed it is—quite that; see, here's your money. Good day." Scarcely, however, had the painter quitted the room than he was back Again. I have forgotten something. What is your Jute to me if I have not your book of airs?" 4‘ Ah, Master Gainsborough, I cannot part with my book." "" Nonsense. You can make another at any time. see..here's the book I want. _a n d here's another ten guineas for it." The transaction Seemed now com- plete; but at the last moment it would seem suddenly to have occurred to Gainsborough that he did not know how to play upon the lute. He accordingly returns once more. "Dear me, what is the use of your book to me if I don't understand it, or of your lute if I cannot play on it? Come home with toe a once, and give me the ffrst lesson." "I will come to-morrow." "Come now." "I must dress." "You are admirably dressed." "I must shave." "1 honour your beard.", " I must, how- ever, put on my wig." "Confound your wig! Your cap and beard become you well enough. Do-you think if vandyck wanted to paint you he'd let you be shaved? Come at once." And so the poor prVessor was dragged • off, and all earlier musical passions were forgotten in the new enthusiasm for the lute.—l7te English Illus- trated Magazine for December. A young man being, in the habit of "just running round the corner to see his friend Tom," his father said to him one day, "I've no objection to your frequent visits to Tom so long as Jerry is not there; but Tom and Jerry I should decidedly object to." About .twenty such Spaniards arrived in this port recently from Havana. Their speech was not the purest Castilian. Said their spokesman: " 'Melican law no good. • We pay 25 clonal in Havana fol papel that make us Spanlads. Ilelican man got no law 'gainst Spanlads." ROMAN-NOSED Ser.stox.—Probably few of the many people who like and eat the salmon concern themselves about the shape of his kse. It is hardly possible that , anybody has ever dreamed of a salmon with a Greek or a Roman nose, or with a pug. Napoleon could not have, required long noses on his salmon as he did on his gene- • rals. And yet there is a Roman-nosed salmon—hook- nose is a more common name for hien—and he is not very good to eat. Complaint is made of the appearance, of a large number of hook-noses in Oregon waters. It, was at first supposed that this fish was a distinct spe- cies, but it is probable that he is only an especially ill- favoured male—the hook-nose is always a naale—of the Chinook variety. " Pexcies" PLACE coA POWER.—On 17th July, 1841, appeared the first number of an illustrated weekly paper that has had down to this day a career so honourable that Englishmen may justly feel pride in its success. Punch, or the London Charivari, has made itself a neces- sity to the people of these islands. Our mental life would be poorer, wanting Punch; the innocent gaiety of the nation would be eclipsed, if Punch ceased to laugh with us, and to make us laugh. The position of Punch is unique in the world. The best comic papers of the Continent, those of Paris, for example, are roor beside it. . . . . The satire of the French journals is, for the , most part, either ferocious or indecent; they gibbetl their adversaries to eternal infamy, or they grin with a double meaning that suggests all things that are unholy and impure. Punch is, and always has been, healthy, manly, and honest. Mistaken, we may, think it some- times; it looks at life, perhaps, too much through Cock- ney spectacles; it does not, except at rare and very , happy moments of inspiration, quite understand a Scotchman but it has never been mean or vindictive. It is a standing proof that gaiety and innocence go gadly hand in hand. Grown men find amusement in its pages, and it ilever brought a blush to the cheek of an innocent , girL Think of the abuses it has exposed, the absurdities it has ridiculed, the reforms it has advocated, of the merry laughter it has caused, of the kindly feelings it has promoted !—Good Words for December. "PUNCH'S" PICTURES Now AND AT ITS START—When Punch started it was rather a dead time for English caricature, and the new journal gave new impetus and a new tone to burlesque art. The little black Silhouettes, with punning titles, of the earlier volumes are clever certainly, but they become monotonous, while the larger illustrations are comparatively thin, forced, and man-j tiered. The demand for the work, however, produced ere long the men who were ready and able to supply it. The contrast is great between the drawings in Punch and those of the caricaturists a century ago. They show us a different life, almost a different national tempo"- ment, or at least a temperament modified very much mi its manifestations. The old ferocity, the old rough-and- ready horseplay have given place to the grace of life, and to dignity and purity of manndrs. Among those who have drawn for Punch are Birket Foster, "Crow-s quill," Sir John Gilbert, and Kenny Meadows; but the artists who have made its fame in the past are pre-, eminently John Leech and Richard Doyle. The artists* of to-day on the staff of Punch sustain splendidly the reputation of the paper. Du Maurier, Keene, Sam- bourne, are household names among us, and we are their debtors for many a pleasant moment. One of the most illustrious of the band is John Tenniel, who is to-day the foremost living political caricaturist, not of this coun- try only, but of the world.—lbid. UPPER CLASS TRAINING OF CHILDREN.—What a mis- take parents make in bringing up their daughters with I the solo practical object of marrying them off. It seems that this is the leading characteristic of English edu- cation amongst the upper classes. It shall be my en- deavour to bring up my girll in such a way that they shall not regard marriage as the one thing needful in their future, and that they may feel themselves equal to em- ploying their lives just as usefully in other directions. Marriage for marriage sake is surely the greatest error a woman can commit I know what an all- absorbing feeling devotion to parents is; as long as I was in the house of my father and mother that feeling ' filled my whole soul. So it does now to a great extent, and my 4onging for home has not ceased despite my long a ,W.bnce. Nothing is more disadvantageous to children than to make too much of them. They ought to be unselfish, unspoilt, and easily satisfied. Up to the present this is the case with mine. That they occupy a , more salient position in my life than is often the case] with families of our rank is simply because I have never been able to employ persons enough of a responsible kind to look after them; upon this account certain things remain undone unless I do them myself—and the children would suffer were they not done. But child- worship, or having one's children always about one without intermission, is by no means the right thing ;1 and women are intolerable who continually talk about their own children.—Letters of the Princess Alice. "CURRENT Cone IN ABTSSINIA.—There are no shops in Adowa or in any other Abyssinian town. All trade is done within the trader's home or compound over a glass of tedge or mattic. Flour is ground by the women of the house; on the premises bread is made; tedge and mead are brewed in each household. Each house rears its own cattle as well as children—baby, goats and lambs, fowls and chickens are brought up together, and are playmates from their youth. The Marie Therese dollar-piece is the only coin. Cloth and bah; of rock salt ten inches long by two wide and deep, bound with a reed, serve as their ordinary medium of barter. Mem- bers of our mission traded a good deal with empty beer bottles, receiving two chickens and a dozen eggs for a quart. I made everlasting friendship with a village chief by making him a present of an empty Worcester, sauce bottle; the glass stopper appearing to be a source of delight and comfort to him. Abyssinians seem to require "but little here below" as regards variety in their diet, and are very conservative as to the paucity of vegetables. Onions, with another unsavoury plant almost as obnoxious to the nasal organs, with the addi- tion of capsicums, are all they seem to care about. Potatoes were introduced some time ago, but are never allowed to come to maturity, and are eaten green. M. —' the only European resident in the country, who came to Abyssinia to repair muskets, introduced water- creases, which now grow near all the brooks round about Adowa, but the natives do not patronise it. When the gunsmith called upon the Admiral to pay his respects with that flowery politeness proverbial to Frenchmen, he presented him with a bouquet of these pungent little leaves, and supplied us ever afterwards while we re- mained in Adowa. This solitary man of Marseilles had lived in the country over fifteen years, and had only been once back to his native land. He was now making good money out of his smithy, and seemed quite content.— Frederick Villiers, in the Illustrated English Magazine. "FAITHFUL JACIL.—A touching incident in dog life is told by Samuel Smiles in his sketch of George Moore, the merchant and philanthropist. Whitehall was the Cumberland seat of Mr. Moore. It was an old Border tower, in which as a boy he had many a dangerous' climb in search of birds' nests ; and when he became a prosperous man he often thought of buying the White- hall property. In 1858 the property came into the mar- ket, and he became the happy possessor of this splendid estate. Mr. Moore had a favourite dog named Jack. Says Mr. Smiles:—" Jack was a thoroughbred bulldog, much under-hung, and though rather ferocious, looking as gentle as a kitten to those whom he knew. Jack's devotion to his master was quite touching. Mrs. Moore on saw him get up a wall quite eighteen feet high by scratching up with his paws and hanging on to the pro- jecting pieces of stone with his teeth, in order to get to his master, who was overlooking some building on the other side. But though kind to those around him, he was suspicious to strangers and savage to other dogs that came about the place; and many were the serious adventures that took place in consequence. Jack never began the fight, but if another dog growled at him or insulted him he gave no quarter. Mr. Moore had been two or three times bitten in trying to separate the dog's: but as he really loved Jack, he gave him, as was his wont,, "one more chance." At length the last chews came. One day some ladies called at Whitehall, bring- ing a little mongrel terrier with them. The dog went into the yard, and occupied himself with barking and snarling at Jack, beyond the length of his chain. Jack was, of course, very much provoked, but he was tied, and could do nothing at that time. He could only show his feelings by suppressed growls. In the afternoon Jack was loosed to go out with his master. He first went to the study door to make his greetings. Then fie r. tt lllasrleota ft ho. snlimdo ahsiorie er, andw as a couldts eonsnte went to the bowling-green to find out the strange ag- cpefaorprai, tneanne thekwif mongreltrho from groat the dog t7h effort, he separated them by force. He had to strike the dogs to make them loosen their hold, and Jack was ter- ribly hurt. Yet he crawled to lick his master's feet. George Moore went into the house quite unmanned. Ile shed bitter tears over his faithful dog, and he could not sleep that night. But the order was given that he must be shot. It was carried out next day. Twenty-five years ago the freight on wheat from Chi- ca..° to Liverpool was 38. a bushel. This season it has ben carried for 7-id. a bushel. A farm in Lincolnshire was sold recently at £22 per 'acre. A few years ago this land cost £BO per acre, and over £l,OOO has since been expended on buildings: .: • A FIGHT BETWEEN COINS.—The other evening a very remarkable fight took place between two cows, the pro- perty of Mr. T. Vl'illiaths, farmer, of Allaston Court, near Lydney-on-Severn. The animall had for some time past exhibited a dislike to each other, and, meeting in a quiet spot, fought with such desperation that one was killed. The brute was terribly maimed, and its head was beaten to a pulp. The victor was also severely mauled, one of its horns being broken. DECLINE lit THE VALUE or FARMS.—In the Chancery ' Division, London, lately, an action was retied which re- vealed the extent to which the agricultural depression ' has diminished the value of farming property. By ad- vice 'of Mr. R. Howes, solicitor, Mr. J. Atterbury, of Rugby, seven years ago lent £2,500 on the security of a farm near Bedford which was valued at £14,000, but upon which there was a first mortgage of £5,000. When the farm was sold four years later it realiSed only £5,950, Mr. Atterbury thus losing £1,633, which sum he now sought to recover from his solicitor, Mr. Howes. Vice-Chancellor Bacon said there had been no neglect on the part of Mr. Howes, the property having depreciated in value, and he dismissed the action, but withouticosts. Rrancricas OF RENT.—In a speech at Alford, on Friday week, Mr. Chaplin, MT., acknowledged as inevitable the reduction of rents which must, follow a diminished money produce from the land. His proposal virtually recommended the reduction of corn rents. He had often thought that a fair and legitimate arrangement between all parties would he this—tp make a rule of three sum with regard to lands which grow wheat, and to say if land was worth 40s. per acre when wheat was making • 40s. per quarter, it should only be worth per acre as • much as wheat was now making per quarter, and this arrangement would, he believed, fulfil all the conditions of fairness. The proposal is that the rent of wheat- • growing land should always be the value of one ginner of wheat per acre, whatever that might be. What will • clay-land farmers'say to this?. --• ' SUGGESTION FOR LOIJNTY LAND COURTS.--TIIC mem- bers of the Executive of the Scottish Farroers'. Alliance • have .Committed themselves to the proposal of a Land Court for every county in Scotland, "to regulate the conditions of occupancy on the application of either landlord or tenant, and to deal with the allocation or allotment of land- to working 'men both in town and country." Each court, it is suggested, is to consist of three commissioners, two of whom are to be practical • agriculturists, well acquainted with the soil, climate, and conditions of occupancy in the ootuatry. The power of these commissioners is to be so great, that , "there is hardly any questiOn connected with the land which they Ihould not be empowered to adjust." A right to appeal on pointa of law only is recommended. • Whether the General Committee of the Scottish Alliance will agree to this or not remains to be seen. Some kind of court would be essential to prevent the renting of tenants on their improvements; but it would not no-, cessarily have power to interfere with rents in any other way. _ , IA DELIGHTFUL Stamm, or- FErnamsx.—A novel case was recently heard at Bolton County Court before Judge Hutton, the old feudal system turning up, by 1 which personsltholding in feud, feed, or fee were bound ' by oath to sefie the owner of the fee-simple at lieme, or' abroad in all military expeditions when required." The• l defendant in the action, a Mr. Wilson, occupies Eatock Farm, Westhoughton, holding the farm on lease from the Hon. Algernon Egerton, who is 'feudary to the Bridg- water trustees, and bound by virtue of his tenure to supply.each year a man or horsEl to the Worsley troop of the Duke of Lancaster's Own Yeomanry Cavalry in, respect of that farm. Defendant is bound by a similar deed drawn up between him and Mr. Egerton. . Defen- dant failing to comply with the agreement, Mr. Egerton had to supply the want in the shape of a substitute named Hart, the plaintiff inthe case, who claimed £6 as expenditure incurred in 1883 and 1884 as a trooper in the yeomanry. The deeds in proof of defendant's liabi- lities were submitted, and his Honour found that the defendant was liable to Mr. Egerton, who ought to have been the plaintiff in the case. By consent Mr. Egerton's name was substituted for that of Hart in the summons, and defendant promised to pay the amount claimed to the regimental sergeant-major. GLANDERS.—Dr. N. H. Paaren, State Veterinarian of Illinois, read a paper before the Chicago Eclectic Medical Society on the subject of "Glanders in Man and Animal" Glanders, he said, is a specific febrile disorder peculiar to solipeds, and is capable of transmission to man and other animals. The disease may appear in different i forms—simple glanders and acute farcy. In reality, I however, glanders and farcy are identical, glanders being I the, more malignant form, and invariably fatal. There ' is a form of simple chronic glanders, Which may exist in the human system, as has been demonstrated in cases that came under the doctor's observation. He cited a' ease where a farmer, living near Elgin, became inocu- lated with the most malignant form of glanders from a diseased horse by getting some of the virus from the horse's nostrils on his -finger. The farmer 'died a hor- rible death a few days after the disease had asserted it- self. The man's wife, who attended him in his sickness, became inoculated with the disease in the form of farcy, and, while she is stilt alive, after one year's suffering from the disease, she drags out a miserable existence,' excluded from the world. There is no such a thing as a cure for glanders or farcy, but it may be temporarily arrested by antiseptic treatment. The only safeguard to society, the doctor said, is the destruction of any animal that shows symptoms of the malady. Nonni LANCASHIRE.—A few days ef fine weather has enabled winter wheat-sowing to be pretty well com- pleted on most farms, and on some the plant is showing through. Turnips, also, are mostly off the land, except such as are to be eaten off by sheep; but as winter pro; vender is likely to be short this year, fewer roots will be eaten on the land, and chaffing and pulping food for stock will more resorted to as tending to eke out the available supply. The present look-out is not ,of the brightest in this district, for everything that the farmeg has to sell is at the lowest prices, whilst his stock of food for the animals of the fasm is less than for several 'years past. This state of things presents a difficult problem from which to nnng out a profit. The trade of the district is as fiat and depressed as it can well be, an 4 the bulk of the artisan class are on about half wages this 'hag had a serious effect upon the price of farm pro- duce. Next we have American and New Zealand flesli meat poured into the markets, and during the past fort; night butchers' prices' have receded about 2d. per lb., and the rates paid to farmers are in corresponding ratio. Rents keep at about the old rates, and there has been very little relief in wages paid to labourers. There is a general feeling amongst farmers that, unless an im- provement sets in shortly, northern rents will have to fall to a somewhat corresponding rate of thOse now existing in the south.—R., in Agricultural Gazette. Curie AND &roar Puosracrs.—Winter-proud wheats have been checked by frost, which is salutary, and yet the cold has not been so severe as to hinder the comple- tion of root-saving. Not only is all pre-winter seeding of wheat finished, except in special cases, but ploughing for fallow and other tillage operati-ms are so forward that the horse teams have little left to do on the land. This must lead to a serious diminution in employment for labourers; and reports from many quarters tell of lowered wages and of men thrown out of work for pro- bably most part of the winter.—A valuable contribution to the science of feeding is sgpplied in experiments made in the growing and fattening of various kinds of animals. Thus, the average result of feeding young shorthorn steers is given, from the calf 2 months and 25 days old, havingla live weight of 2921 b., valued at 21d. per lb., till it ended:As a fat beast 2 years and 2 months old, with a live weight of 1,4391 b., or 920 dead weight, at aid. per lb. In a little short of two years the cost of feeding was £.22 88. 2d., value of calf £3 6s. 2d., total cost R. 25 14s. 44.; amount realised for the finished animal, £25 17s. ed., leaving a gain of only 3s. 2d., plus the value of the manure left for producing crops. The hay, barley-meal, oil-cake, and buck-wheat consumed were stated at cost price the vetches, clover, &c., put it the assumed price realised, namely ss. per ton, and swedes, rnangolds, and cabbage at 7s. 6d. per ton. The average weekly increase of the beast in live weight was 114 lb. Trio Gnowrit OF FAILH RENTAL.—Major Craigio writes to a contemporary ;—" May I ask to be allowed to point out to your readers that Mr. Bear's estimate of a 40 per cent, increase in land rental between 1855-4 and 1879-80 is entirely erroneous? He has, no doubt inadvertently, but none the less unfortunately, failed to observe the change made in 1874 in the mode in which Irish rental is stated in schedule B. Only the ' net ' Irish rental ap- pears in the so-called ' gross ' column in 1853-4, whereali gross rental from all the three kingdoms appears in the figures for 1879-80. As the gross Irish rental exceeded the net in the last-named year by £7,258,000, were We 'now to state the figures for 1879-80 in the form in which those for 1853-4 were made up—the only course bk which a correct comparison could be made—it wound be at once apparent that the increase between the dates referred to was one not of 40,, but only, of 25 per emit, and a reduction must 'consequently be made of no less than A 17,700,000 from the aggregate addition assumed to be made to the landowners' capital in the years of general inflation of values selected for the comparison," In reply, Mr. W. E. On examining the figures for 1874 I see that Major Craigie is right. div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING

The frog, if it continues—though as we write thereis I every sign of a change—will render the ground in a fit state to wheel manure over with ease and comfort. Nothing can be more tiresome than having the soil con- tinually carried by the feet and the wheel of the barrow on to the walk, which must unavoidably occur more or less when the surface of the ground is moist and ad- ' hesive. If any length of walk is traversed, the labour of cleaning it is considerable, especially if it be graveL One way of getting over these unpleasant experiences is to have a few boards placed on the soil for the wheel- barrow to run upon. If in short lengths they are more convenient, as they can ,be moved and placed more readily in any direction. Manure is not always a plentiful article on the cot- tager's premises, and we have in this column shown how it can be increased. The Gardening World has some very sensible remarks on the subject of "Home Manures for the Garden." The materials for the preparation of the compost may, it says, "be considered under four heads: —lst. Earthy refuse, such as ashes, building rubbish, clay, quicklime, gaslime, scrapings of roads, mud from ditches, ponds, or sluices. 2nd. Vegetable refuse, com- prising all fallen and decaying leaves, whether of trees, shrubs, or kitchen vegetables; seaweed, potato haulm, trimmiags of hedges and trees, peat rubbish, mowings of lawns and trimmings of garden paths, weeds, moss, heather, sawdust, soot, and stray rubbish in general. 3rd. Animal refuse, including blood, dead animals, feathers, bones, nightsoil, and slaughter-house refuse of all kinds. According to Boussingault, 301 b. of blood, 841 b. of bone or 291 b. of cow hair, contains as much nitrogen as half a ton of stable manure. 4th. Liquid , refuse from dwelling-houses, soapsuds and wash water, drainings from stables, cowhouses, and piggeries, and gas liquor. In fact, whatever contains the constituents ' of which the living fabric of plants is composed will be found useful to promote future plant life.' Cottagers k have not all these, articles within their reach, but there are some of the materials which are contemptuously thrown away, and we have had frequent evidence of great waste of fertilising material in the cottage garden and farm.

_ THE norm GARDEN.—Cottagers that have not intro- duced the Chrysanthemum into their front garden have missed a rare treat, for they have never before been finer. For a month they have been developing flowers rapidly, and they are of various sizes and colours. Elaine has been the best amongst whites, and it has maintained its purity, beyond a little yellow which tip- pears to intrude itself as the flowers advance, as well as a smoky atmosphere would allow it. Jardine des planteS is a bright golden yellow. Mrs. Sharpe is a rich pink rose; Bob is a dark brown crimson, and very profuse but smaller flower. There are several others represent- ing all shades of the above, and none seem to have suffered from the frost during the past few nights. It is easy to protect the plants if planted against a wall, and so prolong their flowering season. Fuchsias that may have been turned out of their pots into beds or borders may be taken up and placed in pots, or packed together in boxes, or placed on a cellar floor with any light stuff round the roots. Cocoa-nut fibre would answer very well, or short litter. The object is to pre- vent the rood; drying up. Those in pots or boxes can be stored away in the dark or in the light, provided they are not expoSed to too much frost. No frost that we have had this season has damaged them yet, even outside, but to expose them to a continuous 1.0 deg. or 12 deg. for a fortnight would- be too perilous. The length of the shoots may be reduced, as they will not be so liable to be broken in being moved when they are moderately short. It was once the' practice to keep these plants unusually dry during the winter, and in spring many were found to be dead and several partially so. The plants should, upon no account, become dust dry, and sufficient water must be given to preserve the shoots from shrivelling. Tax Witinow.—All Fuchsias grown in pots in the win- dow should be brought to a state of rest by gradually Withholding water till every leaf turns a natural yellow and falls off. The wood, also, will turn toe nutty 'brown colour. Water may be withheld till the plant flags, when as much may be given as will moisten the soil half-way down and after two or three applications of this sort, another reduction may be made in the supply, when the plant will appear to go to rest in the most natural manner. Fuchsias are not to be grown well by keeping them in a continuous state of excitement, as is usually done by cottagers.

div.head: MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY.
div.p: THE MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY.

THE CRYSTAL PALACE SHOW. I The whirligig of time has once more brought round I the Crystal Palace stow, to the growth of which there appeared to be no limit, for this year it is two or three hundred pens larger than the show of 1883, in itself the largest by far that had ever been held. The grand total was 5,645 pens. Nearly all the classes are for single birds, but there are a few in which pairs are exhibited, so that the actual number of birds at the show will have been at least 6,200. This number would probably have been considerably larger, but for the fact that the Birmingham Show opens to-day, and as the Crystal Palace Show only closed on Thursday night, it was utterly impossible for many birds to appear at both places. And if it had been possible, the being penned , up for two whole weeks without any rest, for the day I spent in journeying from one place to the other cannot be called a reat,:would mean the death of many speci- mens. Doubtless some may be at both, but we should not like to be owner or purchaser of them. But for this clashing, and it is only fair to say that the blame of it must be laid on the Crystal Palace authorities, who changed the date of their fixture to a week later than usual, it is more than likely the total of pens would have reached 6,000. When we consider the vast efforts made for the show, the preparations for enonths and years, the large number of exhibitors who send, and the thousands who attend the show as visitors, it will be seen how wide are the ramifications of the poultry fancy. If we take the value of the birds at £2 each, which, as there are very few entered at a less sum, and many would not be sold tor £2O or even £5O, is a very low estimate indeed, the value of the poultry and pigeons exhibited, would be upwards of £ll,OOO. The prizes offered, amounted to £1,600, including 135 silver cups, ranging in value from two guineas to thirty pounds. There were 170 classes provided for poultry and 183 for pigeons. It may be interesting for readers of The Guar- dian to know the number of entries in the various sec- tions, and we, therefore, give them. Pounaiy.-Dorkings 241, Cochins 214, Brahmas 340, Spanish 71, French 134, Hamburghs 144, Game 253, Aseels 3, Malaya 23, Polish 58, Leghorns 54, Plymouth Rocks 114, Andalusians 46, Minorcas 71, Langshans 79, any other variety 22, Game Bantanis 245, Bantams not Game 149, Ducks 105, Geese 23, Turkeys 16, Table Poul- try 31; total, 3,226. PIGEONS.-Pouters 243, Carriers 273, Dragoons 302, Short-faced Tumblers 99, Barbs 78, Jacobins 141, Fan- tails 59, Owls 103, Nuns 13, Trumpeters 14, Turbits 131, Oriental Frills 105, Frill Backs 13, German Toys 24, Swallows 11, Magpies 91, Archangels, 49; Runts 23, Muffed Tumblers 18, Flying Tumblers 69, Antwerps 120, any other variety 10, Homers 223; total, 2,419. The Show was held in the centre transept as usual, and the poultry pens stretched in two double rows from one end to the other. The pigeon pens occupied the great square lying between the pantomime stage and the Handel Orchestra. It may be of interest to nots that the staging occupied by the pens was upwards of 8,000 feet, or nearly a mile long. To erect pens for all these birds, which was undertaken by the well-known firm of Spratt's Patent, to receive, pen, judge, and de- spatch them again was no light task, but it has been carried through most successfully. Only a long experi- ence could teach anyone how to provide for all the thousand and one matters involved in so great an under- taking. Amongst the judges we note the named our fellow- townsman Mr. Richard Teebay of Fulwood (who has acted at this show since its establishment), Capt. Heaton of Worsley, and Mr. Geo. Hall of Kendal; and the fol- lowing are the names of some Lancashire prize winners: -In Poultry, Mr. Forrester Addie, of this town, wins the twenty-five guinea Challenge Cup for the best Game Bantam, cock or cockerel, with a beautiful black red; also, amongst other prizes, first and second prizes for black red hens, first for a Duckwing cockerel, and first also for a pullet of the same breed. Messrs. Ainscough, of Parbold, near Wigan, win first and cup for black red Game Bantam cocks, second and third for Duckwing pullets, second for Pile cockerels, and second for Pile Bantam Pullets. Mr. J. Ainsworth, of Darwen, takes second in Houdan cocks, first and cup, and second in the other French varieties. Mr. Gr: ,Anderton, of Grim- shaw-street Mill, wins first in any other colour Game Bantam cock; Capt. Heaton;of Worsley, wins second in. both black red Game cocks and cockerels, first and third in black red Game hens. Messrs. Saul; Harrison, and Saul, of Ashton, win second in any variety Bantam hens. Messrs. T. H. and A. Stretch, of Ormskirk, win first in brown red Game Bantams, second in black red Bantam cockerels. Mr. E. Walton, of Ravrtenstall, obtains second in black Polish hens. second in brown red Ban- tam cocks, second in black red Game Bantam pullets, third in brown red Game Bantam pullets, first in Pile Bantam cockerels, and the same in Pile Pullets, first and cup in black Rose-comb Bantam cocks, and second in white Bantam hens. Mr. J. Wood, of Bruiscall, Chorley, takes third in Partridge Cochin cocks, s'econd in hens of the same breed, second in Spanish cocks, and second in golden-spangled Hamburgh hens. In Pigeons, Mr. R. 11. Leach, of Thornhill, Wigan, takes second in chequed Homer cocks; •Messrs. Stretch, of Ormskirk, obtains third in each of two of the Owl classes, second in bled, pr dun Turbit cocks, and second in-red or yellow Turb;t cocks.

- DISORDERLY PROCESSIONS. - The minutes of the Watch Committee contained a resolu- tion that the Town Clerk be instructed to prepare bye-laws to prevent disorderly processions in the public streets. The MAYOR moved the adoption of these minutes. Councillor MACKIN asked the Committee or Town Clebk If they would give the Council the slightest idea whether that minute referred to the procession of the Mayor, alder. men, and councillors to church on Sunday, or whether it referred to the poor Salvation Army. If the resolution re- ferred to the crowding of the streets, especially on Sunday evenings, he had not arfother word to say, but if there was to be any special arrangement for one party more than another, whether it was the Mayor or the Salvationist% he should like that they should see those arrangements before they passed under the authority of the Council. The MAYOR said he would take upon himself to answer Dr. Mackie in this way—that whether it was the Mayor i and Corporation in their procession to church, or whether t was a procession of the Salvation Army or any other proces- men, if there be elements of disorder in it be (the Mayor) took it that that procession would come under the influence of the proposed rules. ([tear, hear, and , laughter.) The minutes were then passed. FINANCE COMMITTEE.

• This Committee's minutes contained the following : ResAution that Mr. Councillor Broadbent be appointed chairman and Mr. Councillor Platt the deputy-chairman of this committee for the ensuing year.—Recommendation that the following plans be approved :—Plan of proposed new streets near Wellfield-street; plan of ten houses in new 'street off Lovely-lane for Mr. John Appleton.—Orders for ' payment of accounts amounting to (including the sum of £7O law costs Fairhurst to Corporation) £7l es 41—Re- commendation that the town clerk be instructed to offer £5,250 and law charges for the purchase of Messrs Layland's property in Bridge-street. COancillor PLATT moved the adoption of these minutes and said that with regard to Messrs Layland's property the price named was rather under the mark of the estimate given to the Council in the first instance. Councillor BOLTON complained of some of the lamps be- ing shifted almost every other month. He thought it would be much less expense if they were kept in one place. Alderman CITANDLEY, referring to a proposal by the com- mittee to place a new 60-candle Bray's lamp opposite Rylandsltreet, said that the cost of lighting the town was very serious, and although be would not move against this proposal he thought the conamittee Ought to bear in mind the expense when they multiplied the number of these lamps. Councillor BURGESS said that although he had ever wished the town to be lighted as economically as possible he hoped Alderman Chandley'e remarks would not induce the Light- ing Committee to cease from making the town as light as possible. (Hear, hear.) He thought there was nothing that made it more easy to keep good order in the town, than hav- ing the streets well lighted. (Hear, hear.) I The MAYOR said he was going to remind Mr. Alderman Chandlev that the Corporation were customers of themselves with regard to gas. He had no doubt that it did not cost them one half what it would have cost if they had to pay a private company. He was a great advocate for more light, both materially and metaphorically. (Hear, hear, ind laughter.) Councillor Purr, in reply to Councillor Bolton, said the Committee never shifted any lamps without having first examined theepot, and they were sometimes compelled to shift them because of the making of new streets. With re- gard to Alderman Chandley's remarks, he thought they would findthat there was only one 60-candle burner andthat was in Bridge-street, which was, he thought they might venture to I say, the most important street in the borough. i Alderman WEBSTER: And the worst lighted. (Hear, hear.) The minutes were adopted. SANITARY COMMITTEE —IMPORTANT SEWAGE PROROSALS. In the minutes of the Sanitary Committee it was stated that Alderman Burgos had been appointed chairman of the committee for the ensuing year; and Councillor Sutton deputy-chairman. It was also recommended_the adoption by the committee of the amended report of the Borough Surveyor with regard to the present mode of manufacture carried on at the Corporatiore Depot, Longford, and the collection and removal of the town's refuse thereto with suggestions for alterations and improvements. Jo this report, which is of considerable length, the borough surveyor (Mr. T. Lengdin) deals in an exhaustive I manner with the sanitary system of Warrington. In the in- troduction he refers to the inquiry into the sanitary condi- tion of Warrington instituted in 1872 by the Local Gov- ernment Board in consequence of the apparently high death- rate obtaining from fever then in the tpwn. At that time the population of Warrington was 30,000 and the death-rate about SO per 1,000. Dr. Ballard, the Local Government Board inspector at that time, traced very clearly the cause of the several kinds of fever prevalent in the town, one source being "the constant foul exhalations from the badly-constructed and neglected middens." One of the consequences of Dr. Ballard's recommendations was the ad- option of the present pail-system in Warrington. After the Introduction the Borough Surveyor sketches the history of the depot at Longford. The amount of money expended in the erection of buildings and machinery at Longford up to date is stated as follows, viz. :—Purchase of land £5BO Os Pd; Shed' s cottage, walls, eke., previous to 1879, £2313 lie; buildings erected for machinery since 1879, , £2543 2s 8 ; flagging, paving, erection if machinery and sundries in connection tliere- with, £985 19s lid; machinery for destruction -of refuse and evaporation of excreta, 43,428 Els 10d. In ac- cordance with the instruction of the committre, Mr. Longdin also reports as to what machinery and plant he considered would be requisite to enable them to treat the whole of their collection. After giving the data ef his calculations he reports that the machinery which will be required is two destructors and boilers; one vacuum pan; one dryer; one new air pump engine; condensers; one rotary blower; two new screens; one steam ram ; save-ails to existing and pro- posed vacuum pans and dryers; shafting, pullies, belts, dm.; small engine to mortar mill; donkey pump for water. Thu, increased plant will not require any additions to the present buildings excepting the erection of a store room, which will be Wit out, of the old material from the sheds proposed to be taken down, for the purpose of erecting the destructors and platform to receive the ashes and the formation of an Incline road to the said platform. The cast c3pital and outlay is estimated as follows:—The total cost for the before-named plant, including erection and fixing and over- hauling present machinery, £3,065; alterations to buildings forming incline road, and erecting tanks and platform, • £1,628; sundries, say £300; total, £4,993. The annual working expensee, to treat the whole of the material de- livered at Longford, based upon a careful estimate will be: —Wages £845; materials used ia manufacturing, including vitriol, oil, bags, and sundries, £270 8s; repairs, £120; total, £1,235 Bs. To the above must be added interest on capital expenditure as follows :—Land (£580), at £4 13s lid per cent, £27; building and machinery erected previous to 1879 (£9,271 2s sd), at £4 13s 1/d per cent.. £432 lls 81 ; proposed machinery and buildings (£4993), at £4 13s lid per cent, £232 8s 8d; total £692 Os 44. According to analy- sis the i manure is worth commercially about £9 per ton ; but tak ng the value of the product at the price at which it is sold by the Committee' viz.:—se lOs per ton the revenue derived will be, Manure, 520 tons at £6 103, £3380 • Sales of rags, glass, iron, &c., say £2O; Rent of field adjoining works, t 5; total £3405. Thus the cost of working the depot, including interest and repayment of capital outlay for plant, buildings, etc., will be, Wages and Materials, £1235 fis ; Interest and Repayment of Capital outlay, £692 Os 4d•' total £1927 So 44.—Therefore Revenue as above, £3405; Wages, Materials, Interest and Repayment of Capital Outlay (as above), £1927 83 4d; Shewing a net profit of £1477 Ils Bd. With regard to the collection and removal at night-soil the surveyor gives elaborate statistics to show the working cost of the present system, ard states that for some time past he had been carefully considering the whole question, and now had pleasure in submitting a scheme which be claimed had for its principal objects :- Ist, Reduction of cost in cellection and removal ; 204, Less liability of nuisance from the collecting vans in the Muni- cipal Borough; 3rd, The prevention of nuisance on the roads of the rural districts; 4th, Better supervision of the collect- ing without increased cost.—The great cost of the present system was caused by horse haulage, therefore his (the Sur- veyor's) main object is to reduce the mileage that the vans travel, and to that end he purposes to erect two new intercepting depots in the town, one to receive the collection from the south east, south-west, and Latchford wards, and one for the north-east and north-west wards. Each depot will be provided with a tank of sufiloient capa- city to bold one day's collection of excreta, and to each . will be fixed one of "Shone's" pneumatic ejectors, similar to those which have been working for the past two years in connection with the Latchford drainage, for the purpose of transmitting the liquid to the manufacturing depot at Long- ford.. The total annual cost of the proposed scheme is esti- . . .. .. . .

I mated to be as follows :—Collectiti ad delivering refuse 'to intercepting depots, £1,400 14c; interest on capital ex. penditure and cost of working and delivering refuse to man- ufacturing depot, Longford, £644 15s 5d ; credit interest t on the re-sale of 17 horses and 12 vans, say £3O ; total, £2,015 9s sd. Thus comparing present and proposed system: Annual cost of present,system, £3.201 2s 8d ; ditto proposed wrstem9 as above, £2,015 9s 5d ; showing an annual saving )f £llB5 13s 3d.—Alderman Brraoass, in moving the con- irmation of the Sanitary Committee's minutes' spoke in lomplimentary terms of the way the above report bad been )repared by the borough surveyor, as did also Councillor •4utton and other members. Several members said that as hey had only had the report in their possession a day or .wo they could not be expected to vote upon it thakeVening,

and it was consequently decided to pass the remainder of the 1 minutes and leave the report over for consideration at a special Council meeting. PAVING AND SEWERAGE COMMITTEE. The minutes of this committee recommended that Alder- man Kean be appointed chairman, and Alderman Davies deputrchairman for the ensning year. It was also recom- mended that the question of compensation to be paid to Messrs. Parkinson, of Latchford, in respect of the public sewer through their land be sailed on certain specified terms.

Councillor BROWN proposed, and Councillor HUTCHINSON seconded, the adoption of the minutes. Councillor W. PIERPOINT was surprised that no explana- tion had been given regarding the question of compensation to be paid to Messrs. Parkinson. Councillor WRIGHT said that the committee considered the conditions laid down to be fair and reasonable. The cost of the whole matter would be trifling. In answer to a ques- tion from Councillor Platt whether the necessity for com- pensation arose from the committee having made the sewer without the permission of the owners of the land, Councillor Wright said that due notice was given to Messrs. It was recommended that the Mayor be appointed chair- man and Councillor Crosfield deputv.chairman of this com- mittee, that a sub-committee be appointed to report as to the most appropriate places for forming open spaces and recreation grounds, that a sub-committee to act as a Parliamentary committee be appointed, and that a memorial be presented to the Postmaster- Cienc at to aff rd to Warrington direct telegraphic com- munication with London.

In answer to Councillor Dixon, Councillor Dr. Macxix stated that he had seen the postmaster with regard to affix- ing in a prominent place notices of the times of despatch of mails, and that tho matter would be attended to when a re-ar.angernent of the despatches that was going on had been concluded.

Connelllor PLATT hoped that some arrangement could be made whereby the sub-office at Market-gate could be kept open until 9 30 in the evening, or whereby letters could be collected at a later hour than at present. Referee, Mr. Dewhurst, "Athletic News." WARRINGTON ASSOCIATION (A Tram) V. MANCHESTER CLIFFORD (A).—This match was arranged for second teams, but in consequence of the Hartford St. John's match falling through, Warrington were able to play four first team men. Warrington won the toss, and chose to play with a slight wind in their favour ; and, after a very few minutes' play, the ball was passed to the left wing, when Matthews and Roach worked it up, the former getting an easy goal, which the Clifford custodian should certainly have stopped. The ball being re-started was again taken in the neighbourhood of the visitors' for- tress, and repeated shots at pal were the consequence, but without success, till Allen (who improves each time he plays) played the ball nicely, and put it through a second time. Nothing further resulted before half-time, and the visitors were two goals to the bad on changing over, but they pulled themselves t:,gether, and after a splendid bit of play In the vicinity of the home goal by Gleave, the sphere was neatly, placed through the posts. The downfall of the

home fortress raised a general cheer, as it was unanimously agreed to, both by players and spectators, that such good play deserved the recompense it obtained. Shortly after- wards, from a corner kick, Davies pat the ball through his own goal, thus making matters equal. Matthews then had an easy chance of scoring, bat he put the ball over instead of under. Warrington tried hard to score again, but their efforts proved futile, as their shots were most erratic in front of goal ; in fact, they played well till they got a chance of scoring, and then seemed to lose their heads. The visitors played well, except upon their left wing, which was certainly not all that could be desired, but we cannot help congratu- lating °leave, Ball, Harrop, and Hutchinson for their very steady play, and the whole team upon the gentlemanly ' style shown throughout the game—far different to the epi- sode we had to chronicle last week. Tearns—Clifford : Goal, Sankey; backs, J. Harrop and Ball ; half-backs, G. Dutton, Jenkins, and J. Dutton ; forwards, Walkden, Mellor, Wrightson, Hutchinson, and Gleave. Warrington : Goal, Hocton ; backs, Davies and Royston; half-back., A. Dillon, Shaw, and Pearson ; forwards, Matthews, Savage, West- brook, Allen, and Roach.

"Doctor," said an old lady the other day to her family physician, "kin you tell me how it is that some folks IS born dumb?" "Why, mem, why, certainly, madame," replied the doctor; "it's owing to the fact that they camn into the world without speech!" "La, me," remarked the old lady, "now just see what it is to have a physic education; I've axed my old man more'n a hundred times that ar same thing.'
FOLLOW YOUR NOSE. Kate's nose was retrousse—her husband's a Roman;

One day in a passion he bade her "Begone!" "Where to ?" said she. "Follow your nose, silly woman !" He answered with pointed and petulant scorn. Kate smiled as she answered: "The taunt is forgiven— It implies hut a compliment, dearest, you know; I'll follow my nose with pleasure to heaven, If you'll follow yours to the regions below!" INQUEST AT rtaxgrura, ASYLUM. On Wednesday Mr. Brighouse held an irquest at Kainhill Asylum on the body of Charles Hollis, aged sixty-nine years, tailor, of 88, Farnwotth-street, Liverpool, who was admitted into the Asylum on September 19th, 1883, from the West Derby Workhouse, and who died on Monday.—John Best said he was an attendant in charge of No. 1 Infirmary Ward, in which deceased had remained since his admittance. On IThursday, the 27th ult, witness heard a noise, and entering the room he found deceased lying over the foot of a bad on his side. Witness helped him to bed, and as he felt no worse, witness did not thick he had received any injury. Deceased had suffered from paralysis and fits, and was not able to walk. There were two other pitients in the same room who were confined to their beds. The patients were harmless. It was not possible for either of the other pat- ients to have got out of bed and done anything to deceased. Dr. Rogers said there was not sufficient attendants Tor each room.—Mr. Albert Higson said he was assistant medical officer at the Asylum. lie examined deceased on the morn- ing after the fall (he not being informed of the occurrence the night previous), and found that he had three broken ribs. Witness made a post-mortem examination. Deceased would soon have died from natural causes, but the shock of his fall might have accelerated his death.—The jury re- turned a verdict of "Accidental de,th."

IMPERIAL PARLIAM HOUSE OF LORL)S.—MONDiY. The House met at 40. The Royal assent was given by Commission to the Addi- tional Income Tax Bill. Tux FRANCHISE BILL. The Representation of the People Bill was on the paper for Committee, but Lord SAL- ISBURY observed that it would, perhaps, be more convenient to carry out the arrangement he had originally proposed, and take the Committes on Thursday, on which day, he believed, the Government proposed to move the second read- ing of the Redistribution Bill in the House of Commons. --Lord GRANVILLE stated that the Government did not oppose the suggestion of Lord Salisbury. After soma conversation, the Committee was then deferred till Tisurs-
ENT.

-dal% The Tramways and Public Companies (Ireland) Bill was read a second time. Their lordships rose at 4-55. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MoernAY. The Speaker took the chair at 3-15. THE ARMY IN EGYPT.—In reply to Mr. O'Kelly, the Marquis of lIARTINGTON said there was only one Coin- mander-in-Chief in Egypt, Lord Wolseley. General Ste- phenson commanded in Lower Egypt, and General Wood commanded the Egyptian army. ANGIJA PEQUINA —ln reply to Sir M. Hicks-Beach, Mr. ASHLEY said that the protectorate proclaimed by Germany In regard to Angra Pequina would extend from Angra Pequina a distance of 50 geographical miles. The settle- ment would embrace 1,000 equate miles, measuring from a point 20 miles inland. Mr. Caine for ecarborough, and Mr. Sutherland for Greenock, took the oath and their seats. THE REDISTRIBUTION BILL. Mr. GLADSTONE introduced the Redistribution Bill. He I said it would be in the recellection of the House that a fort- night ago he intimated that if the Government found it pos-1 3ible to receive adequate assurances that the Franchise Bill would pass forthwith it was far from being alien from the disposition of the Government to submit at once to the House a Bill for the redistribution of parliamentary seats, and to prosecute it with all reasonable and convenient des- patch. He was glad to find himself under these circum- stances in a position to give the Bill for the redistribution of seats, and to recognize the circumstances under which he approached the execution of a task that was neither diffi- cult nor disag-eeable. Ile then proceeded to give details of the features of the Bill, which will be found in the sum- mary of the schedules. With regard to the question of I boundaries, he would not attempt a minute description as to what was being done, but would state that a commission had been appointed and the names of the English Commis- sioners were Sir Joha Lonleert, Mr. Pelham, barrister-at- law, Sir Francis Sandford, Mr. J. J. Henley, Colonel Owen Jones. and Major H. Tulloch. This Boundary Commission was already at work, and its labours would occupy about two months. There would have to be a considerable recess after their autumn labours, and he had no doubt that in the Committee on the Bill there would be no difficulty In in- seating absolutely the results of the labours of the commis- ' Rion, se that they might be brought under the judgment of the House. Viewing the nature of the Bill, and its not in- I volving grave and broad principles, the House might be in- dined to proceed to its s mood reading with a rapidity greater than usual. Therefore they were disposed to ask the House to read the Bill a second time on Thursday. They believed there was no broad and vital difference of opinion on the subject between the several sections cie the House. They oonfilently trusted that the Bill would be found lobe nitable, and considered neither regardless of ancient ar- rangements and ancient rights nor disposed to respect those ancient arrangements up to a point which would allow them to preclude the attainment of the great purpese of a widely poooler and national representition. (Cheers.) Sir S. NORTHCOTE did not propoie at the moment to enter lamely in the question, and would only ask the right hon. gentleman whether it would be in his power to communi- cate to the House the nature of the instructions which had been given to the Boundary Commissioners. Mr. GLAD- Mem assented.--Mr. CHAPLIN, Mr. Oteseow. and other members thought the second reading of the Bill should be delayed to a later date than Thursday.—Sir J. HAY and Sir J. CAMPBELL urged that Scotland should have 21 new members instead of 12. Alderman FOWLER thought the Bill should be proceeded with at once.—Sir H. Woevrasked whether the Boundary Commissioners would make any alter- ation in existing borouahs ?—Sir H. DYKE said it was like hustling the Bill through the House to a-k the second read- ing to be taken on Thursday.—Mr. GLADSTONE thought the evident sense of the House was to proceed with the seoond] reeling on Thursday. The addition of 12 members to Scotland WAS the result of the application of the uniform principle of electoral areas, and therefore the Government could not deviate from it. It was proposed to make the metropolis into one-member districts, excepting the city. The Government proposed to take the population from the census of 1881, but did not intend to go into the grouping of boroughs.—Sir CHARLES DILKE explained that the second reading would only mean an assent to the prin- ciple of redistribution, and any difference of opinion as to this partial scheme could be raised on the motion to go inte committee after the recess.—ln answer to Mr. SEXTON, Sir C. DILKE said Belfast would receive two new members. —ln reply to Mr. Picton, Mr. GLADSTONE said the question of university members had been considered by the Govern- ment, who adhered to the provisions of the Bill. The Bill was then brought in by Mr. Gladstone amid cheers, and the second reading. was fixed for Thursday.— The House adjourned at 6-45 p.m. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TUESDAY. The Speaker took the chair shortly before 4-0. A new writ was ordered to be issued for Knaresborough. THE CROFTERS --Mr. MACFARLANE moved the postpone- ment of the second reading of his bill for suspending evic- tions in the Highlands of Scotland, which stands for De- cember 17th, to March 7th.—Agreed to. Queestriotes —Mr. GLADSTONE, answering Mr. Bartlett, said he had no hope of being able to submit to the House before the recess the results of the communications to the Powers in regard to Egyptian finance. A number of ques- dons were asked about the Seats Bill, and in replying to one of them the PREMIER declined to state what points would be considered vital and what would not. As to the recess, he said he had no doubt that if the Seats Bill was read a second time the Hones would adjourn this week. THE NAVY—Sir THOMAS BRASSEY moved for returns re- specting naval shipbuilding during the past four years, and made a statement on the condition of the navy and the pro- posed additions thereto similar to that made in the House of Lords.—Mr. W. H. SMITH complained that there was to be no acceleration of shipbuilding until next year, and said that our navel harbours were in a condition to give us cause for anxiety—a condition which was known to every foreign officer sent to this country to Require information for the use of his own Government. He protested against the de- partmental policy of concealment,and he asked the House to alter a system which was dangerous to the country.—Sir W. Lawsme said this was hardly the time to come to the House and ask for moreey when they were on the eve of a winter which was likely to be one of severe distress in all our large towns, when the agricultural community were making very small profits.—After a few words from Mr: Puleston, Mr. Parnell, Mr. Illingworth, and others, the motion was agreed to at ten minutes past one. The Consolidated Fund (No. 1) Bill was reed a third time, and the House adjourned at a quarter past one. HOUSE OF LORDS..--TUESDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at 4-15. The Tramways and Public Companies (Ireland) Act Amendment Bill passed through Committee. THE NAVY: IMPORTANT STATEMENT. The Etrl of NORTHBROOK moved for returns respecting ships built for the navy since 1880 or now building, and in SO doing went somewhat at length into the condition of our naval defences. His Lordship was glad of the opportunity to make such a statement, because there had been lately go- ing on an agitation upon naval matters upon which no one of official authority had joined. On behalf of the Govern- ment, he could assure their Lordships and others outside the House that Her Majesty's Ministers were determined, as far as in them lay, to maintain the naval eapremacy of the country. They did not desire that this question should be treated as one of party, but in view of what had been said he wished to make clear what had been the policy of the Board of Admiralty since 1880. During that period the construction of armour-plated ships had pro- gressed at a rate as rapid as was consistent with economy. The Government had sought not to multiply types of skips, but to construct vessels as far as possible of the sime class, though varying in power. All the ships were designed for an average speed exceeding 16 knots, or greater than that of the vessels built or build- ing by France. Comparing the English with the French fleet, he stated that so far as modern ships went we had 30 vessels, with a tannage of 210,412, whilst France had 19, with a tonnage of 127,828. Of ships of older types England had 16, with a tonnage of 115,600, and France had 12, with a tonnage of 53,000. He was satisfied that at present our expenditure in the construction of armour-plated and other ships was in excess of that of France, and he did not be- lieve there was any extraordinary activity in the French yards. With regard to the future, the progress of artillery had made it essential that very large sums of money should be spent on particular types of ships. In our building yards there would soon be three vacancies created by the comple- tion and launch of three ironclads on hand. The Benbow would also be launched soon, and then four new ironclads Would be laid down, either at the beginning or in the course of the next financial year. The first would be a turret-ship of the Conqueror type, carrying two 110-ton and six smaller guns, protected by 18 inches of armour' and having a speed of lee knots. The design of the other three ships was not vet decided, but they would have a ton- nage of about 10,-000 each. It was also proposed to build at once two "torpedo rams" of the Polyphemus class. Two torpedo cruisers were in course of construction, and it was inteeded to build ten more moderately armoured and armed, to do duty as scouts. Then they proposed to build thirty first-class torpedo boats and five non-protected swift cruisers, armed with torpedoes and guns, for the pro- tection of our - commerce. These additions to the navy woeld cost about £3,100,000 in excess of the ordinary esti- mates, excluding the three ironclads, and it was calculated that they would all be completed in five years. To a large extent the additional ships would be provided by contract with private firms. This estimate did not include £l6OOOOO which had to he provided in the five years for armament, so that with the £825,000 for the protection of coaling stations there wouldhe in that time a total expenditure of £5525000. The necessity of arming our home ports ageinst possible attack was under consideration. The Earl of Carnarvon, whilst not condemning these proposals, thought them hardly adequate to secure the national safety. Lords Alces-

ter,Dunsany, Camperdown (who considered that the English navy was undoubtedly the strongest in the world), Clan- william, and Sidmouth continued the discussion, which was wound up by Lord Northbroook intimating that the ships would be commenced before the Select Committee appointed by the House of Commons met.—The motion was agreed to, and their lordships adjourned at 8-5. HOUSE OF LORDS—WEDNESDAY. Their Lordship met at one o'clock. Lord Monson, in , the absence of the Lord Chancellor, occupied the woolsack. , —The Consolidated Fund (No. 1) Bill, brought up from the House of Commons, was, on the motion of Lord Tnuneow, read a first time.—Their Lordships adjourned at ten minutes after one o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. The House was made at 12-35, there being at that hour only forty members present. The Law of Evidence Amendment Bill was read a first time. REDISTRIBUTION.—Mr. ARINOLD gave notice of his inten- , Bon to move an instruction to the Committee on the Redis- , tribution Bill regarding the proposed increase in the number , of members in that House. He would propose that all , boroughs having fewer than 25,000 inhabitants according to the last census should be disfranchised, and that one seat each be taken from the Oxford and Cambridge Universities. , —Sir C. DILKE said that though power Was given to appoint assistant Boundary Commissioners the chief Commissioners , only would be responsible for fixing the boundaries.—Major Noteet promised to draw attention to the exclusion of Ireland from all participation in the bentfits to be derived from the large additional expenditure on the , navy. DOURS OF POLLING.—The Hon. A. ELLIOT moved the second reading of a bill extending the hours of polling in counties, as had already been done in regard to boroughs.— Mr. Stanhope, Mr. Collings, Mr. Staveley Hill, and Mr. , Duckham supported the motion, which was opposed by Mr. Warton.—Sir C. DILKE said the extension was urgently re- quired, and would have been supported by the Government last year had any general expression of opinion in its favour been given by county members.—Lord E. FITZHAURICE , promised that the bill should on reaching Committee be taken over by the Government, who would consider the expediency of amendments in it.—The bill was then read a second time without a division. Mr. BROADHURST introduced a bill to legalise marriage with a deceased wife's sister.—Sir W. LAWSON gave notice that he would ask the Prime Minister whether steps could not be taken to ascertain the feeling of the Great Powers in favour of a general reduction of expenditure on warlike pre- 'aerations. The House adjourned at two o'clock. HOUSE OF LORDS.—Tnnusnev. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a quarter-pest four o'clock. The Yorkshire Registries Act Amendment Bill Was brought from the Commons and read a first time. THE FRANCHISE BILL PASSED THROUGH COMMITTEE The Earl of KIMBERLEY moved that their lordships go into committee on tee Representation of the People Bill—The Earl of WEMYSS took occasion to characterise this measure to admit two millions to the franchise as a peedefal but great revolution.—Speaking on an amendment (which was negatived) moved by Lord Denman in favour of the exten- sion of the franchise to women, the Marquis of SALISBURY said he looked favourably on women's suffrage, hut he thought the present was not a suitable occasion for raising the question.—The third reading of the Bill was fixed for Friday. The House adjourned at half-past seven o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Trecasnev. The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. QuesrioNs —Mr. ASHLEY, replying to a question, said the Cape Ministers had reported by telegraph the conditions on which they could effect a settlement of the Bechuana difficulty, but the conditions, as at present understood, were not such as could be accepted by her Majesty's Government. Mr. M‘Coeer drew attention to the inflammatory writing in United Ireland, of which Mr. Parnell, Mr. Justin M`Certhy, and Mr. Bigger are the registered proprietors, and Mr. O'Brien the editor.—Mr. CAMPBELL•BANNERMAN said the fact of some of those concerned in the paper being members of Parliament would not influence the Government in de- ciding what they would do in the matter. While they were sensible of the evil such publications might do, they had to consider whether a prosecution would not intensify the evil. Lord E. Ferzeteueice replying to Mr. Salt, said her Majesty's Government hoped that the steps which they had taken and were taking at the Berlin Conference would secure the due protection of British trade on the Congo and in the adjacent countries. Sir W. LAWSON having asked if the Government would use their influence to bring about a diminution of European warlike forces, Mr. GLADSTON.I assured him that the Government sympathised with his views, but said he thought no,good would be done to anyone by giving any pledge. In a state- ment on the business of the House,Mr. GLADSTONE said he thought the House might on its rising on Saturday adjourn till the 10th February. A definite date would be named be- fore the adjournment. THE SEATS BILL.—On the motion for the second read- ing of the Seats Bill, Mr. COURTNEY explained at length his reasons for resigning office—his strong disapproval of the proposal of the Government to create single-member districts as areas of representation. The hon member ad- vocated the one man one vote principle, and, said that by that system all classes would be represented in their propor- tion, while at the same time it would secure the representa- tion of minorities.—Mr. GLADSTONE replied to Mr. Courts- ney's arguments, and in the course of his speech be said he did not say the judgment they had arrived at in this matter was necessarily an irrevocable one.—Sir H. TYLER moved an amendment affirming that the principle of representation in proportion to population should be adopfed in place ot arbitrary figures as a basis in order to obtain a logical, judicious, and permanent settlement of the question of re- distribution. The amendment was negatived without a division, after a long debate. The motion for the second reading was agreed to, and the Committee stage was fixed for Thursday, 19th February. EDUCATION IN IRELAND.— Mr. J. WCARTHY moved the second reading of the National School Teachers (Ireland) Bill, which proposed to increase the pay and improve the condition of teachers. Mr. C. BANNERMAN objected that the Bill was only in the hands of the members this morning, and moved the adjournment of the debate. —The debate was adjourned. HOURS or POLLING. Mr. A. Ermorr moved that the House go into Committee on the Electors in Counties Hours of Polling Bill. Mr. SEXTON moved the adjournment of the debate.-A discussion ensued ; eventually the House went into committee, and progress was reported. It was agreed that the House, at its rising on Saturday, should adjourn until the 19th of February.—After another long discussion which ensued on the proposal of the Irish section to debate Irish questions, the House adjourned at, 5-20 a.m. until 1-15 p.m. on Saturday.
SHOCKING TRAGEDY AT BURY.
MURDER OF THREE CHILDREN AND SUICIDE OF
I.HE MOTHER.

A shocking tragedy, involving the death of four persons —a woman and her three children—occurred in Bury on Wednesday. The victims are Hannah Mason, aged 37, the wife of John Mason, waste bleacher, who lives in Milton- street, Elton, Thomas Mason, aged four years, Nelly, aged three years, and Gertrude Mary, aged eight months; in each case death was caused by the hand of Mrs. Mason. Mr. and Mrs. Mason, it seems, have always lived on good terms with each other and with their neighbours, but of late Mrs. Mason has been suffering from an attack of melancholia, and notwithstanding the assurance of her medical attendant (Dr. Mellor) that her condition was not at all serious, she appears to have laboured tinder the irnproision that she had an ailment from which she would never recover. Her state was not such as to cause much anxiety to her friends, and she showed ne signs of mental aberration. On Wednesday morning she appeared to be in her usual condition, and having had breakfast with her, her husband at half-past eight o'clock left the house and went to his work at Bury Ground. Almost im- mediately after his departure Mrs. Mason went into the house of the next door neighbour with a bottle which she bad borrowed some time ago and having left it without making any special remark, she returned to her own home. The husband upon going home to dinner about noon found the blinds at all the windows down, and the back and front doors locked from the inside. With the assistance of his bro- ther-in-law he burst the back door open, and not finding any of his family about, went upstairs, when he found near the window of the back bedroom his wife and three children ly- ing dead with their throats cut. Mrs. Mason was fully dressed, and the children were in their night dresses, with their stockings and clogs on. Near to the woman lay a razor eavered .with blood, and there can be no doubt that with this instrument she killed her children and then committed suicide. The horrible work seems to have been done very deliberately and very quietly. The fact that a utensil in the room con- tains a large quantity of blood, and that there is compara- tively very little on the carpet or on the clothing of the children suggests the idea that Mrs. M isort held them so as to allow the blood to Row into the basin, and, then, when they were dead, laid them in a row where they were found, afterwards placing herself near them ; and the other fact that no cries or sounds of straggling were heard by the neighbours on the other side, leads the police to think that probably before she attacked her victims with the razor she stupefied them by the use at some narcotic. The bodies of all four were warm when the husband found them, and they remained so for two hours afterwards. On a table in the sitting-room downstairs the following letter in her handwriting was found, together with the policies of insurance issued upon the lives of Mrs. Mason and the chil- dren : Dear John,—You must forgive me for doing this ; I have been a good wife to you. You must bury all of us with George [her eldest child, who had died some years ago]. I cannot leave my children behind me to be knocked about. I say good-by to you. I have done nothing wrong to anyone. The Lord forgive me. I kave been a true wife to you. The cause of my illness Ido not know. You have been a good husband to me. You must forgive me and try to forget. On another scrap of paper was the following : I have prayed to the Lord to take me. I cannot lie on a sick bed and die and leave my children. I know they are gone before me. I know the end of them. I watched them die, and am happy. Good-bye. The occurrence has caused a painful sensation in the locality, both Mr. and Mrs. Mason being greatly respected by their acquaintances.
