TITE REDISTRIBUTION BILL. The following ale the main outlines of the Redis- tribution Bill as explained to the House of Commons ,by Mr, Gladstone on Monday night. The two chief features of the Bill in its dealings with the boroughs were the division of the large boroughs into single- member constituencies, and the merging rather than grouping of the smaller boroughs, except in Scotland. All the boroughs under 15,000 inhabitants will be merged in the counties, though the county districts will, in as many cases as possible, be named after the boroughs which form their centre and place of elec- tion Boroughs with lees than 50,000 inhabitants ' will retain only one member. Between that limit and a population of 165,000 the two members will be re- taim.d, and they will constitute, with the city of Lon- don two•membered constituencies. Boroughs above the limit of 165 000 will receive an additional mem- ber or members, and will be divided into wards, each returning a single member. In Scotland there are no boroughs which will lose a member under the rule re- quiring a town having two members to give up one for insufficient population, and there are in Ireland only the cities of Limerick, Waterford, and Galway. Two members will be taken from London, one from the county of Rutland, which now now returns two, and one from Hereford- shire, which is no'w represented by three mem- bers. The Irish county of Carlow will also lose one member under the 50,000 rule. There are s6o seats which Mr. Gladstone stated would be

gained under Schedules A and B. These 160 seats, togethhr with six which have been liberated by the disfranchisement of Irish and English boroughs for corrupt practices, will be given to new county dis- tricts, new barcughs, and new divisions of boroughs. Seven new boroughs will be created round London, and the existing London boroughs, like the other large boroughs with more than r 63,000 inhabitants, will be divided into wards. The addition to the re- presentation of London will be 37 members. The counties will gain 96 more seats, of which 64 will go to counties in England, distributed on the same one-member principle which is to be adopted in the large towns. There will be sixteen new members for county districts in Yorkshire, fifteen for Lancashire ; Middlesex will receive five, and the county of Dur- ham four. The county of Cork will also receive five new members, and Lanarkshire four. In the largest towns the additions will be of an equally liberal char- acter. Liverpool will get six more members, and will be cut up into nine wards; Glasgow will have four more, and vote in seven divisions. Birmingham will also receive four more, and be divided in a similar manner ; Manchester will double its representation, mid have six members; and Leeds and Sheffield will have in all five members each ; Dublin and Belfast will each have four members, and will be divided into, as many wards. On the whole England will have tax more representatives than it has at present, and Scot• land will receive twelve additional members. The six for England are provided by the disfranchised constituencies, but the twelve for Scotland will be an addition to the numbers of the House of Commons, I which will henceforward consist of 670 members, instead of 658. The bill for the redistribution of seats at Parliamentary elections and for other purposes relative thereto, which was ordered by the House of Commons on Monday night to be brought in by Mr. Gladstone, the Marquis of Harlington, Sir Charles Dilke, the Attorney-General the Lord Advocate, and Mr. Campbell-bannerman, and which was then read a first time, was issued to members on Tuesday morning.

The Times.eave :-The redistribution proposals are even more extensive than those of the first Reform Bill. By that measure 143 seats were liberated for redistribution, 56,two- member constituencies being wholly disfranchised and 31 losing one representative each. By Mr. Gladstone's pro- posals 160 seats are now set free, six now in abeyance are revived, and twelve new members are added to the House of Commons in order to meet the claims of Scotland. There is thus a total of 173 seats available for distribution, or 26,5 per cent of the whole representation of the three kingdoms. Of this number 96, or more than half, will be given to the counties, which become numerically strong by the absorp- tion of small boroughs. The number allotted to them by the first Reform Bill was 57. Of the boroughs now disfran- chised 20 were reduced by the first Reform Bill to one member each, and two-Kendal and Whitby, which were created boroughs by that bill-are now deprived of their separate representation. There will be considerable displacement of well-known men by Mr. Glaistone's proposals. The disfranchisement of Bridport will probably throw serious obstacles in the way of Mr. Warton continuing his favourite amusementof block- ing Bills, and Mr. Ashmead-B triett will be compelled by the extinction of Eve to look out tor some other constituency appreciative of his restless activity in foreign affairs. Lord Kensington will no longer_be able to woo the Haver- fordwsst District, a contingency Which he no doubt contem- plated when he offered himself to the eleators of Middlesex, and Caine, which once returned Mr. lanwe, and is now repre- sented by Lord Edmund Fitarnaurice, will no longer offer a comfortable Liberal eeat. The disappearance of Woodstock would possibly have proved inconvenient to a less prevenient representative than Lord Randolph Churchill, who has al- ready taken stepa to procure his reception in one of the wards of Birmingham. Mr. A. J. Balfour, with an equally keen perception of coming events, has already prepared for the loss of his seat at Hertford, by wooing Manchester. After the trouble Sir Hardinge Giff ard had to find a seat, it is hard that he should be turned out of Launceston;, and the disfranchisement of Liskeard compels Mr. Courtoey also to seek another constituency. He is not likely to find much difficulty in obtaining a new seat, nor can we suppose that the abolition of the privileges of Ripon will occasion much anxiety to Mr. Goschen. Warwick with its two members disappears from the electoral roll and leaves the Speaker homeless. while Truro, which also suffers a double bereave- rnent;will no longer shelter the Chairman of the Metropoli- ten Board of Works. Of the disfranchised boroughs, 37 at present return Liberal members, and 87 Tories. Of the seats which lose a member, 17 at present are entirely Liberal in representation, 3 en- tirely Tory, and in 13 the representation is divided. The Houma, previous to the Reform Act of 1832, con- sisted of 489 members let England, 24 for Wales, 45 for Scotland, and 100 for Ireland. By that Act the number became 482 for England, 28 for Wales, 53 for Scotland, and 105 for Ireland; while by the Act of 1867 the number was made 463 for England, 30 for Wales, 60 for Scotland, and 105 for Ireland. Under the new scheme England will re- turn 465 members, Wales 30, Scotland 72, and Ireland 103. It may be noted that of the bo.oughs lobe disfranchised by the preeent Bill-Buckingham, Eve, Malinesbury,Midhurst, Petersfield, Wareham, and Woodstock-were proposed to be disfranchised by the first Reform Bill introduced by Lord John Rusaell in 1831. As regards England and Wales, the scheme is greater than that carried out in 1832. By that Act 56 boroughs were totally and 30 partially disfranchised, while by this scheme 75 will be wholly and 38 partially dis- franchised. Lancashire will occupy the position of premier county in respect of the number of members it sends to Parliament. Yorkshire has previously enjoyed that distinction. At pre- sent Yorkshire sends 38 members, against Lancashire 33. Lancashire, on the whole, gains 25 members. Of these, 15 will be new county members. The losses at CI itheroe and Wigan are compensated for by the new seats at Barrow and St. Helens, and the other ten seats are accounted for by the additions to Liverpool, Manchester, and Salford. The total representation of the county will now be 58 members. Of the present members, 21 are Liberals and 12 Conserva- tives. ' Yorkshire has an addition of 16 members to the county divisions, but otherwise makes no gain. Six small boroughs are abolished, and one member is taken from Pontefract, thus absorbing the extra representation which is given to Sheffield, Leeds, Bradford and Hull. The total number of members will be 54. At present they send 31 Liberal and seven Conservative members. Cheshire loses one member. The addition of two mem- bers to the county representation compensates for the dis- franchisement of Macclesfield, but the city of Chester has its representation reduced by ~one. The total number of members for the county will now be twelve. At the Gene- ral Election the county returned six Liberals and seven Conservatives. Derbyshire gains one seat by the increase in the number of the county representatives to seven. The total number of members will now be nine. Derbyshire at present sends seven Liberals and one Conservative. Notts loses four seats by the merging of East Retford and Newark into the county, and the representation is decreased from ten to six. At present Notts is represented by seven Liberals and three Conservatives. The labours of the Boundary Commissioners in taking evidence with regard to the division of electoral areas in connection with the redistribution of seats will begin with a sitting at Bedford on Thursday next, and the work will be carried OR continuously except for a few days at Christmas. It is stated that some consteenation has been caused in various boroughs by the 25th section of the Seats Bill, which proposes to perpetually disqualify from voting in Parliamen- tary elections in the constituencies in which the offences were committed all persons who were scheduled in the Coni. missioners' reports on corrupt practices in 1880. In the borough of Chester there are about 800 such persons, and al Boston upwards of 400. The changes in Lancashire caused by the Bill are as 'ollows

That man,l think, has had a liberal education who has been so trained in youth that his body is the ready servant of his will, and does with ease and pleasure all the work that, as a mechanism, it is capable of; whose intellect is a clear, cold, logic engine, with all its parts of equal strength, and in a smooth working order, ready, like a steam-engine, to be turned to any kind of work, and spin the gossamers, as well as forge the anchors of the mind; whose mind is stored with knowledge of the great and fundamental truths of nature and of the laws of her operations; one who, no stunted ascetic, is full of life and fire, but whose passions are trained to come to heel by a vigorous will, the servant of a tender con- science; who has learned to love all beauty, whether of nature or of art, to hate all vileness, and to respect others as himself.—Hur/ey. EGYPT AND THE SOUDAN. GENERAL WOLSELEY'S ADDRESS TO THE SOLDIERS. DONGOLA, SUNDAY.—latelligence received here states that the Mandi continues calling upon General Gordon to surrender, and that the General replies with his guns. On one occasien he is reported to have told the Mandi to dry up the Nile and come across if be were a real prophet, and that then he would surrender. The rebels are intrenching themselves at Wady Gamer. Lord Weiseley has offered a prize of £lOO to the- regiment which makes the quickest passage in the whalers from Sanas to Debbah. The following general order has been issued :—" To the Sailers. Soldiers, and Marines of the Nile Expedition.—The relief of General Gordon and his garrison, so long besieged in Khartoum, is the glorious mission which the Queen has entrusted to us. It is an enterprise that will stir the heart of every soldier and sailor fortunate enough to have been selected to share in it, and the very magnitude of its diffi- culty only stimulates us to increased exertions. We are all proud of General Gordon and his self-sacrificing defence ef Khartoum, which has added, if possible, to his already high reputation. He cannot hold out many months longer, and he is now called upon to save his garrison. His heroism and his patriotism are household words wherever our lan- guage is spoken' and not only has his safety become a matter of national importance, but the knowledge that our brave comrade needs help urges us to push forward with redoubled energy. Neither he nor his garrison can be al- lowed te meet the sad fate which befel his gallant com- panion in arms, Colonel Stewart, who, when endeavouring to carry out an enterprise of unusual danger, was treacherously murdered by his captors. We can—and with God's help will—save General Gordon from suclra death. The labour of working up this river is immense, and to bear it uncomplainingly demands the highest soldier-like qualities—that contempt for danger and that determination to overcome difficulty—which in previous campaigns has so distinguished all ranks of Her Majesty's Army and Navy. The physical obstacles that impede our rapid progress are considerable; but who cares for them when it is remembered tbat General Gordon and his garrison are in danger. Under God, their safety is now in our hands; and, come what tnay, we must save them. It is needless to say more to British soldiers and sailors.—(Signed) WOLSELEY.;' DONGOLL, MONDAY.—There :rave for some little time been rumours in the bazaars of a gathering of the tribes beyond Merawi with the intention of opposing the British advance. It is now reported that the assemblage is taking place in a day and a half's march beyond Merawi. It is said that the tribes are under the leadership of a daughter of Mahmoud, one of the Mandi's leaders, whe was killed in a late battle with the troops of the Mudir.— Standard. Cam% SllNDAY.—Duplicates of General Gerdon's last message have been received via Massowa, teigether with another message, dated Angus.. 28th, in which the General states that it is imperative for the prosperity and tranquil ity of Egypt that the whole course of the Nile should ne re- tained, and that any evil effects which might have arisen were "attributable to the word abandonment." The Khe- dive has received a telegram from Lord Wolseley that the Mandi is reported to have run short of provisions, and that much sickness and general discontent prevail amongst his regular troops, 500 of whom have sulemitted to General Gordon and have arrived at Khartoum. SUAKIM, SUNDAY.—A company of Marines is encamped two miles beyond the lines in a zariba. The enemy hres on them every night; and on Saturday the town was closely invested, the ships and forts shelling all day. This morning 500 of the enemy came down and attacked the cavalry and patrols, but were repulsed. Donoota, TUESDAY.—Six whale boats have arrived here, conveying the 26th Company of Royal Engineers. CAIRO, Tussnay.—The Court has decided against the Government in the action brought by the Caiese respecting the suspension of the sinking-fund, and hold the Ministers end railway directors responsible for the sum they paid over to the Government. REPORTED DEATH OF THE MAHDI. DONGOLA, WEDNESDAY.—The MEdir Of Congola has received intelligence that the Mandi is dead, and that his followers continue dying of sickness very fast. Since the arrival of the British troops here seven deaths have occurred, two being from small-pox and the other five from various causes. No invalid have been forwarded to Cairo, none of the cases being serious enough. CAIRO, WEDNESDAY—NO news of the reported death of the Mabdi has been received from Lord Woleeley or the Mudir of Dongola either by the Khedive or Sir Evelyn Baring. THE WEST AFRICAN CONFERENCE. BERLIN, SONDAY.—Yesterday'a sitting of the Conference lasted four hours and a half. A unanimous decision was arrived at in favour of freedom of trade within the limits of the newly defined Congo basin. BERLIN, MONDAY.—A plenary sitting of the Conference was held to-day, when the Projet de Declaration regarding the territorial extent of the Congo baein and the establish- lishment of free trade within its limits was finally adopted, after an immaterial amendment proposed by the committee had been agreed to. FRANCE AND CHINA. PARIS, SUNDAY.—Tbe Government have just chartered three new vessels to be employed as transports for the con- veyance of troops to Tongan in case of necessity. At a Cabinet Council, held yesterday, it was decided to raise the import duty on foreign corn by 2f. The amount of duty, which has hitherto been 60c, will therefore be 21. 60c. HONG-KONG, SUNDAY.—OD the 14th instant the French attempted to drive some Chinese sharpshooters from a bill close to Kelung, but were repulsed with a loss of 20 men killed. Steamers and junks are now running the blockade, the blockading fleet being insufficient. PARIS, WEDNESDIY.—II is announced by the Paris that the Secretary of the Chinese Legation in London laid before Lord Granville on Monday last some proposals for a settle- ment with France which the latter could well accept. THE PRESIDENTIAL ELECTION. Nnw YORK, WIIDNESDAY.—The electoral colleges of the various States have cast their votes for the President in accordance with the results of the elections held in the different States on November 4. EXPLOSION ON AN IRONCLAD.-14 KILLED. PARIS, SATURDAY.— A. boiler explosion occurred on No- vember 11th on board the French Man-of-war Rigault de Genouilly, one of the veesels of Admiral Courbet's squadron. Two quartermasters, one engineer, and 11 seamen or stokers were killed. Admiral Courbet has had the five remaining boilers tested, the result of the examination being quite sat- isfactory. DISTURBANCFS IN MADRID. MADRID, MONDAY. Owing to demonstrations by the Students the authorities have taken very severe measures, which are resulting in a very exasperated feeling. No papers • are allowed to appear without being first submitted to the censor, and in Madrid 46 journals have been seized and , prosecuted.

HONOUR TO LORD RIPON. BOMBAY, SIISDAY.— A monstre meeting of the native in- habitants of the Bombay Presidency was held yesterday, in the Town Hall here. The hall was densely crowded, while upwards of twenty thousand persons assembled out- side. It was resolved to present an address to Lord Ripon on his arrival, and to found a Ripon Memorial, to take the form of an industrial exhibition. A sum of 80,000 rupees was subscribed on the spot. The greatest enthusiasm pre- vailed throughout the proceedings. UNITED STATES.—THE PRESIDENT'S MESSAGE. WARRINGTON, MoNner.r—President Arthur's Message to Congress says the closeness of the late contest sharply calls the attention of the Congress to the necessity of haying more precise and definite regulations for counting the electoral vote. The foreign relations of the United States are amic- able. The recent purchase by the united States of the large trading fleet, heretofore under the Chinese flag, has considerably enhanced our commercial importance in the East. Intercourse with Great Britain is most friendly. The Message recommends that the scope of the neutrality laws should be enlarged so as to cover all patent acts of hos- tility committed in America aimed against friendly na- tions. THE BECHUANALAND DIFFICULTY. CAPETOWN, TUESDAY EVENING.—Mr. Upington. the Premier, addressing a meeting at Rool Grout, identified himself with the Dutch party. He expressed sympathy with, and warmly eulogised, the Goshen freebooters. The speech has caused intense excitement and great popular Indignation in Cape Colony. The second detachment of Methuen' Horse for the Bechuanaland expedition left Waterloo Station, London, on Thursday morning for Southampton. The contingent numbered 300 men, many of them being members of the British Volunteer Corps. A large crowd cheered them as they departed. CAPETOWN, THURSDAY EVENING.—Sir Charles Warren arrived here to-day, and was most enthusiastically received. A dense crowd assembled to welcome him, and the streets were decorated in his honour. Meetings are being held, or are announced, in all parts of the country,- to express indig- nation at the interference of the Colonial Government in the Bechuanaland question. OUTRAGE IN BRITISH WATERS AT GIBRALTAR. GIBRALTAR, WEDNESDAY.—A epanish revenue critter having attacked and captured a felucca close to the Rock of Gibraltar and in British waters, was pursued by a steam launch from one of the British war vessels here. The cutter at first inclined to show fight, bat upon a shot being fired at her from the fortress she surrendered, and together with the felucca was brought into the dockyard.

Stanley, who is paying a brief visit to this country during an interval in the Conference proceedings at Berlin, arrived in E iinburgh on Wednesday to fulfil one or two public engagements which he has made. Professor Tyndall on Thursday night distributed the prizes won by the students attending the Harris Institute, Preston, and delivered an address dealing with the conserva- tion of energy, the principle of evolution, and the germ theory of epidemic disease. LEN.
Ismail Paha, ex-Khedive of Egypt, arrived in Landon on Sunday evening from Paris. Two boys have been drowned in Forfar Loch, and another in a pool near Anna, Scotland, through sliding on the ice.
Captain E. Billinge has been appointed to command the steamship Great Eastern on her forthcoming voyage to New Orleans.

Professor Roscoe attended at Windsor Castle on Satur- day, and her Majesty conferred upon him the honour of knighthood. Several of the leading railway companies are arranging for the instruction of their employes in " First Aid to the injured," by the St. John Ambulancs Association. News has been received at Durban from Madagascar that ten thousand rifles and a million rounds of ammunition, with some field guns, have reached the interior from the coast. For the vacancy in the representation of Knaresborough caused by the death at Mr. Torn Collins, M.P., Mr. Angus Holders (L) and Col. Gunter (C) have been selected. There will be a contest. THE WHALLEY WILL CASE oncluded on Tuesday. The jory returned a verdict of gulty against. Thomas and Nash, who were each sentenced to 15 years' penal servitude. Gun- nell was acquitted. It pilot who, with two other men, drifted out to sea in a skiff from Lewes, Delaware, denies having eaten a portion of one of the party who died of starvation. The other sur- vivor, a seaman, admits baying done so. A speeial meeting of the Proportional Representation Society was held on Wednesday, in Westminster, Sir John Lubbock, M P., presiding. It was agreed that a fund of £5,000 should be raised for promulgating the views of the society. Sir Alexander Grant, Principal of Elinbugh University, died on Sunday night from an apopletsc fit which attacked him on Saturday. Sir Alexander was 58 years of age, and held various important educational positions in India, from which country he returned in 1969. THE MERSEY TUNNEL.—The last section of rock in the portion of the tunnel under the river has been knocked away, and 2a miles of the railway been completed. The works have never been in abeyance for a single working. day since the contractor took them in hand. DORSETSHIRE LABOURERS —Mr. Gladstone, writing in re- ply to 40 resolutions of confidence from Dorset labourers, says he much values such an untnisteleible sign of the opinion prevalent among the labourers of Do/set. The right hon. gentleman has received in all between 60 and 70 resolutions from Wilts and Dorset. A SINGULAR STRIKE has occurred at Walker Colliery, near Newcestle. The miners had been asked to take down Marsant lamps instead of the old Clanny and Davy lamps. The Marsant is believed to be safer than the old lamp, and it costs more money. The men objected to the new lamps, and struck to the number of 300, laying the colliery idle. THE MIGNONETTE CASE —The arguments in the points of law involved in the special verdict in the Mignonette "cannibalism "case was heard before five of the judges on Thursday. The verdict of the assize jury was confirmed, and sentence will be pronounced on Tuesday. The accused men, who bad been out on bail, were sent to Holloway Gaol. DESTRUCTIVE FlRES.—Damage to the amount of about £lO 000 was done by fire on Saturday morning on the pre- mises of Messrs. Barclay, Perkins, and Co., the brewers, in Southwark. On the same morning fire brake out in-the extensive premises of Messrs. Alderman Stephen and Sons, shipbuilders and tanners, Dundee, and the damage will not be less than £35,000. Swoon-en Hoesr Aompaeor.—An inquest was held at Padiham, on Thursday, on the b sdy of George Also)°, a boy who was employed as a weft carrier at the Britannia Mill, Padiham. He entered the hoist in an upper room of the mill while it was standing, and shortly afterwards it began to descend. He evidently tried to get out on arriving at the next room, and was caught by the top of the cage and his back broken. Exraostox IN A CHAPEL.—A.n explosion of gas occurred at Broadmead Baptist Chapel, Bristol, on Monday. Mrs. Thomas, the wife of the chapel keeper, and her two sons, ' aged 27 and 23, went into the vestry carrying a light, when immediately a loud explosion occurred. They were all thrown down and sustained serious injuries. They we now lying in the infirmary. The building was much damaged. The gas had escaped from a pendant in the middle of the room. THE LATE Ma. Fawoorr.—An interesting and apprecia- tive article on the late Postmaster-General appears in the Christmas number of On and Of Duty, the policeman's monthly journal. The writer says:—"Rich men are settling what memorial to erect to Mr. Fawcett; the one he would have most prized can be raised in the heart of every man, rich or poor, who for his s Ike is more than ever careful to protect the weak, the helpless, and the blind." A GLASGOW SMIPBUILDER AND HIS MEN.—Mr. Pearce, of Glasgow, whose offer of work, at reduced terms, to un- employed men, was refused by the unionists, writes a cau- tion against the abolition of the naval dockyards, lest the 1 nation, in an emergency, should be left at the unionists' mercy. Mr. Pearce's offer meant 50s. weekly to 1,500 men. He bad purchased materials for a steamer of 5,000 tons. This statement, though received with ioeredulity, has not yet been contradicted. RESIGNATION OF MR. COURTNEY.— Mr. Leonard Court- ney placed in Mr. Gladstone's hands on Monday evening his resignation of the office of Secretary to the Treasury.' Mr. Courtney, we understand, has taken this step because, in his opinion, the system of one-membered districts propo- sed in the Government Redistribution Bill does not afford sufficient security for the due representation of minorities, and will tend to deteriorate and degrade the HOLUM of Come mouse and the political life of the country. THE SUPPOSED MURDER By A WlFE.—Elia4beth Gibbons, who is charged with the murder of her husband by shooting him with a revolver, appeared again before the Uxbridge magistrates on Monday. Dr. Bowlby. a medical expert, gave it as his opinion that one of the ballet wounds found on the deceased could not possibly have been self-inflicted, while of the other three on the front of the body one would have been almost instantaneously fetal. On Wednesday, a verdict of "Wilful murder" was returned against Gib- bons. Mae. WELDON AND Da. Wierstow.—After five days' trial the action brought by Mrs. Weldon against Dr. Forbes Winslow was brought to a close in the Court of Queen's Bench en Saturday. The claim was for damages for tres- pass and assault on the part of Dr. Winslow when he entered' Mrs. Weldon's house to remove her to a luaatic asylum, and for a libel upon her in a letter written to a medical news- paper. Mr. Justice Denman having summed up, the jury, after a lengthy deliberation, found for Dr. Forbes Winslow as to the alleged trespass, gave nominal damages for the as- sault, and awarded £5OO damages for the publication of the libellous letter in the newspaper, when evidence was at hand proving Mrs. Weldon' s sanity. THE FLOODING OF THE MOSTON COLLIFRIES.—Water is peurlog into the Moston Collieries of Messrs. Platt, Brothers, and Co., at the rate of 4,000,000 gallons per day, and all efforts to cope with it having proved fruitless, pumping operations have been stopped. It is now three I weeks since the water began to pour into the mine in in- creased quantity, and during the whole of that time the supply has never fluctuated, but has entered the shaft in a well-sustained volume, estimated at 3000 gallons per minute. The manager (Mr. Greenernith) is of opinion that the stream will prove itself an unfailing supply, if any means can be found of utilising it. All work at the colliery being now suspended, over 400 men and boys are thus thrown out of employment. IMPROVEMENT OF THE IRWELL AND MERSEY NAVIGA- TION.—At a recent meeting of the directors of the Bridge- water Navigation Company it was decided to carry out cer- tain improvements in the navigation of the Dwell and the Mersey. The scheme adopted has been under consideration for a long time, and we understand that the directors already possess the necessary statutory powers enabling them to pro. ceed with the work. It is proposed to straighten and deepen the water course, remove a number of the existing weirs, and erect large locks at certain Vanes. The locks will be sufficiently large to accommodate vessels of 500 tons burden. As a matter of fact, boats carrying more than 60 tons can- not be brought up to Manchester at present. The distance ny river from Manchester to Warrington is now 25 miles, but by means of channels which will be cut it will be brought down to 17 miles. The plans show that it is in- tended to make 10 of these channels at various places. The first, going from Manchester, will be made at New Barnes near Mode Wheel; three more will be cut between Barton and Flixton ; another near the confluence of the lrwell and the Mersey; another at Butchersfield ; another from the existing floodgates at Woolston to the old lock-house; ano- ther across the Oakland Ease; another near the Latchford lock; and the tenth from Halton Point to the terminal basin at Runcorn. With regard to the first nine, the water will be passed into them as soon as they are made, and the old circuitous course will be filled up. According to the plans, there are to be some six or seven locks instead of 11 as at present. The weirs which will be removed are those at Holmes Bridge, Stichens, Woolston, and But- ohersfield, and a new weir will most likely be erected near Woolston. All the new weirs will be built on the "tilting "e principle which has proved so satisfactory in the case of the Throstle Nest weir, which was improved some time ago. It is believed that by constructing the weirs on the "tilt- ing" principle the -flood level will be materially reduced. When the work of deepening and widening the river has been carried out according to the plans, and the new weirs are erected, it is estimated that the flood line will be lowered Oft. between Manchester and Warrington. As a result of these alterations it is almost certain that the trouble and annoyance to which owners and occupiers of low-lying land have frequently been subjected by the overflowing of the river will be entirely prevented in the future. The plans provide that locks may be made large enough to allow a flotilla of four of the boats at present in use between Man- chester and Liverpool to pass in a single lockage. It will also be possible for steam barges of a draught not exceedino 10ft., a beam of 30f1., and a length of 150 ft., to pass through the docks. The width of the Latchford and Runcorn Canal, at present 561 t., will be extended to 76it. There will be a large terminal basis at Runcorn, I,looft. lone by 200 ft. wide. This will serve as a dock for the transhipment of merchandise, and also as a tidal basin for vessels waiting to enter the tideway. From Halton Point to this basin a new canal is to be made, SOft, wide and sone 10ft deep. A meeting of the shareholders of the company will be held shortly for the purpose of considering the seheme,and should the plans be approved, as doubtless they will be, the works will be at once proceeded with. A LOCAL BOARD meeting was held on Wednesday, but there was no business of special interest. SLEEPY CARTERS.—At the Prt scot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, before Messrs. W. Blinkhorn and W. L. Evans, Richard Hal, a carter, residing at Rainbill, was summoind for being asleep in his cut in Liverooo'-oad, Huyton, the 14th ultimo, and was fined 5s and costs.—Charlea Massey, a carter, living at St. Helens, wag summoned for a similar offence committed at Elayton, on the 18 la ultimo. He did not appear, and the B nch imposed a fine of 5s and costs. WORKINGMEN'S SOCIETY —The first annual tea party and entertainment of the Prescot Workingmen's Sacie,y was held on Monday in the Assembly Rooms, whee about 150 persons sat down to a very substantial tea.—Aftetwards Mr..Wro. Bennett, of Liverpool, gave one of his iitezary and musical entertainments, which occupied the attentiot, of the audience for nearly two hours. Toe chair was occupied by the president, the Rev. H. A. Macnaghten, and Mist Quick ably presided at the pianoforte. A SOLDIER IN Tuoretar —At the Pi escot Petty Sessions, on;Tuesday, before Mr. W. Blinkhorn d Mr. W. L. Evans, Walter Russell, dressed in regimentals, was charged with being absent without leave from the 40th Regim-nt of Foot. A constable met the prisoner on the previous day, and asked him if he had a pass. The prisoner replied that he had, and produced one which, however, expired at a quarter to twelve on Saturday night last.—The Bench ordered the prisoner to be handed over to the military authorities. ALLEGED GAME TRE3PASS.—BeIore Messrs. W. Blink. horn and W. L. Evans, at the Prescot Petty Sessions, en Tuesday, Thomas Wright, a labourer, residing at Widn, a. was summoned for trespassing in search of game on land et Croaton, in the occupation of C.)lonel Plerkes.—The defen- dant did not appear.—Mr. McKenzie, salicitor, Prescat, peered for the complainant, and stated that Colonel Parks a bad certain " covers " for game on land at Cronten, and rn the Bth November a keeper named lihnehton, w hen feedirg the game. saw the defendant trespassing on the laud &me 400 or 500 yards from the highway —Samuel Hough'on, gamekeeper, was then called. He stated that whea the de- fendant 83W him he (defendant) ran away, and witness called out "Oh Torn, my lad, you're there.' The defen- dant had something in his hand, but witness could not say what it was.—The Bench rematked that there was no evl- dence to show the defendant was trespassing in search of game.—Mr. McKenzie observed that thst was the inference. —Mr. Evans, J P., said the defendant was only trespassing. There was no evidence at all that he was in sea,cla of game. It was only a very suspicions cas..—Mr. McKenzie said be had no more witnesses, and the Bonen thereupon dist:Lined the case.

PRBSCOT HIGHWAY Boenne—The monthly meeting of this Board was held on Tuesday forenoon. Present : Messrs. W. L. Evans (in the chair), Lowe, Tyrcr, H. Cross (clerk), and IV. Goldsworth (surveyor) —The minutes of the last meeting were read and confirrned.—Expenditure: The Sur- veyor's statement of expenditure for the four eteks October 30th to Nove.nber 27th showed the following totals :—Bold, £26 17s; Knowsley, £7 as 4d ;:Rainhill, £lO 63 61; Whiston. £147. 41; team labour, £TI44 sil; new materiale, £29 15s lid; incidentals, .51. Ta 4d; total, £9B 41 -Against the Board: The Clerk reported that after the last meeting of the Board he wrote to Mr. William Tvrer solici- tor, with reference to the claim made by his client, Mr. Frith. farmer, Whiston, in ressect of damage alleged to have been done by the Board. He informed Mr.-Tyrer that the Board would be willing to pay to Mr. Frith £3 Os 81, being a third part of the amount of damage done.. The sum was off-red without prejudice. He (Mr. Cross) had not received a reply since.—St. Helens Corporation and its Traffic: Mr. Tyrer said he thought the St Helens Corpora- tion should bs called upon to pay something for the extra- .ordinary traffic upon the roads at Know iley.—Mr. Guide.. worth remarked that the Board hid entered into an mere, ment with the St. Helens Corporation, and the time would not be up until May next. He had been putting stones along the road, so that when it came to be repaired the trench would be in a satisfactory state. So far as the cartage of coal was concerned he did not think they could make any claim, but they could for the carting of tee engine beds, and when that class of carting was done then a claim could be made. He had the thing in mind, and at the proper time would amain bring the matter up.—This was the cnly business. BOARD OF GUARDIANS,—The fortnightly meeting was held on Thursday week, present—Mr. J. I'. Hall (chairman), Revs. T. Chambers and Barnacle ; Messrs. W. Newsome, J. Leatherharrow, T. Sadler, IV. Gerrard, W. Birchall, W. A. Meadows. W. Tyrer, J. Lowe, W. Holm, J. Kenwrigh., R. Leigh, E. Syder, T. Eatock, W. Swift, P. Longton, W. B. Longton, and H. S. Hartley (clerk).—Master'e Report : The Master reported that there were 437 inmates in the workhouse against 446 in the preceding week, and 438 in the corresponding week of last year. During the week 45 vagrants had been relieved, as compared with 51 in the corresponding week of last year. No able-belied men from Widnes bad been relieved during the seek—Mr. Meadows said he had understood there were a great many people out of work in Widnes.—The Chairman said it was not so.— The Clerk said a special meeting of the committee appointed to consider the question of relaying able.bodied poor, re- commended that adult persons not suffering under tempor- ary or permanent infirmity of body should be relieved out of the woikhouse' we'll set that the tasks of we' set forth in a resolution of the Local Government Board should be ex- acted.—The recommendation of the committee was ap- proved. Christmas Dinner: The R-v. T. Chamber moved that the inmates have the usual dinner of roast beet and plum pudding on Christmas Day.—Mr. Newsome seconded the motion, and it was carried unanimously.— Appointments A. letter was read from the Local Govern- ment Board, assenting to the appointment of Dir. Peter Chorley as vaccination-officer for the St. Helens registra- tion sub-district of the Prescot Union, with a fee of four- pence in respect of each case of successful vaccination re- gistered by him.—Mr.Leatherbarrow moved that Mr. Henry Fogg be appointed vaccination-officer for the Prescot sub- district, with a remuneration of sixpenee for each case of successful vaccination registered by him.—Mr. Newsome seconded the motion, which was agreed to.—The Guardian- ship of Ditton: The Clerk read a lette: from the Local Goverement Board authorising the election of a guar- dian for the township of Ditton, in the room of Mr. Willoughby Gilbody resigned. —The Charges Against Union Officials : The Clerk stated he had written to Sir R. A. Cross. M.P., and Colonel Ireland Blackburne, M.P., requesting them to bring the question of proceeding against Dr. O'Hara for refusing to give evidence at the recent inquiry before the heeds of the Local Govern- ment Board. Sir R. A. Cross replied that the Local Govern- ment Board had promised to lay the matter before Sir Charles Dilke. A further letter be (the clerk) bad since received stated that the Board did not feel that the case was one in which it was necessary they should institute proceedings against Dr. O'Hara —A rote of thanks to Sir Richard Cross was passed.—Resignation: The Clerk read a letter from Mr. David Swallow, assistant-overseer for the township of Rainford, resigaing the office on account of old age and bad health, such resignation to take place on I the quarter-day ending December 24th, 1884.—The resigna- tion was accepted, the Chairman remarking that Mr. Swallow had been a faithful servant of the Board for nearly 23 years, I and was highly respected.—The Board adjourned. RURAL SANITARY AIITRORITY.—k meeting of the Prescot Rural Sanitary Authority was held at the Workhouse, Whitton, on Thursday forenoon. Present: Messrs. J. Leatherbarrow, W. Newsome, W. Tvrer, W. Swift, W. A. Meadows, E. Svder, and S. Hartley (clerk).—The minutes of the last meeting were read and confirmed —The Sewerage of Ecolestown; The Clerk read a communication from the Local Government Board enclosing two memorials from rate- payers of Ecclestown with reference to the sewerage scheme for Eccleston township, and asking for the observations of the Rural Sanitary Authority in refarence thereto. The first memorial, signed by 150 ratepayers, asked that the scheme in question be not carried out according to the plans of Mr. Goldsworth. The township consisted almost entirely of agricultural land, with the exception of Lane Ends, Eccles- ton Park, Portico, and Helen Nook, which they wished to be declared a special drainage district, and thereby provide for its own expenses, so that the great expense which would be for the benefit of a small portion of the township might be borne by those who benefited by it, and not by the general body of ratepayers. The second memorial w, I signed by 84 persons, and stated that the property owners and ratepayers of Lane Ends had hold a meeting to protett against the proposed sewering of the township the existing system of sewerage being found to meet the full require- ments of the neighbourhood and to work efficiently and to the satisfaction of the serveyor. They prayed the Local Government Board would refuse to sanction the proposed , scheme and thereby save the township great and unneces- sary expenses the execution of the work would entail.—Mr. Meadows said the Authoity had asked the Local Govern. merit Board to send down an inspector to irquire into the scheme, but they declined to do so. He thought it was only fair that the people who were to ben; fit by the scheme should pay for it. lie thought the memorials were only reasonable, and it was hardly fair that a straggling district like Focleston should he compelled to pay for what would only benefit one portion of it.—Mr. Newsome disclaimed the right of Mr. Meadows to champion the ratepayers of Eccleston. He disclaimed the right of Mr. Meadows to champion the part of the ratepayers of Eccleston, and charged Mr. Meadows as a former chairman of that Autho- rity with being the cause of the nuisances that had arisen in that township by signing and passing plans for the erec- tion of property without looking ft)t a sewerace outlet.— Mr. Meadows did not understand Mr. Newsome's remarks, and stated that when he sigsed the plans for the property to which Mr. Newsome had alluded they were in conformity with the bye-laws in force at that time.—The Clerk added that that was so.—R was ultimately decided that the clerk should write to the Lecel Government Board stating that the Board would give their observatmas upon rthe memorials when the Local Government Board hold the I Thquiry.-21fedical Ofeer's Report: The Medical Officer (Dr. Hall) reported that there had been several itailatrd cases of fever in the district since the last meeting, one death frenl diphtheria in Halewood, a case of scarlet fever in Eccleston, and a whole family with the same disease in ' Crouton ; they were nearly well again.—The Surveyor (Mr. Twist) handed in his monthly report, which contained no item of public' interest.—Claint Against the Board: The Clerk read a further letter from Mr. W. Tyrer. solicitor, on behalf of Mr. Frith, farmer, Whiston, who claimed £lO as compensation for damage dene to his land by the overflow of a sewer. He (Mr. Hartley) advised the Authority that they were not liable for any damage that had becn done, and the matter dropped.

div.head: EXAMINER
div.p: THE EXAMINER
I

merged in county representation. It is some- thing gained when leading Tories can be brought to consent to such ancient places as Hertford, Shaf tesbury, Tewkesbury, Lich- field, &c., losing separate representation, for we can fancy the pathetic appeals that would have been made on their behalf if the Go- vernment had taken this course siegle-handed. The 15,000 limit is a good one : 20.000 as suggested by Mr. BRIGHT, would have been better; but we must get to heaven by de- grees. The next important point is that one member will be taken from towns under 50,000 inhabitants that have hitherto been over-represented by having two members of Parliament. The necessity of this is ob- vious when it is pointed out that, taking the av rage of the country, there would. be one member to 54.,000 inhabitants. Wigan, under this provision, will lose a mem- ber, its population according to the census of 1881—which is to be taken as the basis— being just under 50 000. If our neighbours should think they are being hardly used, see- ing that they are on the border line, let them reflect how much harder has been the lot of St. Helens to have had no representative at all, though its population is nearly 6o 000 ! St. Helens will, of course, become a Parlia- mentary borough under the new Bill; and so will Barrow, another large Lancashire town which has up to now had no direct re- presentation. Towns with a population be- tween 50.0c0 and 165 000 that have two members will be left undisturbed; but, go- ing beyond this, all large towns and cities are to be broken up into single-member consti- tuencies. Liverpool, for instance, Will gain six additional members, making nine in all ; but the city will be divided into sections, or wards, each ward returning a member. Man- chester will gain three members, making six, and the city will be divided into six sections, each returning a member. Salford, gaining one, will have three members, but the same principle will apply in dividing the borough, so that there will be an end of what is usually understood as three-cornered constituencies. Counties are to be treated in the same fashion; they are to be no double-barrelled constituencies, except, as already stated, in towns of between 50,000 and 165 000 inhab- itants at present sending two members to Parliament. The change is undoubtedly a great one, and already this feature of the bill is being keenly canvassed. There is much to be said against as well as in fitigy çflyllat are called ward representa- tives. It is fear that it will tend to de- C 4 n terioration in the class Ca" didates, seeing that it will give greater play to purC',7 legal influences, and that it will be so much easier to " nurse " a part than the whole of a town. On the other hand, prov4oll. 4 made for the representation of minoritio in a way which; to say the least of it, is less objection- able than by the three-cornered system which is about to receive its quietus London has previously been cut up into sections, and with the 5o odd members which will in future represent that vast community it is not desir- able that it should be otherwise. We cannot conceive of anyone saying that the metro- polis should be regarded as one constituency, and that an elector should have the privilege of giving so votes. This would be to give the elector's vote 5o times the value- in the way of representation to that, say, of a voter in Warrinoton which has only one ineinh,- And if this holds good as to the 'Metropolis, it applies, though with dimknished force, to such large centres as Liverpool, Manchester, Birmingham, an.',3, Glasgow. The Redistri- bution Bill. 'we may add, will place no less than 166 seats at the disposal of the Govern- ment; Ireland is to retain her present repre- tentation, less two seats lost through corrupt practices; Wales will remain untouched as to the number of her representatives; Eng- land will gain six seats—the six disfranchised for corruption—and Scotland, which is under represented, is to have the balance restored by an addition of twelve members—the total number of members of the House of Com- mons being increased for this purpose from 658 to 670. We give in another column de- tails as to the various places affected by the Bill. Warrington is let alone, not being ' touched even as to boundaries; but Chester loses a member, which will be a loss to that extent to the total representation of the county. Lancashire, on the other hand, will gain 25 seats, and will thus stand, with 58 representatives, in the proud position of returning more members to Parliament than other County in the Kingdom.

Lord RIPON has been a much-abused man as Viceroy of India, the Europeans who! should have stood by him having been amongst the first to endeavour to weaken his authority when it was seen that he thought less of class privileges than of the well- being of the community. The Anglo- Indians predicted the worst results as the outcome of the trust which he showed in the natives of our great Dependency; for they have no faith, it would seem, in any rule but that of force. His lordship must have had a disagreeable time of it in his efforts to carry out principles of local self- government, seeing that the permanent offi- cials were for the most part disposed to place stumbling-blocks in his path rather than re- move them. But he is having his reward ; the people have not been slow to recognise that he was actuated with the highest motives in his endeavours to promote their advance- ment; and now that he is on the eve of leaving India they have become demonstrative in their expression of regard. At Bombay, on Sunday, there was a monstre meeting in the Town Hall, at which it was resolved to present his lordship with an address and to found a Ripon Memorial, which will take the form of an industrial exhibition. Such was the enthusiasm of the populace, and so great was the crowd, that it is stated that upwards of 20,000 persons were assembled outside the hall. On Wednesday the VICEROY paid a visit to Calcutta, and met with a reception which kings might envy. The city " cast its people out upon him," over 100,000 assembling in the streets to do him honour. The route he had to traverse— z distance of two miles—was all along beau- tifully decorated with "flags, festoons, and , evergreens." "The VICEROY," the telegram ' goes on to say, "was received by a deputa- tion from the Ripon Reception Committee, beaded by the MAHARAJA DURBHANRA, who welcomed his lordship cordially on behalf of the natives, the band playing See the Con- quering Hero Comes.' The VICEROY and Lady RIPON walked through the middle of the crowd amid deafening cheers." How paltry, how contemptible, in view of this spontaneous outburst of feeling is the recollection of the slights to wllich Lord RIPON was subjected by the official classes when in the interests of justice and good government he was sseeking to make headway with the Ilbert Bill ! It is kdident that the people of India are grateful and warm-hearted. Good seed sown amongst them has fallen on good soil, and has already

THE IRON TRADE.—An award has been made in the dis- pute as to wages in the iron trade in the North of Englanl. The employers proposed a reduction of 5 per cent and the men claimed an advance of 5 per cent. The arbitrator— Dr. Watson—decided that the wages shall remain un- altered, but strongly urged the adoption of a sliding scale. IMPROVEMENT CLASS AND GYMNASIUM.- The adjourned de- bate on" Oliver Cromwell: Is he worthy of our admiration ?'' was resumed in the National Schools. Widnes, on Wednes- day evening last. The Rev. C. Rumfitt, Rev. A. H. Wilson (the vicar of Widnes), Mr. J. W. Machin, and Mr. Williim Cook took part in the discussion. A motion for a further adjournment being negatived, the question was put to the , meeting, and was carried in the affirmative ky a large majority. MISSIONARY MEETING AT KINGSLEY.—The annual meet- ing has been held in the Wesleyan Chapel, en behalf of the Wesleyan Foreign Missions. The choir was taken by Mr. , Sanderson, of Wallerscote, near Northwich, and the follow- ing other gentlemen took a prominent part in the proceed- ings:—Rev. H. T. Bramwell, Middlewich ;Rev. E. Moscrop, circuit minister; and other local friends. The meeting was , well attended, and at the close a collection was made in aid of the above society. WATER FAMINE IN CHESITIRE.—A mee'ing of inhabit- ants of Malpas, Cheshire, has been held, to take into con- sideration the water famine. There was for six days a total failure of the supply. Mr. Tomlinson said he had been un- able to obtain water for three months. Dr. Jordison said he bad been without water, except what he begged privately, for over a week. Such a lamentable state of things has never been experienced before It was decided to endeavour to provide an additional supply. SUDDEN DEATH AT RUNCORN.—Yesterday morning Jane Isabella Boyle, aged 6 years, daughter of Joseph Wilson Boyle, ship's carpenter, Percival'e-lane, died under the I followingcircumstances. The child was taken ill on Wed- nesday, and the father, who is a herbalist, treated her for croup. She became much worse yesterday, and Dr. Robin- son was sent for, but the child had expired before his arri- val. The doctor states that there is no doubt the child died from croup and that the father treated the child in a proper manner. The coroner has been acquainted with the case. TEA PARTY AT RUNCORN.—In connection with the Preston Brook Circuit ot the Primitive Methodist Connec- tion a tea party was held on Monday evening in Regent- street Schoolroom, Runcorn. There was a very good attend- ance. Tables and contributions were given by Mrs. Pick- well, Mrs. White, Mrs. Midwood, Mrs. J. Broadhurst, Mrs. Gittene, and the Stubbs' family. Subseqaently a meeting was held under the presidency of Mr. T. Stringfellow. Ad- dresses were delivered by the Rev. J. Miles and Messrs. Patin and W. Stott. The choir rendered several anthems under the leaiership of Mr. J. Poole. The proceeds will be added to the circuit funds. BANKRUPTCY CASES —On Thursday, at Warrington County Court, Mr, Mather, of Weston Point, came up for his public examination, which was adjourned till the 12th December.—Application was made to His Honour, Judge Ffoulkes for a warrant to arrest John Yapp, corn dealer, &c., of Halton, near Runcorn, who has failed to appear to pass his public examination, on the ground that he had disposed of some of his goods and books.—His Honour adjourned the application for further evidence to he pro- cured. At the Liverpool County Court, yesterday (Friday), the Registrar, on the application of Mr. A Browne solicitor, Warrington, made a receiving order in the estate of John Pye, of Widnes-road, Widnes, toolmaker and hardware dealer. RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE. The monthly meeting was held on Thursday afternoon, at the Town Hall, Waterloo-road. The Rev. Canon Barclay presided, and there were present—Dr. Steele, Messrs. P. Briecoe, W. Hargiley, and J. D. Jones (librarian.) The Librarian's re- I port stated that 1,482 books had been issued to borrowers er consulted by readers in the reading-room, classified as fol- lows :—Reference history 4, science and art 4, miscellaneous 9. Lending Department : Theology 24, philosophy 6, his- tory, dm., 195, science and art 43, poetry 13. fiction 1,128, miscellaneous 56. The receipts for the month amounted to £2 2s 9d. Books had been presented during the month by Mr. Simpson, Mr. Handley, and the representatives of the late Dr. Hodgson. AN ALKALI WORKS FLOODED AT WIDNES: 1,000 MEN lOUT OF EMFLOYMENY.—For several days past the important and extensive works of the Widnes Alkali Camnany have been and are now standing idle, in consequence of th-e main sewer which drains the premises having become stopped up. In some parts of the works the ground is covered with water to a depth of several feet, and as under such circum- stances it is impossible to carry on the various operations, no less than 1,000 men are temporarily out of employment. Yesterday a number of workmen were engaged in remedying the defective sewer, which is known as the Bower's Brook culvert, and it is expected that work will be resumed at the Ibeginning of next week. It is supposed that chemical deposits have caused the stoppage of the drain.

THE Redistribution Bill is now before the country, and, speaking of it as a whole, it has met so far with a most favourable reception. It is not theoretically perfect—nobody expec- ted that it would be, for the country is not yet quite ripe for equal electoral districts or proportional representation. It is in the nature of a compromise with existing institu- tions and anomalies ; but it goes further—it is more radical in its changes—than is usually the casewith measures shaped to suit opposing parties. Indeed, the Bill is wider in its scope than was hoped for as possible a few months ago ; and there can be no question that if it had been introduced in its present form by the present Goveznment apait from consul- tation with the leaders of the Opposition, it would instantly have been d.inounced as re- volutionary, and fought tooth and nail. As it is, the non-contents are likely to be few, comparatively speaking, and there is reason to hope that the measure will become law without undergoingmaterial changes in either of the Houses of Parliament. Lord SALIS- BURY can be counted on to cirty the House of Lords with him when it is not a case of desperate fighting; and a 3 to the House of Commons there is little reason to fear that it will go seriously wrong when Mr. GLAD- STONE and Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE are practically in agreement as to the course which it is best to Like. There are some, of course, who will fume and fret at everything that is vital to the Bill having been " arran- ged" beforehand ; but what does it matter so long as that which has been " arranged" is good in itself ? Take the Bill on its merits, and it must be admitted that it is admirable. To begin with, there is to be no separate re- presentation of towns with a population of less than 15,000, which means that the fusty musty little places with a good deal of anti. quity, but very little vitality, are to "go under" in the matter of representation, as they have long since gone under in other re- spects. It is not that their little light is to be entirely snuffed out ; they will have their place, but no more than their place, in being

It is, too. with a pang as at the loss of a near friend that they have heard of the death of MiE FAWCETT, and the idea has quickly been taken up to establish scholarships in his memory. All this is most hopeful for the future of India; it is an encouragement to statesmen of high character to spend at least a portion of their energies in striving to better the condition of the 250 millions of people committed to our care in our Eastern Empire.

IF any ratepayers ever had any doubt as to the willingness of the bulk of the inhabitants of Warrington to levy a rate upon themselves in aid of the promotion of the Ship Canal, they can have none after seeing the result of the poll on Saturday last. A majority of more than ten to one is certainly a most emphatic expression of opinion on the subject—quite as emphatic in its way as the decision of the Town's Meeting a few weeks ago in favour of laying the rate. We know it can be urged that the promoters of the Ship Canal scheme had active agents at work drawn from the ranks of both political parties; and that ' there has been no such organisation on the part of the opposition ; but, making due allowance for this, it must still be admitted that there is a vast preponderance of opinion in favour of a rate-in-aid. This doe 3 not of course touch the issue which has been justly raised as to whether it is wise on the part of the Corporation to step out of the beaten track in matters of this kind; but the subject has been fully discussed—we have given both sides a fair hearing—and if there are any ratepayers who are still in the dark it must be, as " Festus " has it, because they are "blind as never bat was bind." The question as to the legality of the course taken by the Town Council in confirming the decision of the ratepayers is of one which we shall yet, most likely, hear something more ; though it must be said that, seeing that the HOME SECRETARY has this week given his sanction to the levying of the rate in Manchester, it is hardly likely that it will be withheld in the case of War- rington. Runcorn, as we observe from a report of a meeting of the Commissioners on Thursday, is carefully watching the Bill, in so far as its provisions will affect that district. It is alleged that, as the plans are drawn, they will seriously affect the drain- age—a matter, we need hardly say, of vital moment to every community. But the Pro- visional Committee of the Ship Canal having had so many ups and downs will doubtless be I found to be accommodating, and we do not therefore anticipat, Any difficulty ii this respect. Warrington, it should not be for- I gotten, is securing what was required as a I Cem§eqUence :of the material support which is being accorded; and when it is considered that conflict would soon cost the town more I than the total of the ra'.e, it will be some consolation, we trust, to those who contend that it is neither wise nor necessary to levy a tax upon Warrington to aid in promoting the ; Manchester Ship Canal. • .

A NEW LAMP has been placed at one of the darkest parts of the bridge. It will doubtless boa great boon. DISTRESSING FATALITY ON THE MERSEY.—A distressing fatality occurred during a heavy gale which prevailed at Widnes on Thursday. A flat, owned by Mr. John Marshall, who lives at Penketia, manned by the owner and his son, essayed to leave the docks on a voyage down the tiver. Owing to the high wind the flat Was driven underneath the bridge, and at this point the boom of the vessel broke. The heavy piece of timber struck the younger Si irshall on the head, splitiittg his skull and knocking him overb) ant. A strong tide Was running and the body instantly disappeared. The father Was helpless, and was an agonized witness of his own son's painfie! death. On Thursday night the river Was ; being searched for the body, but its recovery Was considered very doubtfel on account of the high tides. WinsEs &moor. The annual tea party in connection with the Newtown Mission Chumh took place on Thursday evening in the Mission Room, Shaw-street. There was a very large attendance a' tea, and at the subs.quent proceedings the room was crowded. The Rev. B. He mentioned that the communicants had increased from 8 to 16, and the evening collectione from £lO to £2O. Addresses were also delivered by the Revs. T. M. Ammon and J. Madden, and Messrs. Run- corn Police Court. on Tuesday, Martha Riley, a married woman living at Halton, was charged with stealing three chemises and a pair of drawers, the property of Martha Janes, of lialton.—Ernena Wilkinson, a single woman, who lives with the prosecutrix at the Prospect Inn stated that sae missed the articles from the clothes line on the night of the 25th November. She identified one of the chemises pro- duced.—George Henry Graham, assistant to Mr. Edward Imison, pawnbroker, Church-street, deposed that the pri- soner, whom he knew very well as a customer of his master's, on the 26th ult. brought the chemises to the shop, and asked for 61 upon them.—P.S. Loundes said he appre- hended the prisoner on Monday, at her own house. She de- nied having pawned anythine with Mr. Imieon, but the as- sietarit was re-called. and said he was sure she was the woman.—The Bench imposed a fine of 20s including costs, or 14 days hard labour. ADVENT SERVICE AND ORGAN RECITAL AT FRODSDAM. —The first of a series of Advent services was held in the Frodshain Parish Church on Tuesday evening, when an ad- dress was delivered by the Vicar on the Gospel of St. Mat- thew, and was attentively listened to by the congregation. The fine quali- ties of the organ were brought out in a most effective man- ner by Mr. Dolby, and the choice combination of the stops displayea rare judgment and a thorough acquaintance with the instrument, as well as an appreciation of the feeling and spirit of the cempesers. Mrs. G. Hubi Newcombe, Warrington, ' makes a further bid for popularity in the publication of this song, in which she appears in the double capacity of corn- poser of the music and the writer of the words. As will be gathered from its title, the sang is neutieel in character, and the music is of that ordintry type which, if we have not already a repletion of sailor ditties, is likely to gain the ear of vocalists with a predilection for saunas of this class. There in the usual story of the absence of an object of en- dearment, the ultimate and happy return, and a fairly good sentiment expresseel in the inevitable refrain. Such material calls for no great skill in musical treatment, and j it is, perhaps, sufficient to say that Mrs. Newcombe, though by no means at her best, has given a melodious and ade- quate setting with such diversification as the subject allows. A Song of Sixpence' composed by Mr. Henry Pontet, is another sailor song which, while in ro wise pretentious, has , a fair amount of " go" in it. Far Away in Dreams I. 1 music and words alike—from the pen of Mr. W. M. Hut- ! chinson. It is nicely set, very tuneful, and quite in the vein of his celebrated "Dream Faces." "The Guadal- quiver," also by Mr. Hutchinsan, is lees likely to be success- ful. The last-named songs are published by Messrs. W. Marshall and Co., London. A Wummes APPEAL CASE.—In the Court of Appeal, London, on Saturday, before the Master of the Rolls and Lords Justices Cotton and Lindley, the case of Hall Bros. and another and Chadwick and another was heird. This was an anneal by the defendants against the judgment of Mr. Justice Cave at the trial in Liverpool. The plaintiff's ; are chemical manufacturers allaying on business at Widnes,' and the defendants are piper makers, of the Ordeal Hall Paper Works, Manchester. The action was brought to re- cover £174, the belance of the price of certain bleaching powder supplied to the defeatants. The defendants ad-I mitted the claim, but set up a counter claim of £260 for damages said to have been sustained by them in respect of the non-delivery of part of the bleaching powder with which the plaintiffs were bound under the contract to supply them. —The Master of the Rolls said that in his opinion the re- quest made to the plaintiffs to hod over delivery was noth- ing but an alteration of the mode and manner of delivery, which had been expressly provided for in the contract. Be, therefore, thought that, wnile the plaintiffs had a right to the amount claimed by them, the defendants were entitled to the amount of their minter-claim, leasing the judgment in favour of the defendants for £45 2s s.3.—Lord Justice Cotten and Lord Justice Lindley concurred, and the de- cision of Mr. Justice Cave was therefore reversed. ATTEMPTED SUICIDE AT WIDNES.—AY WicineS Police Court on Tuesday, Edward Fitzgerald, 19 years of age, was charged with attempting to commit suicide. It appeared that the prisoner worksal at the Widnes foundry, and lodged with John Coogan at 19, Charlotte-street, Widnes. There had been some disagreement between the landlord and the lodger about the manner in which the latter paid for his board, and Coogan had told him that he could not afford to keep him. On Monday night the prisoner several times entered the house and made a "bother," and broke a pane of glass in the kitchen window. He afterwards went out although the weather was very inclement, but returned in a state of intoxication at midnight and asked lobe allewed to come in "for God's sake." He was permitted to come in and went upstairs, telling his sister that she would not see him alive again. Heariug a noise in the room some time afterwards Coozan and the prisoner's sister went to the room but found the door blocked ins the interior by a large table, which it took all their united power to remove. On effecting an entrance they found the prisoner hanging by a strap from a clothes book. He was insensible, but Coogan immediately cut him down, and he recovered. The pri- soner informed the Bench that be had no intention of com- mitting suicide. He added that lee had got injured on the head at the Widnes foundry, and was out of work for some time. Because he could net pay Coogan the money he owed him all at once, he hat kept nagging at him. The prisoner was remanded to Kirkalale gaol for a week. BREAKING UP A SALTATION ARMY MEETING LT RUN- CORN.—Henry Moores, a young man, was brought up at Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, charged on remand with having, on the 23rd November, been guilty of riotous and disorderly behaviour ill the Runcorn Public Hall, during the celebration of divine service ; and he was further charged with assaulting P.C. Smith. Defendant pleaded not guilty to both charges. Evidence was given by Wm. Greenwood, " captain " of the local corps of the' Salvation Army; Richard Herschel, " lieutenant "; John Heys, a painter; and Constables Smith and Fryer. It appeared that the Public Hall is licensed as a place of public worship, and on the Sunday afternoon in question the members of the Salvation Army were holding a service there. Shortly after the commencement of the proceedings Moores, who was in a half intoxicated condition, entered the room, and took his seat among several young urea, who were inclined to be hilarious. He shouted and laughed, and otherwise disturbed the harmony of the meeting, snd the captain having several theme requested him to behave himself, or leave the room, at last asked " Who shonld conduct the meeting ?" The defendant insolently replied "The one with the biggest mouth." The captain and his assistants were unable to Pacify the defendant, who was three times requested to leave the building, but he refused, and as a lest resource the aid of the police was invoked. On seeing P.C. Smith arrive the defendant quietly retired, when requested, but in a few moments rushed back with a great noise, and cursed in a violent fashion. The officer then forcibly ejected him. In the vestibule and the street the defendant acted with great violence, and struck Smith twice upon the jaws, besides un- successfully attempting to throw him to the groand. Con- stables Smith and Fryer then conveyed him to the police station, batt the affair had caused so much exitement that the service was broken up in disorder.—Captain Hazlehuret said the Bench considered both cases proved. In the first he would be fined 103 and costs 16e fad; and in the second £1 and costs ss. The officers of the army could not have treated him more fairly, and the Bench hoped taste srntence would be a warning te hint and other young men who at- tend the Salvation Army meetings simply to create a dis- turbance.

His eyeball was cut open and an eye-lash taken out, which had been thrust in at the paint of the sword of the man I whose household he had ravaged, and whose pretty chicks be hd slain. Within a fortnight after this curious opera- tion B trry Sullivan was walking about as if his eye-lashes had always retained their proper place. It is curious to think of the divine Sara a prey to the bitterest anguish for the love of man. -It was but a month or two ago that Damal. entranced her. Daraala disap- peared, and for a time Richepin reigned in his ateati. He speedily tired of the passionate angularity, and Sara lies in the profoundest depths of despair. When she found that Richepin had really left her she was taken violently HI, and the rumour went abroad that she had poisoned herself. However it e she recovered, and there is now some talk cf her returning to her work on the stage. THE

When it opened iii the last week of October the most sanguine man could not have looked for the great results achieved. At most it was expected that the Franchise Bill would be pis- sed. Before the House rises not only will the Franchise Bill have been added to the Statute book, but the Redis- tribution Bill will have been read a second time, with every prospect of passing its remaining stages early in next ses- sion. B can', pea., and Indian corn are al to political topics of the day, and nothing more saccessful. 8 On Monday, amid the drizzling sleet, all that was left of 1 poor Tom Collins was laid under the snow. He was not a very old man as age is counted in these days. But it seemed almost time for him to be gone. On the very day cf his funeral the House of Commons witnessed the memorable spectacle of Mr, Gladstone introducing a Radical scheme of Rsdistribution which crowned the edifice of the largest Re- form Bill ever brought in. and this not only without oppo- sition from the Conservatives but with their active conni- vance. This was a very different kind of business from that to which Tom Collins was accustomed, and he was well out of it. It is more than teirty years since he entered Par- liament, and though he did not eit uninterruptedly through- out that period he was a frequent and p-alonged visitor. The heyday of his time was between 188e-74, when he sat for Boston. Those were the days when churches were being disestablished and land enfranchised. Tom Collie:a " Jimmy " Lowther, and Cavendish Bentinck formed an alliance offensive and defensive, against the progress of all reforms. They were realer to make speeches if need were, but were always prepared with interjections. Tom Collin's chief glory was to brine businese to a sudden end by means ' of a count, an art in which Mr. Samaras his only grotesque - imitator. Collins was a most extraordinary man in personal appear- ance; thin sallow face, large mouth, whence was emitted a Btentorian voice. He alaays dressed in the shabbiest clothes, and, morning, noon, or night, spring, easel:nee, autumn, or winter, was never without his f athful umbrella. Ile bought it btand new, in all the gicry of gingham, when he was returned for Boston in 1863. It saw the Irish Church disestablished,lhe hisa land frted from landlord rapacity, the ballot introduced, education brought within the reach of all, a spirited foreleg policy enacted, the fall of Mr. Gladstone, the rise of Mr. Disraeli, ane once more Mr. Gladstone at the head of a triumphant majority, and Mr. Disraeli merged into Lord Beaconsfield. 'Like its matter, it was a curious concern. But Mr. Collins's-- affection for it ,vas almost pathetic. He never left it in the cloakroom, but always arought it into the lobby under his arm, where in its time, I suppose, it Must have poked out many eyes and administered matey serious digs in the ribs to unsuspecting bystanders. It was his custom to leave it in the personal charge of the doorkeeper, who hid it from covetous grasp behind his chair. Extraordinary in his morning dress, Tom Collins was superb on the rare occa- sions when he went out to dinner. It is said that he never Oe ss. Oil had but one evening suit in his life. WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURI. • SATURDAY.—The only case down for hearing was remanded • until Monday, and is reported elsewhere. Moernar.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) in the chair, Mr. John Fakelough, and Alderman Holmes. STEALING "TIT BlTS."—Joseph Holley (12), son of Mertin Heeley, was sent to prison for a month, and ordered to be detained five years in a refOTI3IIIOTV, for steeling four copies of "Tit Bite" from the shop of Charles Henry Pigot, SankeY-street, on Saturday. • DRUNKENNESS.—The following cases were dealt with:— Patrick Mannicn (16;11 appearance), fined lOs and costs or 14 day; John Robinson, 5s and costs, or seven days; John Kelly, 5s and costs, or seven days; Thomas Foy and William O'Brien, 53 and costs; Patrick Brown, dismissed on pay- ment of lock-up fees; David Jones, 53 and costs; 51a7 Demaine, 5s and c•ets; John Galvin, sent to prison for a month. CHIMNEY co F(lll4.—Annie Parker was fined is for allow- ins' her chimney to be on tire. Scnoor. ATTENDANCE CASES —The following cases were dealt with —Henry: Harrison, Samuel Richardson, Robert Stockton, James Finn, .and James Clark, tined 5s each; Thomas Rutter (two cases), fined 10s; Peter Jones, with- drawn; William Sheppard, boy to receive twelve strokes with the birch rod; John Thomason, dismissed; Jane Victrs, CASE adjourned. Mr. G. Riley, school attendance officer, proved the cases. DRUNK es CHARGE Or A HEABSS.—George Buckley was fined 33 6:1 for being drunk whilst in charge of a hearse and pair of horses in Knutsford-road. TUESDAY.—Before Councillor Broadbent. MISCELLANEOUS. Daniel Hennessey, labourer, was charged with using malicious threats to William Egging. ton, on Saturday evening. He was ordered to find two sureties in £5 each, and be bound over in £lO himself, or go to prison for fourteen days —Elizabeth Woods, married woman, charged with being drunk and disorderly in Butte- market-street the previous evening, was discharged with a caution. WEDNESDAY.—There was no business. TM7llsDAL—Before Major Litton and Alderman Webster. MISCELLANEOUS.—Joseph Bibby, jun., a young man, was charged on a warrant with c•minitting a breach of the peace by fighting in Winwick-street ou the 30th August, and was ordered to find a surety to keep the peace for six months, or go to gaol for 14 days.—Joseph Cookson, charged with sleeping out, was dismissed with a caution. FlUDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), in the chair. and Mr. John White. Tun SNovenstatzea NUlSANCE.—ltielarti Jolley and John Jolley were summoned for dtmegiag tee windows and shutters of the dwelling-home 37. Bewsev-street, en Nov. 30th.—It appeared that on the evening of Sued ay. defend- ants, young men of independent mean., amuse 4 themselves by throwing snowballs at the house of M. Gray, 37, Baw• nes' road. Mr. Gray, being weatly aneoyed, informed P.S. Jones of what was feleing place, and the sergeant and a con- stable secreted themselves and SiNY the defendants throwing snowballs at the house.—Mr. Knowles (Wickes). who ap- peared for complainant, said that the c mdriet of the defend- ants had been that of street ronghe.—Mr. Dev'es, who ap- peared far the defendants, contended that no damage had been done.—The Bench found the case proved, and the Mayor said he thought that, after hearing the evidence, they thought that the annoyance bad been intentional.—The defendants were fined 103 each and costs, including advo- , cats's fee, and ordered to pay the damage, 35. ALLEGED Asserer BY MILITIAXEN.—MiChaeI Garrity and Peter Garrity were charged with assaulting a young woman named Ellen Connor.—The case was dismissed on payment of costs.

Murphy did not appear, and a warrant was issued. Sallinger was bound over to keep the peace for three months.—Sanmel Luther, of Havdock, was summoned for a similar offence committed on the Bth ult. The defendant said he was only acting in self-defence, and called a witness who gave evidence to that effect. The sum- mons was dismissed.—John Dearden pleaded guilty to a summons charging him with committing a breach of the peace at Haydock, on the Bth November, and he was bound ov.:r to keep the peace.
