div.head: EARLESTOWN.
div.p: EARLESTOWN.

GOOD TEMPL LEY. —At the meeting of the members of the Hope of Earlestewn Lodge of Good Tempters, on Monday evening, the chair was occupied by Brother John Taylor, W.C.T. Arrangements were made for holding a coffee supper and entertainment. The programme of the evening was" Entel tainment—officers responsible," and in acoardance therewith a selection of songs, recitations, and readings was gilen by the officers of the lodge. Fcratanaa Itnironat AND BURIAL FEES.—The Bishop of idedford, speaking at Carlisle during the Church Congress week, in support of the Church of England Funeral Reform Association, urged that what they wanted to do was to make funerals more bright and hopeful, an rat the same time leesl costly. Now, if the clergy With to reduce funeral expenses they have the means of effecting that object largely in their own hands—namely, by surrendering their often exorbitant fees for the opening of graves, and for the erection of head- stones, railings, &re. That would be funeral reform of a very practical kind, and would be generally approved.—The Liberator. DISCHARGE OF MEN FROM THE VIADUCT WORES.—The continued depression in trade has been seriously felt in Earlestown, and more especially has this been the case at the Viaduct Works, belonging to the London and North- Western Railway Company. From these works over 100 men have recently been discharged or will leave this week end. The "shop" principally affected are the joiners', spring, and smiths', and in some caeca men who hey been In the employ of the company for a good many years have been compelled to give up their situations. Considerable sympathy has been manifested by toe remaining workmen for the unfortunate individuals who have had to leave through no fault of their OHO. GIME TRE4PASS.—James Flayee was SumtnOnea at the Newton Town Hall on Saturday, before Messrs. George McCorquodale, R. Houghton, and C. Pilkington, for tree- pa,sing in search of game on land at Burtonwood, beklaging to Thomas Stone. James Hill, gamekeeper, stated that he saw the defendant with four others on Mr. Stone's land on the 9,11 March last. They had nets "set," and when they saw witness the defendants ran away. one of them had since been tined 20s and costs, and he had identified the de- fendant as one of the ether men who were on the land. The defendant pleaded not guilty, remarking that he was only watching the men, and was not trying to catch the game.—He was fined 20s and costs. THE EARLESTOWN WESLEYAN SLEPDAY SCHOOL—The annual meeting of the teachers and officers in connection with the Wesleyan Methodist Sunday School, Cross-lane, Eariesfown, was held on Thursday evening, under the presi- dency of the Rev, J. M. Fairbourne, resident minister. The at- tendances of the officom and teachers during the past year were briefly considered, after which Mr. Thomas Clare (librarian) read his annual report, showing that nearly 800 , volumes had been taken out of the Brey during the year, which was a slight increase on the previous 12 months. There was a good balance of funds in hand in connection with the library. ihe Band of Hope Becretary (Mr. John R. Barr) read his report, showing the work of the past year. He recommended the Band of Hope to the more energetic co-operation of the teachers of the school, and referred to the institution of a senior band bf hope. The election of officers was then proceeded with, Mr. Barr (superintendent) being re-elected, while Mr. T. Clare was appointed superin- tendent in place of Mr. J. Roberts. Mr. P. Parr having de- clined Is again accept the post of secretary, Mr. b. Barrett was appointed. Oniaaw RECITAL AT NEWTO/L—A. large corpgrega. tion assembled in the Congregational Church, Crow-lane, Newton, on Thursday evening, when Mr. W. 11. Jude, the well-known musician of Liverpool, gave the second of a series of organ recitals in aid of the organ fund. 51r. Suale'a selections were as follows:—" Coronation March " (Meyer- her), andante, with variations (Haydn). Lemmen's fantasia " Tbe Storm", Wely's "Grand Offertoire," Bach's. andante and fugue, and Beethoven's chorus "Hallelujah to the Father." The performance was a masterly one, and. those present highly appreciated the display of the fine abilities of Mr. Jude. The most attractive item on the programme was Lemmen's fantasia, "The Storm," the rolling and reverberating thunder in which, was brilliantly executed. During an interval, the Rev. James Allatt entered the pulpit and announced that the next organ recital would be given on the 15th January. He added that he need hardly say that there was still a debt of £B4 on the new organ, and they hoped, if not to clear it off altogether during the winter, to at least reduce it considerably. A col- lection was then made.

Tnn EARLESTOWN Gosrwr. lilissrow.—ln aid of the rand for purchasing a new harmonium to be used at the services in the Co-operative Hall, Earle-street, in connection with the Earkstown Gospel Mission, a concert was given in the Co-operative Hall on Saturday evening. Mr. C. Ashton presided, and said the committee desired to make it known that the lines upon which their mission was conducted were that there was no rivalry existing between them and other churches. Every denomination WAS represented from time to time in conducting the Sabbath services, and the force of effort which the mission commanded was diverted into a direction which none of the other churches took. It was thought, therefore, that the churches should regard the es- tablishment of a mission like that as a source of strength, increase, and power. The money required to purchase the harmoninm was £25, and they hoped that with the proceeds of that meeting and the probability of similar engagements in future, the money would be raised.—The concert was then proceeded with, the programme being a pleasingly varied one. The artistes were :Miss Jennie Roberts, Mr. and Mrs. Gee. Mr. Picking, Mr. Jones, Mr. Scott (Liver- dool). Miss Jackson (Earleatown), and Miss Hart (Go!. borne).

"A VISIT TO THE BATTLEFIELD OF SEDAN." On Monday evening the Rev. P. Haim', of Liverpool, delivered a lecture before a good audience at the Viaduct Institute, Earlestown, on the above subject. The Rev. J. Allatt presided and briefly introduced the lecturer, who said that in 1870, being incapacitated in consequence of a severe accident from performing his duties in his own church, he was ordered lav his medical advisers to go abroad, and he went for four months to Brosssls and undertook the chaplaincy of Mal Ms. He was there during the whole month of September, and they would remember that it was during September that the battle of Sedan was fought. At the latter end of that month himself and some persons staying at an hotel at Brussels determined to under- take an expedition to the battlefield of Sedan, the battle of which was fought about a fortnight before, in order to in- vestigate for themselves the circumstances and facts sur- rounding tkat contest concerning which such diversities of opinion had arisen. He then proceeded to relate how he and the small party of travellers compassed that desire, describing .the route taken and the chief characteristics of the journey in ready and graphic terms—a route for many a long mile so dreary that the only relief to the mo- notony was the occasional meeting of carts and ambulances containing the wounded and the dying, and a journey full of exciting interest, if not to say lively peril. Although matters of history were dealt with the rev. gentlemen de- tailed the various scenes connected with the battle, its deso- lating effects and terrible destruction, in a vivid manner; and at the same time narrated the adventures of himself and travelling friends—one a Lancashire man and the life of the party—in a way that could not fail to interest, and at times, notwithstanding the seriousness of the subject, to amuse —At the close a hearty vote of thanks was accor- ded to Mr. Heins

By that means they would know their correct position on 'matters of that sort.—Mr. Gillespie had greet pleasure in seconding the motion, which wee.passed. The Chairman then asked Dr. Watkins if he would give them some information with regard to the health of the township and the present state of the fever.—Dr. Watkins said that in the first instance the mortality for the last two months, he was grieved to ten them, had been very high in- deed. In the month of October there were 27 deaths, 5 under 1 year. 7 over lan under 5, a over 5 and under 15 4 over 25 end under 60, 5. over 601 In the month there were 37 deaths ; 3 under 1 year, 18, over 1 and under 5, 8 over 5 and under 15, lover 15 and under 25,4 over 25,4 over 25 and under 60, 3 over 60. From aymotic dieeases there was 1 death froin measles in October, and 12 in November; from scarlet fever 7 in October and 8 in November ; from croup there was 1 death in October ; from bronchitis, pneu- monia, and pleurisy there were 3 deaths in October, 1 in November, and 2 from consumption in October. From other diseases there were 7 deaths under 5 years of age, and 6 over 5 in October ; and there were 6 deaths under 5 years of age and 7 over sin November. The deaths hod thus been 64, which was at the annual average rate of 33 11 per 1,000 oft the population.—Mr. Emmett That is tremendoue.—The Chairman s Yes, it is nearly double what it was.—Dr Wat- kins (continuing) said he would now give the'statement as to the scarlet fever. Of the notified cases there were 25 miles and 31 females, total 59. The ages were:— Under 5 years 20, 5 years and upwards 37; age not stated 2. Of these 11 were under 5 years of age, and 23 above 5 years ; there being 5 deaths, of which 5 were under 5 years of age, and three above. The summary showed total cases as fol- lows: Notified 59, non-notified 34, total 93. The total deaths notified were 14, non-notified 8, making 22. Regard- ing the distribution of the fever, there had been 11 cases in Sankey-street, 4 in Crown-street, 5 in Legh-street, 6 in Via- duct-street, 3 in Crow-Lens, 1 in teeleee-eteeet 9 in Earle. street, west of Sankey-street, 6, itt`Earle-at eat, east of Sate- key-street,. 3 in Haydockettreet, 4 in Chandos-street, 2 in Rathbone-street, S in Houghten-street, I in Lord-street, 5 in Lewrence-street, 4 in Derby-street, 6 in Wood-street, 2 in Regent-street, 1 is Booth-street, 1 in Prinoe's-street, sat Newton Common, 6at the Vulcan, and 5 at Newton, total 93. This they would see taking Earlestown, the remark- able fact that there was the most serious visitation in what they might call the better part of .Earlestowne-Colonel George Mc Corquolale asked if the doctor could give any particular reason for such a mortality.—Dr. Wateins : No, sir. It has jest been disseminated by personal centact.— Mr. Emmett said that only showed the advisability of re- placarding the town with the precautions about scarlet fever. He would give Mr. Brierley permission to post bills on the front of the works in Earle-street and no doubt he (Mr. Brierley) could get permission from Mr, AVeline tO post them on eerttin parts of cottage preperiy beiongine to the company. He (Mr. Emmett) would do all he possibly could in the matter for he thought it was desirable that everything possible should be done to stamp it out. —Mr. Gillespie asked if it was not desirable to send a few copies of the placard to each of the public wores in the district. That would be a good way to dieseminate the information. —The Chairman: Certainly; I think so.—Mr. Emmett said he would propose that a copy of the placard lee for- warded to each house where fever existed, that copies be sent to each of the works in the disttict, and that further placards be posted throughout the town.—Mr. Hunt seconded the motion, which was passed unanimously.—The Chairman (to Dr; Watkins): Is there anything you can suggest that would mitigate the fever P—Dr. Watkins said the question of closing the schools had arisen, but he did not think if that course was adopted that it would interfere with the way in which it was spread. He explained that it was spread by personal contact, and if the schools were closed the children would play about with the same cere- lessness.—Colonel George McCot quoelale said the only thing was to keep children in an infected house from attending sehool.—The question then dropped.
NEWTON COMMISSIONERS: MONTFILY MEETING.

The monthly meeting of the Newton Improvement Com- missionere was held at the Town Hall, Newton, on Monday afternoon, when there were present: Mr. W. F. Gooch (chairman), Lieut.-Colonel George McCorquodale, J.P., Messrs T. J 1 Gillespie, J.P., T. Stone, B. B. Glover, Thomas Runt, J. W. Emmett. R. Brierley (surveyor), and Dr. J. W. Watkins (medical officer of benlith).—The minutes of the last meeting were read and confirmed. THE Assimcs OF THE Law Csassx.—Mr. Brierley read a letter from Mr. J. W. Worsley (law clerk) stating that he was unable to attend that meeting as be was away ha Loa- don on business connected with the Board.

HIGHWAY AND SANITARY COM111.1"/BE.—At a meeting of this committee on the 17th ult it was stated that notices having been served for the ab dement of nuieances on pre- mises at Wargrave and in High-street, Newton, it WAS or- dered that summonses be Issued if the nuisances were not abated within seven days. Plans for two cottages at War- grave for William Lawson were eubmittad and approved-- The minutes were passed. THE NEW Cmagrani.—The Highways, Public IVerks, sad Sanitary Cemmitteeheld a meeting on the 17th Novem- ber, at which the following candidates for the situation of cemetery keeper, &c., were before the committee, viz. : Mesas. Kettle, Langley, and Boothroyde. Mr. John Kettie, of Tarvin, was ultimately selected for the situation.—Mr. Brierley reported that the Special Committee had divided the-order for trees and shrcbs for the cemetery with Messrs. Stead and Son, of Bold, G. Hilton, Jan., Newton-le-Willows, and R. Boardman, of Lowton ; and that a practical gardener (Mr. Holmes) hid been engaged to do the planting. This- was approved by the committee. It was ordered that the oftler of the bell formerly in St. Peter's Church, by Mr. Gillespie for £5, be accepted, and that the bell be fixed at the cemetery chapel.—The Surveyor having certidad that the sum of £I,SO was due to Mr. J. Bothwell, on his contract for the cemetery buildings, a cheque for that amount was ordered to be signed.—The minutes were conSrmed. Mr- Brierley afterwards suggested the ap- pointment of a special committee to go into the queotion of grave-sites, and the charges and regulations connected therewith.—The Chairman said the time was getting on for- it to be done.—Mr. Hunt said the thing meet be pushed on. During the last fortnight they had had 18 funerals at Wargrave church, and the ground at disposal WAS now very limited. If something was not done socn.they would have to apply to the bishop before the new cemetery was opened. Mr. Brierley remarked that that was why he wished to have the cemetery pushed on and the fees fixed.—Mr. Hunt subsequently moved that the whole et the members of the. Board be constitu- ted a special committee to deal with the question, and Mr. Stone seconded the motion, which was passed.

Scnoon. A.TTENDANCE.—The School Attendance Com- mittee held a meeting on the 17th•nitime. at which the School Attendance Officer read his report. His new register of attendances as far as completed was examined by the Chairman (Mr. Pardey). Many absences being attributed to the spread of scarlet fever and measles at Earlestown, it was resolved to invite the attention of the Sanitary Corn- mittee to the deeirability of closing the schools in the dis- trict. In reply to a communication from Miss Paterson, of the District Schools at Earlestown, it was ordered that she be informed that no complaint has been made to, or by the committee of bad management on her part, bat that the attention Of the trustees of the schools had been called to the need for more teachers and additional school accommodation.—Mr. Emmett, said there was one. matter he would like to mention. He had asked Mr. Matthews to give him an epitome of the Deed Trust of the infant school at Earlestownond he also asked Mr. Worsley to do the same, as Mr. Matthews told him he (Mr. Worsley) had that in his possession. He (Mr. Mnmett) had since got what he wanted, and had sent it to the chairman of the London and North-Western Railway Company, and he still had it in his possession.—The Chair- man: lam glad to hear it, for there will aomething be done ,to increase the school accoraraodation.

THE LOWTON WATER QUESTION ANTI THE ALLEGED "BAD " ass.—A meeting of the Gas and Water Commit. tee was held on the 17th November, at which the follow- ing letter in reference to the Lawton Junction water sup- ply was read :—" Crewe, October 25th, 1884. Water supply, Lowten Junction. Gentlemen, I laid your letter of the 22nd ult, before my direcfrrs, and they are willing that you should have a two.inch connection made to their main at Low ton Junction on the condition that you pay the cost of making the connection, 61 per I,GOO gallons of the water used with a minimum charge of 10t3 per quarter, and the usual meter rent, the supply to be continued so long as they have water to spare, and there is no other authority able or willing to do so. Yours truly, F. W. Webb."—lt was ordered that the foregoing terms be accepted on condition thit the Bedford Brewery Company- agree to pay one half the coat of connections and meter hire, and the full mini- mum charge of 10a per quarter for the water. The carbon- izing account of the past month give fuel used 279 tons 1 nen, gas made 2,805,100 cubic feet, averaging 10,052 feet per ton of fuel used, the illuminating quality of the gas being equal to 21 candles at the works. Mr. Glover stated that at the last meetbig Mr. Brierley was asked to take tests of the quality of gas and examine the fittings of the houses from which complaints had been re• ceived as to the gas. He would like to know what Mr. Brierley had ascertained.—Mr. Brierley stated that at the house of Mr. Fardey the pipes were foued choked up more

or less, while the gas at Mr. Gillespie's house had been tested and found to equal 20 candles. The fittings were overhauled with the result that a larger pipe was put down, and Mr. Gillespie would himself tell them whether he was now satisfied or not.—Mr. Gillespie said he had very great pleasure in stating that since their last meeting Mr. Brier- ley and amother man had thoroughly overhauled the pipes acid burners, end the lizht had been much more satisfac• t ry.—Mr. Glover, as the chairman of the Gas Committee, said he had ascertaLled from a statement as to the quality of gas supplied to neighbouring towns that the people in Newton were being supplied with'a better quality than any other town, and Etta considerably less cast, even in com- parison with large r,owns.

meeting of the Finance Committee was held on the 17th ;At, at which accounts amounting to ME) 6s were read and °bellies signed for payment.—The minutes of the committee were passed. This was the only business of interest.

div.head: WESLEYAN METHOD'S T FOREIGN
div.p: WESLEYAN METHOD'S T FOREIGN

Special sermons, on behalf of the W.rsley an F)reign Missio,ns, ivere preached in the Wes- leyan Methodist Chapel, Cross-lane, Earlestowo, on Sunday. The morning preacher was the Rev. George Smith, of St. Helens, and in the evening the pulpit was occupied by the Rev. J. M. Fairbonsn, resident minister. Though the weather was very unfavourable the services were comparatively well attended. Collections were made in aid of the Mission Fund.

Tne annual puldic meeting was held in the chapel on Wednesday evening, when there was a large congregation. The chair was occupied by Councilor Foster, of St. Helens, and he Was supported by the Rev, J. Shlpham (Superintendent minister of the circuit). the Rev. H. J. Sykes., of Wigan, formerly missionary in India, the Rev. J. M. Fairbourn, and Mr. Thomas Browa, of St. Helens (dis- trict secretary). After the meeting had been opened with singing and prayer, the Chairman remarked that he WAS pleased to be present, and he hoped they would have a verY successful meeting.—Mr. Thomas Brown then read a por- tion of the anneal report, from which it appeared that the income during the last year was £150,106 16a 54, whilst the expenses were £150,161 17s, leaving a deficiency for the year of £55 Os 7d. Towards that amount the St. Helens circuit coatrihuted the sum of £223 16e lid, which • was an increase over the previous ye ir of £A 41 Eld, and of that increase £3 7s 1.1 had to be placei to the credit of Eerlestown. Last year Earlestown raised £44 7s 14. The pubec lotions amounted to £lO 8i 43, juvenile association £44 161 24 (one half of which was devoted to the Home Mission Fund), public coll:ctions £ll 10s 81. As would be seen from the report, the juveniles were very active in helping forward the mission cause, the total raised through- out the circuit by the efforts of the juveniles being £213 131 lid. There was another branch which ought not to be ignored and that Was the Ladies auxiliary RI promotlug Chrietien education amongst women and children throughout the various mission fields. The amount raised In connection therewith was £4,644 Os 41, and it was otherwise doing a good and useful work. (Applause )—The Chairman said he was glad to hear that the Earlestown friends were doing so much to help forward the missionary cause. They had met to hear something of the missions in other bade, and to have their sympithies broadened and deepened: and he trusted that the hearty enthusiasm of former days might speedily be revived. If there was not the same amount of eetbusiasm and earnestness that there formerly was he was still glad to find that the prac!ical part of the work was still left behind. The church had a great duty to perform in relation to missienary enterprise, and the more the indi- vidual membere of the Church reeegnised their own indi- vidual duty the more interest they would take in that great work. He pointed out the difficulties under wh'ea the missionaries laboured, and said that the people in other lands were calling upon them to lift them up from the heathenism in which they were. Though much had been accomplished there was yet a great deal to be done, and It would take a long time to do it. (Applause.)—After Miss Eckereley had sung a nice solo, the Rev. J. Shipham ad- dressed the meeting. He was confident that the best way to secure commercial prosperity and prosperity of every kind was for the people to be workers together with God, and especially in that great work they had met to further that evening. (Applause.)—Miss C. Roberts then nicely sang "I know that my Redeemer liveth."—The Rev. H. J. Sykes, of Wipe, said all the great missionary societies of the world had turned their at- tention to India, besides which the Bible and tract societies and special educational societies were trying to improve that great continent. There were men of all creeds meeting to preach the great central truths of the Gospel, and they were not meeting any longer to contend ae rivals for empire, but to win India for the Lord Jesus Clerist. (Applause.)— A collection in aid of the missionary society was then made, and Miss Sykes excellently sang "Not lost, but gone be- fore."—On the motien of the Rev. J. M. Fairbourne thanks were accorded to the Rev. H. J. Sykes and the chairman, and the meeting concluded with the singing of the Dox- ology.

SCARLET FEI ER EPIDE MC AT EARLESTOWN.
EXTRAORDINARY MORTALITY.

The ontbreak of scarlet fever at Earlestown has turned out to be much more serious than was at first anticipated. An importeet discussion in reference to the outbreak took plaoe at the monthly meeting of the Newton Improvement Commissioners on Monday afternoon, when there were pre- sent Messrs. W.. F. Gooch (chairman), George McCorquo- dale, T. J. Gillespie, B. R. Glover, T. Stone. T. Hunt, J. W. Emmett, R. Srierley (surveyor), and Dr. J. W. Watkins (medical officer of health.) After the reading of the minutes of the previous meeting, Mr. Emmett rose and said he had a question or two to ask with reference to the scarlet fever. The first was-, what number of placards with regard to the fever question and warning the public were posted ? —Mr. Brierley: About a dozen and others were sent to public places, such as news-rooms and clubs.—Mr. Emmett said the reason why he asked the question was that be had looked very carefully in all, the places where he expected to find a placard, but he had never been able to see one. He had made many inquiries and he could only hear of one having been seen anywhere. Seeing that the fever had been. very bad he thought more than a dozen ought to have been posted. What was a dozen for a place like Earles- town ? It looked like doing nothing. If the thing was worth doing at all it ought to be dane well—Mr. Brierley stated that there were very few private posting places in the town, and people would not allow the-placards to be posted.—Mr. Emmett said that if he had been asked he would have got permission to have the bills posted On the property of the London and North Western Railway Company all over the town. As it was he had never seem a bill, and it was not likely he would do so long as only a dozen were posted.— Mr. Hen, remarked that there was one in the porch of War- grave Church.—The Chairman They will be posted in all places of worship?—Mr. Brierley : Yes. The billposter had orders to post them where he could. There was no limit to the placards.—The Chairman remarked that a dozen seemed very few for a township like Newton,— Mr. Emmett moved that more placards be posted in places where the people ceuld see them, and not hid under a bushel.—Mr. Stone seconded the motion, which was passed. —The matter then dropped until the minutes of the High- way and Sanitary Committee were read, when it appeared that at a. meeting of that committee on the 17th ultimo, the Clerk salamitted an amount of the Warrington Corporation for the maintenance of George Harris's family at the Infec- tious Hospital amounting to EM Os. 4d.. and stated that Mr. Sutton, Clerk to the Union, repudiated their liability to pay the amount. It was ordered that Mr. Sutton be seen upon the claim, and that "in all future cases of infectious diseases in the district, requiring hospital accommodation, that our-medical officer be requested to order kas represent- ing the Commissioners) the removal only of such patients as are in a position and willing to pay for medical aid, nursing and maintenance in tbi hospital, and that in future no patient who is not in a posi6an to pay for such medical aid, etc., be removed unless such medical certificate is accompanied with the necessary order from the relieving officer."—With regard to the first part of this minute, Dr. Watkins sail it was rendered perfectly nugatory, for there was no power whatever in England to remove patients to hospital. In reference to the second part, he (Dr. Watkins) had to say that the cases sent to the hospital were decidedly those of paupers. He presumed that Baard would contest the payment of the amount demanded. On the 2nd Auamst, being in Earlestown, he heard of three or four cases of scarlet fever in one house in Earlestown—the children of lodgers there. The men was out of work and quite destitute, and he (Dr. Watkins) felt it his duty—it mattered not whether he went as the medical officer of health or as a parochial oflicer—for it was clear to anyone with common sense that it was a case for the immediate re- moval of the children, and they were removed to the hospital. The case simply rested there, but he thought be would have been guilty of a gross neglect of duty if he did not attend the case at once, and not quibble and wait for a parochial order. He hoped the matter would be amicably adjusted between that Board and the Board of Guardians.— The Chairman stated that the Board wished to know before any future removal took place if the parties would pay the expense.—Dr. Watkins said that the case in question was very much like a fire which they could put out with a bucketful of water, but which if let alone mia,dat destroy the whole town. He had simply put on the bucketful of water.—Mr. Gillespie remarked that it had been at the expense of the Newton Commissioners.--Dr. Watkins : I have nothing to do with that.—Mr. Hunt ex- plained that with regard to the terin pauper it simply im- plied that a person had made application to the relieving officer. If the doctor, when he saw the patient required im- mediate attention had sent a messenger to the relieving officer for an order, then the person would have been a

div.head: ALLEGED, FRAUDS BY AN EARLESTOWN WOMAN. . .
div.p: ALLEGED, FRAUDS BY AN EARLESTOWN WOMAN. . .

At the Nevrtoa Sessions, on Saturday. before Messrs. G. McCorquodale R. Houghton,'and C. Mikington, Sarah Ann Walton M. Haskins, a married woman, residing in Regent. street, Earlestown, was cbarg.d with obtaining the sum of 3s by false petenoes from Mr. B. F. Kelly, tobacconist, Queen-street,. Earlestown.—The prosecutor stated that on Tuesday, tba 25th October, the prisoner came into his shop and said she had been to the grocer's for her groceries, but when she got there she found she had forgot her purse. She asked him(,psosecutor) if he would lend her 3s, whereupon he replied4hat he did not know her. She said her husband knew him (prosecutor) very well, and her name was Mrs. Barton.,aad she resided at the Vulcan. She again aged prosecutor to oblige her with 35 as it was a long way to go back for her money, and the prosecutor said he dill not know hoe name, but he would let her have the money as he knew her features. He accordingly banded over 33 to .her, and :the promised to pay it on the Friday. She called again the next day and again asked him to lend her a shilling, but Ise refused.—Superintendent Jackson: I am told that the woman has been getting sums in a similar way from dilerent tradesmen, and I would ask von to remand her to some future day in ordsr that further inquiries might be made.—The defendant was then remanded to the Warring- ton County Petty Sessions.—The husband of the defendant stated that he would be responsible for her appearance, and she was allowed cut on bill. . .

At an Occasional Court, held at Mr. Buckton's office, in Horsemarket-etreet, on Wednesday, Mrs Haskins (Earlestown) was charged before Mr. Maroon, county magistrate, with committing frauds upon Earlestown tradesmen.—Benjulain Kelly, tobacconist, Queen-street, Earlestown, said that on the 28th of October prisoner came to his shop and asked for a loan of two shillings, saying that she had come out to purchase groceries aed had forgotten her purse. She added that her husband purchased his tobacco at that shop, and that he would call and repay the money in the evening. She gave her name as Mrs. Barton, of the Vulcan. Witness lest her three shillings. Next day she called again, and asked for a further loan of three shillings, saying that she would ply it back on the Friday following. She' had, she said, lost her purse, and if her husband found it out he would kill her. Witness declined to lend her the money. A fortnight afterwa-ds he met her in the street and asked her for the money, when she said that she was hard up Then, but would pay it the nest Friday. Subsequently, he went to her house at Batbbone-street, when she admitted that her name was Haskins and not Barton, and he then gave information to the police. Haskins was not a cus- tomer of hid, and the place where the prisoner was living was a mile and a half from the place she mentioned to him, and in a contrary direction.—Tom Ambergate Bell, picture dealer, Earlestown, deposed that prisoner came to his shop on the 28th October and asked for a loan of of 2e 81, atatirg that she had come from home without her purse, and it was a long way to go bock. She gtve her name as Mrs. Barton, of Newton, and said that she and her husband had at d'fferent times paid him a lot of money. He lent her one shillinz.--Prisoner, against whom there was a further charge of defrauding a man named Pugh, was remanded for week, bail 1)025 talliOvrld h her huaband's recognisance&

. . _ SCHOOL ATTENDANCE.—Before Messrs. T. J. Gillespie and A. C. McCorquodale, at the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday last, Ann Carr and Ellis Brown, both of Golbffne, were each tined Si for neglecting to send their children to school, as required by the Elementary Education Act. Tnis CONGREGATIONAL BAZAAR —The Congregational baz jar, which was opened at Golborne last week by Mr. C. Pilkington, J.P„ of Haydock, closed on Saturday evening after having a successful run. The object was to clear the day arid Sunday schools from a debt of agout £lOO, which has been standing over since 1875, when the schools were erected and furnished at a cost of £l,OOO. The gross receipts were £l4l Oa 2,1, the expenses being estimated at £2O. ACCIDENT AT MESSRS. Bawls's MILL.—Two accidents have occurred within the last week at Messrs. Brewis's Got. borne mills. Soon after the machinery started on Tuesday morning a youth named Robert Avery, residing in Leigh- street, had his right hand caught in some carding machinery and three fingers were badly injured. On the previous Thursday a girl named Davies was similarly caught, and bad two fingers badly bruised and torn. Both cases occurred at the " new mill.'

TRESPASSING IN PURSUIT OF GAME. At Leigh, on Monday, William Wonky and John Lythgoe, of Lowton, were charged with trespassing in pursuit of game on land at Kenyon, oo the 14th ult. Mr. Widdows prosecuted. Jas. Clough, of Croft, assistant keeper, and Peter Ball, deposed to seeing the defendants pick up some nets and run away. Woreley stated that be was at Newton at the boar alleged, and Lythgoe said he WAS at home; but they called no wit- nesses, and were each fined 20s and COS/. TIER CONGREGATIONALISTS are to be congratulated on INS success. of their bazaar, which opened on Thursday awd closed on Saturday night. The gross receipts were £l4a There was also a large quantity of fancy articles left for disposal. Amongst those who took part in the "musical evenings' which were given were Miss Lucy Barton, Miss P. Roberts, Miss Jenkinson, Miss S.Travers, Mr. W. Turton and Mr. Sohn Travers (Golberne), the Golloorne Brass Band, Miss Shaw (Oldham), and Misses Martindale (Haydock). ACTION A:I.A/NST A/4 EXECITTOR.-At the last sitting of the Leigh County Court, James Glover' grocer, Golboroe, brought an action against Betsy Whittle to recover the sum of £5O, balance due on shop account—Mr. Calvert, whis appeared far the plaintiff, pointed out that the debt was contracted in Mr. Whittle's time, and when he died he left upwards of,,fl.oo.—The plaintiff was then called, who stated that the articles were generally supplied to the de- fendant. When Mr Whittle died witness as!sed defendant if he had made a will, and she said he had made all to her.— Mr. Brown, for the defence, s tid the account in question was never delivered until after the husband's death, and his client never knew et it.-11 is Honour said there was more than enough to pay the amount sued for, and, he asked the Registrar to go through the items.—This having been done, his Honour gave judgment for £l5 lie 4d, observing that an executrix de Lore tort could not pay her own debts before those of her husband's.

RIVAL ASHTON PEDESTRIANS —RACE FOR 240.—At the Star Inn R,creation Grounds, St. Helens, on Saturday after- noon, the match between William Partington, of Ashton-in- Makerfield, and Samuel Deluce, of Downall Green, to run 135 yards level, for £2O aside, was decided. Partington, who is 23 years of age and sft 9-14 n in height, was trained by Mr. W. Smith of George-street, St. Helens, under the care of F. Lloyd,_ the well-known " ped," whilst Deluce, who is 20 years of age and sft 4in in height, was- prepared by John Lowe. at the Blue Bell Inn, Downall Green. Both men are simply novices, having never previously done any- thing of note; still; their meeting created a good deal of interest, as at least 500 persons were present. Partington, being generally considered to be the more likely of the two to win, was at once made the favourite, odds of 7 to 4 and 2to 1 being freely laid on him. A splendid start was ef- fected, but the shades of evening were falling rapidly when this was accomplished. The favourite at once drew away. He led by about two, yards at the half-distance, and finally won easily by three yards. Mr. T. R. Allison officiated as referee, and Mr. .Ti Pennington, of St. Helens, as starter.

ST. HELENS AND, THE REDISTRIBUTION BILL.—Tho announcement that St. Helens was one of the boroughs to be represented in Parliament under the Redistribution of Seats Bill, introduced by the Government, has this week formed a lively topic of conversation among both political parties. As could only have been expected, the fact has given satisfaction on every hand, and already discussion has been rife as to whom the honour of first representing the borough in Parliament weuld devolve. The remarkable progress of St. Helens in recent years may be judged from the fact that in 1ii1,51 the population was only 28,041, while in 1881 the census returns showed no less than 61,472 in- habitants. Hitherto it has form d a pertion of the South- West Lancashire Division, and there can bo no doubt that the first contest for the representation of the borough would occasion a keen interest. The first reliable informa- tion npn the matter reached the town about noon on Tues- day, when a telegram was received at the Liberal Club from the secretary of the National Lib•ral Club, London, to the cffect that one of the five additional members for South- West Lancashire would probably be for St. Helens. An hour later the welcome news was confirmed hy the following telegram, received from the sante sc-arce :—'• Further examination shows that St. Helens is to be a borough by itself, and to ha reTesented by one member." This intelligence soon spread, and a good deal of speculation was indulged in as to the names of the probable candidates. Amongst the Liberals the name of Colonel Gamble, J.P. president of the St. Helens Liberal Associa- tion, was freely mentioned, though the most popular "can- didate" seemed to be Councillor Richard Pilkington, J.P., of Rainford Hall, who occupies the position of president of the Council of the Liberal Association. No other gentle- men were mentioned as likely to represent tho Liberals of the borough, but as possible Conservative candidates four names were mentioned. They were the Hon.. Wm. Gerard, son of Lord Gerard of Brynn, who would probably secure the Catholic vote—a very strong one in St. Helens; Mr. William Pilkington, J.P., of Roby Hail, president of the St. Helens Conservative Association; the ex-Mayor of St. Helens, Mr. Henry Baxter, J.P. ; and Mr, Thomas Swift, barrister-at-law, St. Helens and Liverpool. -

WARRINGTON AND THE SHIP CANAL RATE. RESULT OF THE POLL. The poll of the ratepayers with a view to obtaining their opinion as to the proposal to assist the promo- tion of the Manchester Ship Canal out of the rates concluled at noon on Saturday last. The count was then proceeded with in the presence of the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) and a number of other gentle- men. The counting was done by a large staff of clerks, and the papers were gone through three times. The final result was as follows For the rate 6,355 • Against

Majority in favour ...... 5,840 About 7. 7c voting papers had been delivered, and of those 7,40 were accounted for. There were 5V papers of no Effect, including those spoilt, invalid, and blank—the latter numbering over 500.—The 3114y0r having declared the result, Dr. MICIIII3 said he thought they would all be pleased at the ex- ;haustive vote that had been given. It was gratify- iing to know that after taking away the number of 1 those papers returned blank ° they had still an ex- !pression of feeling on the part of the ratepayers of Warrington which did both sides the very highest credit. He would have been deeply mortified if the opposition to the rate had been of a merely nominal kind. His own convic- tion was, and the figures would bear him out, that all had been done that could be done on both sides, and that being so they might now safely appeal to their friends on the other side to bury the hatchet and determine to carry out what was the evident will of the people. (Hear, hear.) He knew of nothing that could be more gratifying to.the fair- itlinded people of Warrington than a vote of the kind which had been taken, for they thus saw that several thousands of their humblest fellow-citizens had wil- lingly signed the papers, not to tax others merely, but themselves. He looked upon this as an excellent specimen of what they might fairly expect in the future if there were any other project on foot tending to bless the town. If such ever happened they need never be afraid of throwing the matter upon the ratepayers under the guidance of the Town Coar.cil. He moved a vote of thanks to the Mayor.—Couacillor Roman seconded this vote of thanks, and said that he felt with Dr. Mackie that the result of the poll was a matter of the utmost importance to Warrington, and that he looked forward to the day when the Ship Canal Scheme would be carried to a successful con- clusion. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. GE,OI2E WOODS and Mr. LAwanttox supported the resolution, the latter coup- ling with it the name of Mr. Whittle, deputy town clerk —The MAYOI2, in responding, said that he had religiously adhered to impartiality, and he was glad his conduct had given satisfaction. He believed that if any opponents of the scheme bad been present they would have been perfectly satisfied with the way the proceedings had been conducted. (Hear, hear.)—Dr. MACICIII seconded the vote of thanks to the deputy town clerk, who having briefly responded, the pro• eteedings terminated. SPECIAL ME STING OF THE TOWN COUNCIL.

THE RATE CAilliils. A special meeting of the Warrington Town Council was held at the Town Hall on Monday evening to consider, and if thought expedient, to approve of and direct the promo- tion by the Mayor, aldermen, and burgesses of the borough of Warrington, in conjunction with others, of a local and personal bill in Parliament for the purpose of incorporating a company, and empowering such company to construct a canal from the river Mersey to the city of Manchester, na vigable for ocean steamers and ships of large burthen, and 10 the contribution out of the borough rate the Cost of such promotion of a sum not eneeding twopence in the pound upon the annual rateable value of the borough. The Mayor Oldermatt II irison) presided, and there were also present Aldermen lltiig,eo, Cbandley, Holmes, Pickmei e, and Web- ster ; Councillors J. Croslield, Ashton, Barker, Bohm Brown, Burgess, Dakin, Dixon, Francomb, Fleming, Hutch- inson, Litton, Dr. Mackie, Marsh, J. Pierpoint, W. Pier- point, Roberts, Sutton, Taylor, Tinsley, Whittle, and Wright ; and Messrs. W. H. Brook (town clerk), Whittle (deputy town clerk), Chorley (borough treasurer), and Longdin (borough surveyor). The MAYOR proposed the resolution. Councillor J. PIERPOINT, in seconding it, said that the public had spoken almost unanimously on the question of the rate, and he thought it behoved the Council not to mis- represent their constituents. He thought it their duty to confirm the opinion of the public 'as expressed at the poll.

- Alderman CHANDLEY supported the resolution. It was, he said, their boun,ten duty in that chamber to represent the feeling of the ratepayers. The only course for the Coun- cil to pursue was to confirm the opinion of the public and pass the rate._

• Alderman WEBSTER did not think the Council had power to vote one way or the other. They had obtained coun- sel's opinion, which was that, not being promoters of the Bill, they bad no power to subscribe anything. The power given by the Borough Funds Act was for the promotion of something specially relating to the borough, and not the contribution to the expense of promotion by other parties of a bill only incidentally affecting the Corporation. He did not think they were at present promoters, and asked the opinion of the Town Clerk on that point. The TOWN CIERIE thought that Alderman Webster had misunderstood the resolution, which approved of the pro- motion of the bill and went on to say that twopence in the pound be contributed towards the expense of that promo- tion.

Aid. WEBSTER contended that a resolution should be carried constituting the Council promoters of the bill. If the opinion of counsel was of any value, he said, it would set aside what proceedings might take place that night. The idea of increasing the rates to assist a private speculation was to him altogether unprecedented. At the present time the rates of the borough were seriously high, and tended to make manufacturers pause before they settled in the borough. He. had no feeling of opposition to the Ship Canal, they had given it every legitimate support,cbut had 30 right to assist it out of the rates.

Councillor W. PIERPOINT asked the town clerk if, in the event of the Council sanctioning the rate, and if the bill was rejected, could any contributor compel restitution of the amount he had paid on account of the rate, and would the members of the Council be personally liable. The TOWN CLERK said that his opinion was that they would not be personalty liable. The Council could join iu the promotion of a bill as long as it was in any way in the interests of the town. Counsel's opinion was based upon the fact that the bill bad been promoted, but the circumi- stances as they were at present were that it had not been promoted, and that the Council were joining in the promo- tion. The contribution would not make them members of the company, but as far as the case of the promoters was coneerned they would be-liable beyond the contribution un- less they had souse indemnity against any further expenses, and the promoters of the canal proposed to give- them an agreement to indemnify them against any further lia- bility.

Alderman HOLMES regarded the bill as a private enter- prise, and did not think that the Council had any right to expend money on its promotion. He could not therefore vote for the Mayor's resolution. Alderman BURGESS said that when the bill became an Act of Parliament the promoters would be desirous that the whole matter should be trade into a public trust for the good of the general public. Councillor CnosviEr.n.took the same view of the ques- tion as Sid Alderman flocarEs, and be did so conscien- tiously. He felt that it would be a dangerous thing to set a precedent of that sort. Councillor Malan thoaght that the Council should carry out the expressed wish of the ratepayers. Alderman PICKMERE did not think the scheme entirely a private concern,as it was a national question. The canal, if formed, would benefit in time almost the whole of Eng- land. Warrington would no doubt benefit largely by the scheme, and therefore it became Warrington to amist the promoters. He thought at first that to levy a rate might be wrong, bnt when there was such a majority of the rate- payers-in favour of it be thought they could not do less in the Council than support the views of the majority. Councillor BURGESS. and Councillor Romtnrs.enpported the resolution, the latter remarking that their constituents indemnified them by their unanimous vote, and personally, they took no liability, because they were indemnified by the offer from Manchester with reference to the £l,OOO. The MAYOR said that it must be distinctly underatood that if they paid the £1,030 they did not thereby become share- holders In the canal. Their only responsibility was in the expense of promotion. The guarantee given them by gentlemen in Manchester was the same that had been accepted by Manchester and Salford, and he thought they might fairly commit themselves to what those towns had not hesitated, to do. He believed that if the canal was made Warrington would derive an immense advantage from it. If the contribution was not legal the Local Government Board would never sanction it, which in itself was a suffi- cient guarantee.

The resolution was then put with the following result : For—The Mayor, Aid. Burgess, Pick mere, and Chandley, and Councillors Dakin, Burgess, Brown, Barker, Holton, Hutchin- tion, Fleming, Tinsley, J. Pierpoint, Dr. Mackie, Sutton, Wright, Roberts, Litton, Francarob, Marsh, Taylor, and Ashton (22) t. against—Aldermen Holmes and Webster (2). Coancillors .Crosfield and W. Pierpoint declined to vote.

Twit TORQUAY MURDER.—rhe lengthy inquiry by a coroner's jury into the murder of Mies Keyse near Torquay terminated on Monday. The only witness called was Dr. Stevenson, analyst to the Mome Office, who had examined some clothing taken from the deceased and from tho pri- soner Lee, and found bloodstains upon the articles. He also detected traces of mammalian blood upon a table-kntfe with which it is alleged that Lee cut his mistress's throat after fracturinz her skull with a hatohet. The jury returned a verdict of " Wilful murder " against Lee, who was there- upon committed Zr trial at the assizes. On Wednesday, Lee was further magisterially examined. The testimony given at the inauest was repeated, and the Bench signified their intention Co commit the prisoner for trial. On Thurs- day Lee was formally committed for trial for the murder of Miss lisyse and for setting fire to a house. The prifouer, who appeared in good spirits, reserved his defence,

THE Poon SMIGEON.—A prince of medical science ad- vised one of his patients to submit to a surgical operation- "is it painful?' inquired the sufferer. "Not to the patient," replied the doctor, "but very much to the operator." "To the operator !" ' Yes; because it is an experiment that ie successful only once in ninety times." Dumley had accompanied a friend home to dinner, and, ne they seated themselves at the table, the hostess remarked,' "I trust that you will make allowances, Mr. Darnley. MY servant left me this morning very unexpectedly, and I Wee . compelled to cook the dinner myself." " Oh, certainly', ref dear madam, certainly," responded Durnler, with much ern' pressement, "I can put up with anything." On the occasion of the distribution of medals to ofilcets and men who had served in the Crimea, Lord Malinesburi tells us that Mrs. Norton, talking about it to Lord Panmate,; asked, " Was the Queen touched ?" "Bless my soul no was the reply, "She had a brass railing before her, and Pe one could touch her." Mrs: Norton then said, "I mean vit't she moved ?" " Moved !" answered Lord Pannaure. "She had no occasion to move." Mrs. Norton then gave it up hl despair.

A Pattosorana.—A Little Rock man sold his cooklng. stove to get money enough to take his family to the drone' • When one of his friends remonstrated with him, he said "We had no use for the stove. Hid nothing to cook." "That why didn't you bay something to eat with the money Yes got for the stove?" "Then we would have nothing to cool it on. Don't talk to me. I'm a philosopher." E11131017E8 OF THE BATTLE-FIELD —During the American Civil War many humorous incidents occurred on the battle- fields, says the Cenhtry. A Confederate colonel ran ahead of his regiment at Malvern Hill, and, discovering that the men were not following him as closely as he wished he uttered a fierce oath, and exclaimed, "Come on! Do '9oe, want to live for ever ?" The appeal was irreoistible, on" many a poor fellow who had laughed at the colonel's epleel exhortation laid down his life soon after. A shell struee the wheel of a Federal field-piece towards the close of the engagement at Fair Oaks, and, shivering the spokes, dis- mantled the canon. "Well, isn't it lucky that didn't hap Pee before we used up all our ammunition ?" remarked one of the artillerists, as he crawled from bereath the gun. column of troops was pushing forward over the long an" winding road in Thoroughfare Gap to head off Lee after his retreat across the Potomac at the close of the Gettesburg campaign. Suddenly the signal officer who accompanied the general in command discovered that some of his men, posted on a high hill in the rear, were reporting the presence of a considerable body of Confederate troops on the top of the bluffe to the right. A halt was at once sounded, and the leading. brigade ordered forward to uncover the enemy,e position. The regiments were soon scrambling up the steep incline, officers and men gallantly racing to see who could reach the crest first. A young lieutenant and sonie half-dozen men gained the top; but, at the end of what theY deemed a perilous clim'a, they were thrown into convulsiona of langleter at discovering that what the signal-men took for Confederate troops were only a tolerably large flock of shesP• As the leaders in this forlorn hope rolled oh the grass in a paroxysm of merriment, they laughed all the louder at eeeing the pale but determined faces of their comrades, who. of course, came up fully expecting a. desperate hand-to-hand struggle. It is perhaps needless to say the brigade supPea', ore mutton that evening. As the army was crossing Soul!), Mountain on the day before the battle of ALtietam, General McClellan rode along the side of the moving column. Over- taking a favonrite Zortave regiment, he ea claimed, witn his natural bahamie, '' Well, and how is the Old Fifth this evening itt" "Firs-rate, general," replied one of the Zouaves. "But we'd he better off if we weren't living s° much on supposition." "Supposition ? " said the general. In a puzzled tone, "What do you mean by that?" "Its easily explained, sir. You see we expected to get oat rations yesterday; but, as we didn't, we're living on th! supposUion that no did." " Ah, I understand You shalf have your rations, Zoo-Zone, to-night," replied the Gt putting spurs to his horse to escape the men's, ckcers. An' he kept his promise.

Disiltyss IN trim ICoarn.—At a meeting of the Sunder hod General Relief Committee, on Tuesday, it was stated that 12,000 men, women, and children are at present being relieved with food and clothing, at a cost of £3OO weekly. The sl,ipbuilding trade showed very slight improvement, and employers are likely to ask for a further reduction of

wages. CARELESSNESS O' A PORTER.—A commercial traveller, engaged in the watch trade, was waiting upon customers at Nottingham, on 'Monday, accompanied by a porter with a handcart containing three parcels of gold and silver watches, valued at about £3;Ckio. While the traveller was in the shop the porter left the handcart for a few minutes, and during his absence it was taken away. Sometime afterwards the cart, containing two of the parcels, was lowed in a by-street, and subsequently a man named McLoughlin was apprehended with the third paicel in his possession. ANOTHER ACTION BY MRS. W2,LDON.—The action by Mrs. Weldon against General Sir H. de Bathe, to recover damages in respect of proceedings connected with the plaintifi'd im- prisonment iR a lunatic asylum, on Monday came before Justices Mathew and Day, on points of law raised. Sir Hardinge Giffard argued for the defendant, principally on points as to the trespass, which involved a question of ownership of residence, and, as to the libel, in signing an order for imptisoismont at the request of the plaintiff's hus- band or of Dr. Winslow. The court gave judgment for Mrs. Weldon on the point as to publication of the libel, and against leer as to the trespass. PATNIML SCENE AT A CHURCI.I.—At Rampton on Sunday, the Vicar returned from a visit to the south, in consequence of the Bishop of the diocese (Reading) having refused to grant the curate in charge a license to preach. On the Vicar demanding the keys of the vicarage, the curate in charge not only refused to hand then. over, but actually locked himself up in the house and barricaded the doors and windoes. The doors were forced open, but it being im- possible to get at the surplice, the congregation assembled in the church, repaired to the school room, where the Vicar conducted service. CONVERSATIONAL ENGLISH.—What Interesting and helper- I tant info wallop, often passes as word currency, and c inverse ' upon topics in which no great differences of opinion are likely to arise. Precise rules cannot be established to trace the origi- nal causes cf a prevalent idea or the various seasons why we are content to sink our prejudices when approaching what, nolens rams, has bscome the vogue. Amongst the many we are content ti take one illustration of the rapidity with which the public appreeiateheing well served. The Bradford Manu- facturing Company, having made a new departure, resolved to deal only with consumers direct, as previously the public generally had little option but to pay the regu ation high prices, which it is reasonable to suppose must be put upon dress goods which pass through the hands cf merchants and shopkeepers before reaching the final purchaser. The Company had a keen eye to the requirements of the pubic, and had evi- dently carefully weighed the mattar and the soundness of the principle of direct trading. Few cared to interest them- selves in the matter when the first offers were made through the Press to the public, but those that did avail themselves were not el ;vs to make their friends duly acquainted with the advantages ot buying direct: and err, almost imperceptibly, the system has gained ground until thousands of ladles now pur- chase direct from the looms of the Bradford Manufacturing Company, at Bradford, Yorkshire. , COUNCILLORS' FOOD FOR REFLECTION. Sir,-I see by the ~Ilanchester Guardian of yesterday that it is possible and even probable that the individual members of oar Town Council will render themselves personally liable if they become promoters, with others, of the Man- cheater Ship Canal, so the action of those who voted in favour of it iaet Tuesday was heroic, and of a Marcus Curtius character. The possible suns named is some £1,500,000, and may be mere than that. What will theit wives and families say? Mr. John Crosfield and Mr. William Pierpoint refrained from voting, which was a token of self-preservation, and Aldermen Holmes and Webster voted against. No wonder, for the former alderman vreuld perhaps be the first to be shot, as he would have to sign the cheques as chairman of the Finance Committee. Alde:man Davies,' hear, was "from home." He has often been from home lately. A certaha councillor of the legal profession and one or two other Anowing birds I see were too late to vote.—Yours truly, Warrington, December, 1384. DISCRETION.

THE MAGISTRATES AND LOTTERIEF. Sir,—l wonder whether the magistrates of St. Helens, when they vowed their determination to put down lotteries, were thoroughly in earnest, or whether their words were ac- companied by a pious, but unexpressed, qualification. There .are, as you have pointed out, two chief classes of offenders with respect to lotteries, namely, the publicans and the par- sons, or, rather, perhaps, the managing members of the churches and chaps's. The magistrates have wreaked their vengeance on the former class ; are they equally determined todet the latter class feel the weight of the magisterial fist? If they want an occasion, I would also ask if it is true that at a recent church bazaar at St. Helens a pony, besides other articles, was raffled. Is it true that this bazaar was opened by a magistrate, and that its opening was honoured by the presence of other magistrates, including two of the virtuous trio who sat on the second batch of lottery CAS'S, and also by the legal adviser of the St. Helens bench ? Is it true that the visitors to the bazaar were openly solicited by buy lottery tickets by the wives, the sisters, and the daughters of magistrates, and this in the very building in which the police have their headquarters? It these queries cannot be answered in the negative, I shall be much surprised if the I3mch ate not afforded an opportunity of showing their love of even-handed jestice. The police are often accused of partiality; here they have a chance of proving theirimpar- tiality. Permit me to thank ycn for calling attention to this sub- ject in your colamns.—l am, sir, FAIR PLAY.

FAIR TRADE. Sir,—Will you aliow me to thank your correspondent "Clifford Dix' for the light he has thrown upon the Fair Trade question. Along with many other friend, I have long desired that some qualified writer would take up the que9tino, more from a local trade point of view. " Clifford Dix's" letter will, I hope, completely set at rest the minds of working-men on the Fair Trade question, and those who, like myself, were heverin.: between two opinions, may new have their minds set at ease—Yours, &0., A WORKING MAN.

you permit me, not as a politician but as a British workman anxieus te earn a living at his own trade and in his own country, to say a few words in reply to your correspondent "Clifford Dix." Your correspondent at once admits "that trade is depressed and unremunerative, and that mills ara.running short time," so I am spared the trouble of proving ibis. Your correspondent also throws some light upon the cease of depression in the wire trade of this country when he relates the large quantities of wire imported from Germany into England. A case has just been tried at the Liverpool Assizes in reference to a "Trade mark," vialch also confirms the truth of Wee enormous im- ports. The defendants—a German wire manufacturing firm —it was stated bad sold last year alone £225,316 worth of wire in this country, and thie, remember, is one firm only. There must be someth7ng wrong—something unfair some- where to allow all this work to be done and money made by foreign wiredravvers out oi English orders. The fault cannot real with the British manufacturers, because your corres- pon&nt says "they scarcely get change for a shilling with what orders they are now taking." I believe that unfair trade is at the bottarn of all this mischief. If two clubs are playing a match at cricket or football both must play by the same rules, or it would not be fair play—so this country must trade upon the same rules as other countries, or the trade is not fair. Foreign governments grant sums of money to steamship companies to run at low freights ; if we do not act as others do how can we succeed ? We are "penny wise and pourd foolish;" no wonder we are beaten by unequal circumstance!. Your corresponient refers to cheap wire ; I should like to know what he calls cheap wire—it was cheap a year ago, too cheap for the wiredrawers who had to submit to a re- duction of wages to meet the foreign competition, but it is cheaper still, yet we are worse off for work than ever. So cheap wire will not mend matters. The fact is money is made in a tieing market and not in a falling market. How did the firms your correspondent alludes to carry on busi- ness ten years ago, before German wire came into this coun- try ? Your correspondent says those firms who use wire would take their works to Germany, if we put a duty upon German wire equal to the duty Germany puts upon English wire. I don't believe they would, yet I say act fair ; be- sides, could they not now if disposed manufacture in Ger- many and get the wire even cheaper still. Why also should not English manufacturers of wire take their works and capital abroad if foreign makers can take orders which we cannot get. Your correapondent alludes to the land queetion, but the land question will not salve the difficulty, for wheat at half its present low price even would not help a workman to reduce his weges mere than a few pence per week. Wheat, however, is Cheap now, still trade is bad. It appears to me that Fmglismen pay the trxes or revenue of this country and lose the orders of the country at the same time, by the present poliCty of England ; whereas, if foreigners pay the taxes of their cenntry they secure their own home orders by the aid of a tariff defence, and are able to take our orders also. This is the prazticel truth, aa it stands, in a nutshell. --Yours truly, FAIR PRICE. Warrington, December 2nd, 188.1.
ROYAL MA.NCITESTER, LIVERPOOL, AND NORTH LANCASHIRE AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY.

'flee annual meeting of this society was held on Tburs- day, at the Lion Hotel, Warrington, when the chair was occupied by the Right Hon. Lord Egerton of Tattoo. Amongst those present were Lord Winmarleigh, and Messrs. Lawrence Rawstone, Robert Lonedale, Wm. Scotson, James Birch, James Dickenson, John Haleill, John Hornby, Wm. Derbyshire, 'Rome Wilkinson, R. J. Howard, nos. Fin- - -obett,Wm. Forrester, John. Roberts, J. T. Smith, John White, James Hatton, John Southern, Alfred Srnetham, F.C.S.' George Cooke, Robert Holland, Peter Blun- dell, Catterall, Hodgson, Henderson, Sherwin, Lea, Langton, Peck, ctes , dm. The annual report was read by the Secretary. It stated thst the pre- - &int depression of a.riculture, particularly on arable farms, and the shew being held for three days only instead of four, as was the case the last two yeare, and eaturday, the third day, being wet and unfavourable, explained the reduced amount of receipts for admission, and the show yard requiring double fencing for a considerable length to protect the young hedges with which it was kounded, and the exhaustive trials of traction engines, added to its ex- penees' and to these facts were due chiefly the reduction of the cash balance of led . year from £757 to its credit to £464 as shown in the balance sheet. The show itself was both lanes and interesting. The exhibitions ef dairy cattle and of cart horses were the chief feature at the show, and the fact that the majority of exhibitors were bona fide tenant farmers, and form:d a larger proportion than has been the case for some years, was particularly gratifying to the Council. The society wanted to encourage the enterprise of practical men in improving the character of their own stocks and the cultivation of their farms and crops. The trial of the traction engines excited much interest They desired to extend their operations by proposing that a schelarship or prize be founded by the society to be given annually to any student, from 14 to 20 years of age who should best pass an exami ,alit., a any branch of egricul- tural. science or practice as msy be fixed upon yearly by the Council. The higher education of farmers became more 1 necessary costinually. The large sums now spent in manures and in feeding stuffs, with but limited knowledge of their coletitution anl most etficient action, and the almost entire disregard of book-keeping and of recording results of farm- ing, both common and uncommon, were not creditable to the intelligence and influence of so important an interest. Tee decision of the society at the laet annual meeting to hold no show in 18•5, bet to co-operate with the Royal Agricultural Society to make its show at Preston very suc- cessful, and to contribute MOO to the funds of the Local Committee of that town in support of it, rendered it unneces- sary to revise their prize list, or to do more in regard to the faun than fix upon the division of the society in which its show of 18813 shall be held. A proposal had been very favourably received that the show of 1886 be held at Chester; and the Cheehire and the Denbighshire and Flintshire Agricultural Societies had intimated in an informal manner their willingness to improve the occasion by their co-opera- , rion. Upwards of 30 new members had joined the society this year, but 15 had resigned and six died during the year. The total number of members was now about 700. Lord WINMARLEIGII moved the adoption of the report. Ha believed they would all think it a very sttisfactory one when the circumstances attending it were taken into ac- count. They had had an excellent show at Stocleport, and he knew that it created a great deal of interest in the district and had caused a great improvement in agriculture throughout the district in which it operated. He did not recollect any meeting of that society that had been so well attended as that one, which was a sign that they were pro- gressing and not receding. and if any depression exisited it showed that the farmers of Cheshire and the adjoining counties were determined to meet that depression.—Mr. P. LOSSIDALE seconded the motion, which was carried uneni- mously.—The Rigbt Hon. Lord Winmarleigh was elected preeident, on the motion of the noble CHAIRMAN, seconded by Mr. W. SCOTSON. Mr. Smetham was re-elected analy Ica' chemist, Mr. Holland consulting botanist, anl Mr. T. Rigby secretary, the latter being highly compli- mented on his services.—A number of members were elected on the council, which concluded the business. A substan- tial rep.est was then partaken of.

There was a well. filled room. Mr. W. Clarke, M.A., of the National Reform Union, was present to deliver an address on the subj,ct of " War, taxation, and the Working-classes." Mr. W. (Hear, heir, and ap- plause.) Frequently our wars had arisen from this arro- gance and indifference to the feelings of others, which we Britishers were too much is the habit of displayieg when we got into a distant land. Of the misery of war, the misery caused by the destruction of food, of property, and of life, he need not enlarge. They came then to the conclu- sion of war, and here we saw the ridiculousness of the pen- tion in which we were frequently placed. (Hear, hear) We declared war, the opposing armies marched one against the other, men were slaughtered, and then when one nation expressed itself exhausted, whit hop. pened. Chosen men from from each nation quietly met in the privacy of a Council camber and discussed whit shotild be the result of the conflict. He could not help thinking that to busiuess men and sensible men it would appear that that end might in most instances be the beginning—(hear, hear, and applause)—tbat that council should take place before the fighting, and that when the council had failed to arrive at just conclusions, fighting might then be taken up as an alternative course; bat cer- tainly in the first instance the council,should be adopted. During this century we had been blessed with a great deal of peace. At the conclusion of the great French war, when we had carefully caged the great Napolean, the " tenor of Europe," and placed him on a little island, in which we were quite sure he could do no mischief, there began a period of peace. Our history called this the 30 years' peace, and it was a secti n of our national history which went by that name. Shortly after that 30 years' peace we made great demonstration. We had a great exhibition which toOk place in 1851, and which was largely desigoed to teach all nations of the world that if they would live at peace with one another it would be very much better for each and very much better for all. We thus had two extended eras of peace since the great Europeon war. He thought it would scrpriee most of them when he reviewed the wars thet had taken place between 1816 and 1881. The lat- ter date he took because there was data upon which one could argue—the dote being a document presented to Parliament in the year 1831. He took this period without fear, although, as he had told them, much had been devoted to peace. He found that during these 65 years England was engaged in no lees than 76 wars. Forty- four of them were on a large scale, and worthy of the dig- nity of being called wars. We had four with European nations, 29 with Asiatic nations, 14 in Africe. I only in America, and that in Central America—not, he was happy to say, with our brethren of our own flesh and blood—arid we had five with the Australasian countries, the majority of them having been in New Z !eland; we had 23 wars with various tribes in India, and we had nine with our own fel- low-subjects in the various colonies; making the total he had named. These wars had be-n estimated to cost Eng- land 1,400 millions of money. The result of that very large sum of money which had been spent upon wars was very largely seen in our national balance sheet, represented to a great extent by the figure which st-nds against " National Deb'," the interest we paid every year for the blunders, and, in some instances, the crimes of our ancestors. We paid 23e. million pounds per annum as interest on the National Debt. We had to add to that the cost of our army and navy, which amounted to 26 million pounds. That was not all. We were eeinetimes told that we got very little for our money ; that the army was small, and the result not at all commensurate with the expenditure we incurred —that when we compared our expenditure of our army with foreign countries such as France and Germany, it was seen that they got very much more for their money than we got for ours. This he ventured to doubt. He thought we did not carefully estimate the cost which these large standing armies were to foreign nations. It was not merely taxation which they incurred in so much hard cash. It was the withdrawal of their male population from industriel pur- suits in the most important eras of their lives. In the else of Germany for a very great number of years—he thought about 12 years—the male population between the ages of 12 and 14 years were liable to be called upon for military service ; withdrawing them from more useful occupations, and in many instances requiring them to perform their mili- tary service in districts where they were unable to do any- thing to increase the material welfare of their c4untry Sometimes people thought that in these days we were not at all alive to the glory of our native land ; that those who lived at the beginning of the century were much more fond of military glory than we are, and that it would be well if we could go back to that state. Now, he must ray that he felt very much better pleased that we should be in the posi- tion of expressing our assent or dissent, grum- bling or being grateful, over an extra penny on the income tax when we through our rulers de- cided that we would undertake any particular war. We made much more fuss over an extra penny on the income tax on account of a war than our ancestors used to do over a much greater grievance, and be thought it was a very useful safety valve that we should so immediately have an oppoeuuity of expressing our assent or diseent to the course of action which any particular Government was taking with regard to any particular war. In the time of Our grandfathers it might be that they did not feel the pressure Of what they had to pay so strongly as we did. He thought they in reality paid very much more, and that we very often had evidence of their discontent which we overlooked in the glamour of the victories which our great comman- ders secured over the French and our other foes. They hod to pay for their whistle in dear food. They had to buy that dear food with very poor wages, wages which any workingman in the north of England would not now tole- rate for a single week, or, at any rate, not for a fort- night. He would not give his employer an opportunity of paying him a second time at the poor rate at which our grandfathers were paid. They had then the conscription ; they had then the drafting for soldiers; and there was no "will you ?" or" won't you ' about it. It was all "you must." Then there was the navy. The wooden walls of England had always been our glory. How was the Position of the sailors at the , beginning of the century. How frequently did it happen that there was, a dearth of sailors; an unwillingness on the part of seamen to enlist in the King's navy! They all knew how frequently it occurred that one of the King's ships was in the chops of the channel to meet home com- ing vessels that had been away from England for many years—long voyages were then the custom—that sailors coming home as they supposed to enjoy for a time the plea. sures of femily and home were met in the chops of the channel, were seized there and were not allowed to laud, but were immediately sent off again to fight the King's battles, without any asking whether they would or would not. He thought the condition of affairs which we now had in Eng- land—ties condition of the working classes with regard W our fighting service was vastly preferable to that which we were asked to regard with so much reverence as obtaining in the time of our grandfathers. (Applause.) Mr. WILLIAM CLARICE then delivered his address, which was attentively listened to and frequently applauded, He poiuted out that wars had lowered the moral tone of the ' people of this country to a considerable extent by making them look at questions from the standpoint of interest rather than of principle. War developed a feeling that mieht made right, which was a doctrine that ought to be condemned by every right-minded men. (Hear, hear.) Haling given some statistics to show the enormous cost of wars to this and other countries, he pointed out that the national debts of the European countries owing to were amounted to a no less sum than four thousand million pounds sterling, and the present yearly interest upon that sum at present paid was one hundred and ninety millions

sterling.
