THE CANAL—The CLERK said he had communicated with the Loudon, and North-Western Railway Company with respect to the dredging of the Sankey Canal, and their secretary, Mr. Reay, replied that he would at cnce commu- nicate with the company's divisional engineer on the sub- ject. He (the clerk) also stated that he had written to the Local Government Board on the Sankey Brook, and pointed out that the Authority were still of opinion that the pollu- tion of the brook se -med to have its origin in or near St. 11:eens, and that they considered that so long as the pollu- tion of the brook contioued so long would it remain a source of danger to the public health, and that the Authority in whose district the nuisance arose ought to do everything in their power to prevent the nuisance. To this letter the Local Government Board replied that they would commu- nicate with the Town Clerk of St. Helens on the subject.— The CHAIRMAN: This matter will therefore be left in abey- once for another month, MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.—The MEDICAL OFFICER (Dr. Sephion) reported that two cases of diptheria had oc- curred at Croft, the causes of which he had not been able to I ascertain; and also one case at Glazebrook. The Medical i Officer also referred to the importance of a proper removall ef sewage, and suggested som, improvements in the mode of removal.—Mr. COOPER said he had been informed that the inspector had often great difficulty in getting to kaaw when outbreaks of disease took place, and wished to know if 1 there were no means by which he could get earlier informa- tion.—Dr. SEPIITON said the proposal to make notification of disease compulsory had often been before Parliament, but had always been passed by.—The CHAIRMAN Said he had himself been struck by the need of earlier notification of disease. Farmers were compelled to give information when cattle diseese broke out amongst their cattle, and there I seemed to be at present more interest taken in the cattle than in Christens. (Laughter.)—lt was resolved to adopt the Midical Officer's suggestions as to the mode of sewage removal.—Dr. SEPHTON also reported that during the month of November the births were—males 16, females 16; deaths —males 6, females 12. The death-rate from al ceases being equal to 171 per 1,000, against 12-3 in the correspon- ding month of last year. The CLERKSHIP.—The CLERK mentioned that at the next meeting he would ask the Authority to appoint his son as clerk to the Authority in place of himself. He explained that the emoluments of the office which he now received himself would be turned over to his son. IHE SHIP CANAL AND LATCHFORD DRAINAGE.—The SURVEYOR reported that in fulfilment of the instructions he had written to Mr. Leader Williams, the engineer of the new ship canal, asking for a set of plans of the proposed work in Tbelwall, Latchfcrd, and Grappenball, that he might lay before the Authority a eepart With referenCe the interference with the present drainage. Mr. Williams replied that when their piens were ready he would send the surveyor those affecting the district in question. He (the surveyor) bad net yet got them. This was all the business.
SERIOUS RAILWAY ACCIDENT NEAR

WARRINGTON. Shortly before midnight on Thursday an accident of a serious character occurred near Earlestown station, by which considerable damage was done and the traffic inter- rupted for over four hours. The accident happened at what is known as the "curve," at the point where the line crosses the road from Earlestown to Wargrave and the Vulcan. The 10-30 p.m. express goods train (Great Western) from Manchester to Chester, via Earlestown and Warrington, was approaching Earleatown at a great speed, and just before reaching the" curve" one of the waggons in the front part of the train left the rails it is supposed through some de- fect in the waggon. Other waggons were dragged off the line, and one was turned over and in that condition dragged some distance. The driver of the engine soon brought the train to a standstill, and it was then found that several waggons had left the rails, one being overturncdand smashed ' to splinters, while four others were also seriously smashed. Some damage had also been done to the " fourfoot," which was much cut up by the waggon wheels. Mr. , Young, the stationmaster, was immediately called, and ac- I tively bestirred himself in getting the lines cleared. A tele- gram was sent to Warrinzton for assistance, and about one o'clock a breakdown gang arrived, and, under the directions of Mr. Marshall, and Inspectors Peters and Brooks, were set to work to remove the define and replace the waggons on the rails. At four o'clock this wore had been accamplished, but in the meantime the working arrangements were greatly interfered with, and some delay of the mineral and goods trains was experienced. As cos- . veniently as possible the section was worked On the one-line system until the block was re-In:wed ; and the passenger I train for the North from Warrington was sent along the Winwick line instead of passing through Earlestown. Heavy rain fell throughout the morning, and made the labour of • the railway employe'l very unpleasant, but they went to work with a will, and deserve praise for the way in which • it was accomplished.

div.head: WARRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIEIf•
div.p: WARRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIEIf•
"MOSES IN EGYPT."

'Lee first concert of the season in connection with e I above society was given on Thursday evening in the Public Hall, in the presence of a large audience. The subject chosen for performance on the present occasion was Rossini's oratorio, "Moses in Egypt," by the rendering of which the society may safely be said to have enhanced its well-won reputation. In addition to the excellent solo vocalists which the society sup- plied from amongst its 'OWD members its the persons of Miss M. Wallington, Miss J. Monks, and Mr. W. H. Wallington, important parts were filled by such talented singers as Miss Marian Fenna, Mr. Seymour Jackson, Mr. Brereton, and Mr. Cuthbert Blacow. The society's orchestral band was likewise largely augmented by professional talent, the following gen- tlemen forming the orchestra :—First violins: Messrs. Joseph Harmer (leader), James Dunworth, F. W. Lucas, R. H. Pearson; second violins: Messrs. H. A. Walker and F. Blacow ; violins: Messrs. W. Haw- thorn, T. Rameden, J. Fairhurst, J. Woolman ; violoncellos: Messrs. H. Richardson, U. Bond, J. Leverock, W. Parkinson; double basses: Messrs. T. W. Lucas and Powell; flute: Mr. P. Brimelow ; oboes: Messrs. J.Pardoe and J. P. Reynolds; clarionets: Messrs. James Wadsworth and E. W. Reynolds; bassoons: Messrs. Abel Knight and Knowles. The harp accompanist was Mr. T. R. Ford, hon. harpist ,to the soeiety ; Mr. T. Mee Pattisen was or- ganist ; and Dr. Hiles was conductor: "Moses in Egypt" is a work impressed by many of the characteristics of Rossini's style, and as an oratorio there are somewhat marked differences between it and many other musical com- positions dealing with sacred subjects. There is about it little of that intense and impressive devotional feeling which we naturally look for in works of this class. There are in it indeed passages which are bright and cheerful, and even exhilarating, and much of the mush, is brilliant and wellsalculated to please ' a miscellaneous audience, it is, however, as far as the solo singers are concerned, a somewhat exacting piece, there being no fewer than eight leading char- acters represented, many of the passages for whom make an exceptionally severe demand on their vocal powers. It was, therefore, satisfactory to find that the society had succeeded in securing the ser- vices of a superior class of artists for the principal parts. Mr. Brereton, who represented " Moses," made an excellent impression in the opening solo, an impression which was more than sustained through- out the whole oratorio. He possesses a really splen- did bass voice, which is exceedingly well managed ; his declamation is good, and his enunciation perfect. Scarcely anything could be finer than his rendering of the grand invocation "Supreme Judge! Creator of heaven and earth," towards the close of the first part. On several occasions Mr. Brereton was re- warded for his efforts by the cordial applause of the audience. Miss Farma is the owner of a sweet, clear, and well-trained voice. The music she had to sing was in many places exceed- ' ingly trying, notably in the air ‘• Terrible destiny pursues me," in the second part. On her first appearance in a quartette and chorus she was just a little shrill, but later on her singing was very expres- sive, and her rendering of the passage commencing "My heart is torn" was an excellent specimen of vocalisation. Miss Fauna seemed to soon instal her- self as a favourite with the audience, and was fee- quently applauded Mr. Jackson is a very pleasing tenor singer, and was well received. Like many tenor singers, he seemed somewhat indisposed to throw that dramatic vigour into his part which is of course essential to a perfect representation. As " Amenophis " Mr. Jackson had a conspicuous and important pert to fill, and it is no more than justice to say that on the whole he sang tastefully and effectively, and was highly appreciated. As second tenor, Mr. Bla,cow did not often appear as a soloist, but when he did do so he acquitted himself in a most satlsFactory manner; and with regard to Mr. Wel- lington, who was in the rather trying position of being an amateur amongst professionals, it must be conceded, remembering Oise that he did justice to hlnaself and to the society. Of the local soloists Miss Monks occupied a conspicuous place. Her excel- lence as a singer is well-known and fully admitted in Warrington, and it need now only be said that, although she was placed side by side with vocalists of established repute, her manner of interpreting the music allotted to her as " Zillah " was -such as to advance her reputation as a solo singer. Miss Wal- lington, in the exigencies of the oratorio, did not occupy quite so prominent a position as a soloist, but nevertheless her fine voice added not a little to the effective and dramatic rendering of many fine pas- sages. With respect to the chorus and band, it is satisfactory to say that with one or two exceptions they displayed groat skill throughout the whole oratorio. Many of the choruses were rendered with. grand effect, and in not a few instances called forth the he irty plaudits of the audience. Altogether, the concert was one of the most successful the society has held, and will probably result in lovers of good music looking forward with pie satire to the next concert to be given by the society in March.

div.p: "OPTICAL atrstoNs."—Tbe Wycliffe Young Men's Niutual Improvement Society met on Monday evening, Mr. W. Wallington in the chair, when a paper, entitled " Optical Illusions," was read by Mr. T. H. Yardley, who illustrated his subject with numerous diagrams treating of the illusions of lines, curves, size, distance, position, and motion. He further gave familiar instances of illusions, and some very amusing experiments were tried by the mem- bers. The most wriking IHUAIOTIS brought before the class were " Winer's " and the "Illusions of motion." An in- teresting discussion ensued, Messrs. Brown, George Wal- lington, Coutts, and W. Wallington taking part.

SUDDEN DEATII OP AN INFANT.—On Tuesday the infan daughter of a man named John Knight, tf 5, Back Slam- ford-elreet, died suddenly in convulsions. An inquest was not thought necessary. LiE Iv. W. QUEICETT, rector of Warriugton, has for some thne.b ren indisposed, and on Monday afternoon he fainted in his bedroom from weakness, and has since been confined to Lis house. He is attended by Mr. Charles White. SALE OF PICTURES.—Mr. T. Sutton has this week !wen selling by auction, in the Public Hall, Rylands-street, a valuable collection of paintings from the Bloomsbury Gal. lery, Lyndon. The collection was a superior one, and many of the pictures fetched very good prices.

_ _ r WARRINGTON HORSE Fain--This fair was held On Mon- day, when there was a good show of animals, the number being roughly estimated at about 300. Moderate prices were realised. Most of the horses were of the heavy kind, but there were a few good carriage horses on view. . WESLEYAN YOUNCI MEN'S MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SO- CIETY. —On Wednesday evening a paper was real on "Scenes in every-day life" by Mr. Catterall. Mr. Barran- lough presided. The essayist dwelt chiefly on the effects of drink, gambling, and tobacco, after which a lengthened discussion took place. THE. LIVING OF Si. JOHN'S, WALTON.—We understand that the vicarage of ht. John's, Walton, has been offered by Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., the patrol, to the Rev. Leicester J. T. 1) small, of Oxford. The rev, gentleman is M.A. of Oxford University, was ordained deacon in 1879, and priest ia 1881, by the Bishop of Oxford, and in 1830 was ap.. pointed chaplain of Christ Church and Lincoln Colleges, Oxford. WARRINGTON HARRIERS.—These barriers had a cross- country run on Saturday, in which eight members took part. The hares were G. Hands and W. Gleave, and they laid the trail over some good country. W. IL Salmon led the pack for about three miles, when, having lost the track, they got divided. J. Massey, J. Green, J. Lee, and J. Heyes caine in before the hares, the latter following with W. H. Salmon and J. Bradbury close up._ . . .

COCKREDGE BAND OF HOPE.—The second entertainment of the session was given in the Mission-room. Brick-street, on Thursday evening. An excellent programme, consisting of recitations, songs, duets, readings, and dialogues. was gone through in a most creditable manner. The members were assisted by the Misses Ashley, and Mr. 'f.triner, from Bank Quay Mission, and Mrs. P. Travis. The Rev. W. R. Parry, the president, occupied the chair. . .

, . WYCLIFFE CONGREGATIONAL this church on Sunday evening spccial evangelistic service was held. The Rev. J. Yonge preached from the text "Room in the kingdom for all," and after the service the hymn "Yet there is room" was excellently sung by Miss Podmore, in place of Mrs. It 11. Pearson, who was prevented from sing- ing through indisposition. Sankey and Moody's hymns were u-ed ?Airing the service.

Tits BIRTH AND DEATH BATE OF WARRINGTON.—For week ending Saturday. November 29th, 1884.—The mean temperature was 339 Fahrenheit, and therefore 1.2 degrees colder than the preceding week. The maximum temperature, 58 Fahrenheit, was recorded on the 23rd inst., and the minimum temperature 17 Fahrenheit, en the 25th inst. The rainfall tnetsured 'B2 inches. The general direction of the wind was. N.W. During the week, which was the 48th of the current year, 43 births and 38 deaths were registered. The death rate from all causes was equal to 421 per 1,000, against `", 9 the average of the previous four weeks, and against 177 the corresponding week of last year. The detths included 14 from measles, 2 from diarrhea 1, 3 from plithisis, 2 from cancer, 12 from lung disease, 2 from heirt disease, and 1 from burning. One case of typhoid fever was reported under the requirements of the Act of Parliament.—Jonx H. Goaxatt, Medical Officer of Health.

... Tian SANKEY The Sankey Paper Mill, Farlestown, which has been standing idle for many years past has this week been put under the auctioneer's hemmer, and the sae h occisioned some interest to the trades-people of Earlestown ,t 1 district. The auctioneers were Messrs. Hayhurst and Taylor, of Bolton, and the sale was attended by gentlemen from Manchester, Liverpool, Sheffield, Tam. worth, and other places. Proceedings were commenced on Wednesday, when the contents of the smithy, bleaching, washing, and store-rooms were disposed of, and on the fol- lowing day the general stores, loose fittings, and materials, steam engine, &c., were sold. On Friday the offices, steam engines, boilers, and buildings were offered for sale. On the whole there have been good attendances, and the bidding was comparatively brisk, it is stated that about £3,000 were realised by the sele on the first two days.

GREAT SANKEY SCHOOL BOARD„—The monthly meeting of this Board was held in tha school-room, Great Sankey, on Tuesday afternoon. Mr. Turner, the chairman, presided, and there were also present Messrs Houghton, Kerfoot, and S Sutton (clerk).—The Clerk reported that the balance at. present in the ly dc In favour of the Board amounted to £79 33 91, and the cheques to be signed that day amounted to £l7 83 23.—Two new applications for the post of assis- tant female teacher at the schools had been received, and after a short consideration that of Miss Agnes T. Anderton. 6, Winwick-road, Warrington, was accepted.—The Clerk submitted some information with respect to a site for the pro- posed new Board scbools, and after considerable conversation it was agreed that a committee consisting of the members present should be formed to call upon various land-owners and inquire as to the terms on which a site could be ob- tained and then report to the Board.—This was all the busi- ne3s. _ . .

Sunnim DELTH —A man named Joseph Hough, 45 years of age, a clos•ger, residing at 15, Mersey-street, died rather suddenly at his home on Saturday evening. He had been slightly ailing for Borne time, but became worse and sud- denly died. Deceased was a prominent member of the Sal- vation Army and reference to his death was made on Sunday by several speakers at the meetings of the army. The regis- trar having given his certificate' no inquest will be held. The funeral took place in the Cemetery on Wednesday afternoon. The Army mustered in strong force, and, pre- ceded by its standard and the band playing funeral hymns, marched in front of the hearse. The chief mourners fol- lowed the remains in four mourning coaches. A large and respectful crowd lined Bridge-street and Buttermarket-street, through which the procession proceeded, and it is said that it is some years since a funeral at the Cemetery was wit- nessed by such a large concourse of people as then as. sembled.

div.head: LECTURE ON FREE TRADE AT RUNCORN. •
div.p: LECTURE ON FREE TRADE AT RUNCORN. •

On Thursday evening the second of a series of lectures on political topics, organised by the Liberal Aseociation, was delivered in Bethesda Lecture Hall by Mr. Coancillor Lampard, of Birmingham, who hod at a moment's notice taken the place of Mr. B B. Hackney, who bad been an- I nounced to speak on " Free Trade or Fair Trade." There was a good attendance.—Mr. T. Handley occupied the chair, and, in introducing the lecturer, remarked that during the present lengthened depression ig trade the question of free trade had been very much discussed, and neatly Tolies—he at not sae Whether many weak-kneed Liberals did not hold the same opinion—that the principles of what they called fair trade should be tried. But viewing the countries which lived under a system of protection, such as America, France, Germany, dm., they would find that the depression in trade in those nations was quite as severe, if not more severe, than that in our own. (Applause.)—The Lecturer, who dealt with his subject in a very lucid and interesting way, referred at the outset to the state of the working- classes. He quoted figures showing that while duriog the years between 1810 and 1883 the population hai pro- gressed by about ten or fifteen millions, there wes less pauperism now than there was 40 years I ago. This proved conclusively to his mind that the working classes were in better circumstonces than they ware previously, while in the few years before the repeal of the Corn Laws thOro were no less than fire Royal Commis- sions ep?ointed to investigate the causes of the depression in agriculture. Since these laws were repealed up to 1876 only one commission had been appointed. (Applause.) Fair traders were in the habit of saying England sent more mital out of the country than was being rocsived by her. This appeared so because the English people had so many investments in foreign countriee, and they only received bock the interest upon those investments. He illustrated ths matter by saying a • ship would take out merchsndisa fram Liverpool to San Francisco worth £100,000; th 3 ship was an English ship, the men English eailors ; and when the ship arrived at her destmation the cargo would be worth £125,000. The captain of the ship received the freight, and the sailors re- ceived their wages from the freight; bet instead of bring- log back the value of the cargo in gold, the captain took in a cargo of produce. On returning to Liverpool the p-o- -duce would be valued at £150,000. This £50,000 profit CAWe into English pockets, and England therefore received the benefit. England and Americo, the lecturer stated, were the two greatest manufacturing countries in the world, and he showed that the imports from America were 94 per cent of raw material, and only 6 per cent of manufactured good., whereas from England the proportion of exports was 94 per cent of menufactured goods and only six par cant of raw material. Therefore the working classes of England received more benefit from the exports than did the Ameri- cans from theirs. (Applause.) The lecturer also mentioned that England had two-thirds of the carrying trade of the whole world, and from these various facts deduced that free trade had been a great benefit to the country, and although the principles were not making great progress in other nations, yet, convinced of their truth and advantage, we must still advocate their adoption, and no doubt they would in time permeate the commercial life of other countries. (Applause.)—Mr. J. R. Frith proposed, and Mr. D. Eta- brown seconded a vote of thanks to the lecturer, and the motion was carried with acclamation. A similar compli- ment was paid to the chairman on the proposition of Mr. B. Kniveton, seconded by Mr. Bridgewater.

div.head: PRESENTATION TO THE LATE
div.p: PRESENTATION TO THE LATE
ORGANIST OF THE PARISH CHURCH.

On Thursday evening Mr. C. E. Rowley, of Manchester, late organist at Warrington was presented with a timepiece by those members of the late choir who adhered to their determination to "remain out" when the then choir came to a resolution to discontinue their services, under circum- stances reported at the time. The presentation took the shape of a handsome marble timepiece, supplied by Mr. Joseph Penlington, Liverpool, accompanied with an illum- inated address, and was purchased by Mr. Rowley's friends In tee late choir and a few personal friends alone, though many of the congregation would have been glad to join in showicg their esteem to Mr. Rowley.—The presentation was made at Mr. Rowley's room, in Sankeyestreet by the vcre- tary and treasurer, Mr. J. H. CLanxe, who said that he had been deputed by the members of Mr. Rowley's late chair and a few of his friends to perform what was to him a very piece- ing duty. Mr. Rowley would no doubt surmise that what he had to say was in reference to his (Mr. Rowley's) retire- ment from the position of organist ard choirmaster at the Warrington Parish .Church. When Mr. Rowley informed the members of the choir in June last that it WAS his inten- tion to sever his official connection with the church it was with deep regret that they heard that he was forced by circumstances to take that step,and were not without hope to the last that arrangements would be made to retain his valuable services. Such arrangements, however, were not made, and unfortunately at Michaelmas, when the term of his resignation expired, they found themselves without orgaeist and choirmaster. They felt at the time, and still felt, that the church had parted with a talented organist, and that the choir had lost a kind and efficient master. In reviewing the period of five years during which Mr. Howley had been with them .he could unreservedly state that he bad won the good opinion of them all. His disposition had been kind and genial, and his professional ability invaluable. They should look beck upon the few years that be had been with them with feelings of un- mixed pleasure. Mr. Clarke then made the presenta- tion on behalf of the contributors, saving that they did so not on acceunt of their intrinsic worth, but as a sincere mark of their esteem and regard. They hoped that in the time to come he might look upon them with kindly recol- lections of the many happy and pleasant hours in which they had been associated with him —la reply, Mr. ROWLEY said that he could not but feel himself to be an object wholly undeserving of such warm commendation. Having met with such unvarying kindness from the choir, it was hut the merest act of duty on his part to do all that he could to increase their musical excellence daring his five veers with them. This he tried to do, and it was gratifying to know that his efforts had been appreciated. Those efforts, however, would hive been valueless without the cordial and hearty co-operation of a united choir, and as he had often thanked them before for that, he once more seized the opportuoity afforded of expressing thanks for that good will, without which he could have done nothing. If any help was needed—but it was not—to keep the memory of each one of Clem fresh in his heart, those beau• tifal gifts would be additionally effective in that respect. It was a real grief to him to take that step of resignation which was forced upon him by uncontrolleble circum- stances, and which ended in their separation. He felt bound to say that in apology for what otherwise might ap- pear rank ingratitude for all the kindnees they had shown him in working so harmoniously with him, to exerting themselves to mike the services effective under trying con- dition?, and in being tolerant of his short-comings. If he slid that the Warrington Parish Church choir was the best he ever worked with, be was but giving it, as it was when s,he retired, ite rrere due. div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

Sir Arthur Havelock is ge.zettect Governor of Trinidad. The Gazette announces that the Queen has knighted Pro- fesior Roscoe, of V ctoria University, Manchester. Sir Stafford Northcote, who has been laid up with a cold, was decidedly better yesterday, and was able to leave his room.
H. NI. S. Rambler, which has been hastily fitted for sea, left Sheerness for China, on Friday morning, to strengthen the British fleet.

Mr. Charles Alison, M.P., was chosen yesterday deputy- chairman of the Great Northern Railway, in place off the late Mr. C. B. Denison. The studio of Mr. H. V. Inglis at Rndgwick, Sussex, was destroyed by fire on Friday evening. Many valuable works of art were destroyed. THE BURY TRAGEDY.—The inquest on the bodies of Mrs. Masen and her three children concluded at Bury on Friday, the jury returning a verdict that the woman mrirdered her children, and afterwards committed suicide whilst in a state of temporary insanity.

- GAS EXPLOSION IN LONDON—Several persons were in- jured yesterday afternoon by an explosion of gas at Messrs Woods, opticians, Cheapside. Two men' Robert Wood and John 11.11.01 were so seriously injured that they had to be conveyed to an hospital. DEATH OF A NOTED TRADES 'UNIONIST.—The death was announced yesterdiy of Mr. Thomas Mottershead, the well- known Trades Unionist, who has taken an active part in working-class politics during th% past forte years. He stood in the Radical interest for Preston in 1874, but was defeated.

RIOTING IN IIiELAND.—At Stewartson (County Tyrone) Petty Sessions, on Friday, an inquiry into the rec-mr rioting at Coal Island was concluded. Six women, Catholics, were sentenced to two months, three to three months, and one to fourteen days' imprisonment. Of the Protestant defendants two were sent to gaol for two months, and four for one month.

Barna DOG FIGIIT.—At Wellingboro' Police Court, on Friday, William Lowe, Edward Langley, and ten other men were charged wi h cravlty to animals by inciting two dogs to fiAht. The animals belonged to Lowe and Langley, and the encounter took place in Lowe's shop. The dogs fought with such ferocity that one was killed. Lowe was fined .£5 and Langley £4.

A. , I - • ILLED ON THE RAILWAY AT STOKE.—At an early nour ou Friday morning an accident occurred at Stoke Ittilway Station by which a young man named George Gadsby, 20 years of age, met with his death. The deceased, who was employed on the railway, was engaged in uncoupling some carriages of an excursion train that had come in from Birmingham. He was unfortunately caught between the buffers and crushed so terribly that he died almost immediately. COTTON MILL BURNED DOWN.—NARROW ESCAPE OF WOREPEOPLE.—Messrs. &railways cotton mills, at Moses. gate, mar Bolton, were completely destroyed by fire on Fri- day afternoon. The fire broke out so suddenly and spread 5o rapidly that many of the workpeople were compelled to jump from the windows to escape the lames, several being injured in doing so. The dam tgo is estimated at £50,000 1 and 200 hands are thrown out of employment.

• THE ASTON RIOTS.-At the Birmingham Polic3 Court, on Friday, the charge against Edward Reed, arising out of statements made in connection with the Aston disturbances, was resumed. Mr. Allard was called. and Mr. Matthews asked him to produce documents, including letters from Mr. Chambeilaln. The Stipendiary ruled that this was irrele- vant, and Mr. Allard was, therefore, not examined. Alfred Draycott, a toolmaker, was then examined, and said he was in the hospital when witness was reading Mr. Chamberlain's statement in the House of Commons. The case for the pro- secution was closed. PANIC AT A CONCERT.—On Thursday erehing, a panic occurred at a concert held in the Public Hall, Underhill- road, East Dulwich, in aid of a fund which is being raised to erect a mechanic's institute in the neighbourhood, which resulted in serious injury to several persons. The hall was crowded, and the concert bad proceeded without interrup- tion for some time when it was suddenly observed that the building was becoming rapidly filled with smoke. Some person then raised an alarm of fire, and a panic at once seiz Kl the audience. A general Testa was made for the doors, and the crush and confusion became terrible. Mrs. Anna Dawn iv, of The Laburnums, Underhill-road, had both her legs broken and her skull fractured. The smoke that gave rise to the panic came from the chimney of an adjoining POISONED WITH COUGH LOZENGES AT CHESTED.—OD Thursday night some boys entered a warehouse at Chester, recently occupied by Messrs. Eddy, sweet manufacturers, and finding a 'rib. bag of sweets, consumed a considerable quantity. These sweets were medicated cough lozenEes, made up specially by Messrs. Eddy for an extensive firm of wholesale chemists at Chester. Instructions are plainly affixed to each box that the patient is to suck one lozenge only every two hours, as each lozenge captains a homeo- pathic dose of morphia. The boys, however, continued sucking these sweets until they became very dangerously ill. The parents were much alarmed, all the boys being in great agony. A medical man WAS summoned and the stomach pump applied, but it was only after some hours that danger was over. The greater portion of the contents of the bag were given away to school children, but these lozenges have happily been mostly recovered.

div.head: AMERICAN MILLS RE-OPENED.
div.p: AMERICAN MILLS RE-OPENED.

NEW YORK, FRIDAY.—The North Chicago Rolling Mille, which were recently closed, will resume business on Mon- day, and will continue working till Februtry. Three thou- sand men will be re-employed during that period. FRANCE AND MADAGASCAR.

TAILITAVE, Nov. 23.—Preliminary negotiations are re- ported to have commenced between the Frerch Admiral and the Hovas. The French war vessels Beautemps, Become', and Allier have left with troops for Diego, Suarez Bay. The general situation of affairs is unchanged.

div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF LORDS.-ERMAY.
The House met at 4-0. THE FRANCHISE BILL PASSED.

The Yorksh ire Registries Bill passed, and the Franchise Bill and Consolidated Fund Bill were read a third time.—Reply- ing to Lord Truro, Earl Noratnnuoox said the Khedive thought it undesirable to retain the services of young English culets when experienced native officers could discharge police duties. The Marquis of SALTSBORY complained that this was a departure from former pub- lic policy of the Government to induce young officers to &aye in Egypt. Earl GRANVILLH declined in such civil service matters to interfere with the Egyptian Governtaant.—The House shortly afterwards adjourned.

EXTENSIVE SFIOV Dona ROBBERIES : ANOTgER WATEN.' ING TO TEADESMEN.—TWO women named Catherine Cane and Mary Sinnott were brought up at the Warrington Police Court, on Monday, in connection with extensive shop robe beries that have recently taken place 'in the town. They were conjointly charged with stealing a roll of line*, value £1 15s, on the 22nd November, from the shop Of Frederick Wm. Wright, and Cana was also charged witte stealing from the shops of William Auguetus Hayes anci George Blackhurst. There were four other charges against her that were not preferred. Both prisoners pleaded guiltY and begged for mercy.—Cane was sent to prison for three months, and Sinnett for two months.—Mr. Rant (chief constable) remarked that he wished that something could ho done to induce tradesmen not to expose their goods out- side their shops ; there had been a great deal of felonies from the shop doors. The defence of the tradesmen was tbat they must do so if they were to compete with thole who exposed their goods in the Marktt-place.—The Mayor : It is a strong temptation.—Mr. Hunt : In Liverpool they have an Act of Parliament to deal with them, but we have not.—The statieCt I IBM dropped. WESLEYAN %Z.!, 4R AT RIIRTONWOOD.—OG Wednes• lday a hazier was opened in the Wesleyan Chapel, Burton- wood, for the purpose of raising funds towards the erection lof a new chapel. The bazaar, which was replete with the kind of articles usually sold on such occesions, was supple-. mented by two heavily-laden Christmas trees, one of them which contained a considerable quantity of fowl and fruit, being supplied by Mr. Kilshaw, Bradley Hall, Burtonwood. The other, a holly tree, was supplied by Mr. Stead, of Pres- cot. Prior In the formal opening, the Rev. J. Shipharn, of 1 St. Helens, said be found that their friends at Burtonwood had got the spirit of improvement in them which was char- acteristic of the age in which they lived. They were not content to worship within the four walls within which their forefathers had worshipped these last 20 or 50 years. They wanted something larger to meet the growing wants of the ' neighbourhood. They had not got fa- on with the business of erecting a new chapel, but they had wide a start. They had £4O in hand, and a gentleman (Mr. W. Simms, Bur- tonwood), had promised to- give then a piece of land on which to build the chap. I, an,' he had 110 doubt that with a long mall and a strong pull they would soon have a place to worship in worthy of the times am) sufficient to accom- modate them. (Applause.)—Mr. M. G. Johnson, of Rair- hill, in opening the bazaar, remarked that that was a grow- ing neighbourhood, and as the works round about got dee veloped there would be an increase of population which would need suitable places treworehip in.—A .vote of thanks to Mr. Johnson was accorded on the motion of the Rev. J. M. Fairbourn, of gariestown, seconded by Mr. W. Hewitt. —The four stalls were presided over by the following ladies, viz. :—Mesdames 11: Jones, W. Jones, Wainwright, Makio, R. Simms, Broster ; Misses Hewitt, Forster (2), Martha Heyes, Mary Heves, Simms, Isherwood ; and Mrs W. Hew- itt, and Mrs W. Siml2lB were in charge of the Christmas trees. The very tasteful and appropriate decorations were put up by Messrs Travers' R. Shams, 11. Jones, W. Jones. J. Simms, C. Broaster, J. Ashton Wainwright, and Hatton. Mr. R. Simms was secretary of the building committee, and Mr. R. Kilshaw, treasurer. The bazaar was continued on Thursday, and on each-day was well patronised.

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD

The monthly meeting was held at the offices, Bridge- water-street, on Wednesday. Present : The Rev. Canon Barclay (chairman), the Rev. Father Finegan ; Messrs. T. Norman, P. Briscoe, G. S. Haelehurst, J. Pritchard, It. Lea, and Y. Rigby (clerk).—The Audit—A Surcharge: The Clerk said the auditor had examined the accounts and certi- fied them as correct, with the exception of one item of £4 Is 2d in respect of the treasurer's bond. The auditor said the treasurer ought to find his own bond at his own expense unless it was specially specified otherwise. He (the clerk) pointed out to him that in 1875 he passed the sureties of Mr. Thompson at the expense of the Authority, and that he had also passed a bond on another occasion. The auditor replied that that did not matter, and he had surcharged Mr. Lea, who had signed the cheque, in the sum of £4 Is 2d. The Board would have to appeal to the Local Government I Board, and there was no doubt they would gat the amount allowed.—The Proposed New School : It was stated that the plans of the proposed school were still with the Education Department and on the motion of Mr. Norman, seconded by Mr. Briscoe, it was decided that should the department re- turn them before the next meeting of the Board, the clerk should advertise for tenders in the local and the Manchester and Liverpool papers. In reply to Mr. Pritchard, the Clerk said application bad been made to the Public Works Loan Commissioners for a loan not exceeding £5,500 to purchase the site and erect the building ; to be re-paid in a term not exceeding 30 years.—Mill Brow School : The Clerk said the Board would remember that in his report Mr. Kyneraley spoke of the ante-room at Mill Brow School as a mere pas- sae,e. It was certainly in a disgraceful condition, and Mr. , Briscoe, who bad examined the place with him (the clerk), would bear him out in saying that it was absolutely neces- sary that something should be done. Several doors opened into the room, which was very draughty, and the floor was formed of flags, upon which little children about five years of age had to stand several hours each -day. Several sugges- tions were made by the clerk with the object of ma i- ng the room more oomfortable. A committee was appointed to deal with the question.—Visiter's Report: Mr. Bowyer, the visitor, reported that daring the month of November there had been an increase of SG in the average attendance and of 22 in the percentage of attendance as compared with the corresponding month last year. Forty-seven parents had attended before the committee to answer for the irregular attendance of their children, and the cases were duly dealt with.

The writ for Knareshorough was received on Wednesday morning. The nomination is fixed for Satut.lay, and the polling, for Tuesday next. The Rev, Canon Girdlestone, senior xenon of Bristol Cathedral, and Vicar of Olveston, died on Thursday morn- ing at Canon's House, Bristol, in his 80eh year. General Briere de Lisle, commanding in Tonquin,informs his Government that a Chinese Vieeroy has issued a pro- eamation requesting the people to poison the French. IN PaeLlA,et ENT. SEBBION 18S5 THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. WIIEREA., a Meeting of the Owners and Ratepayers of the Borough of Warrington, in the Counties of Lancaster arid I Chester, was held on Thursday, the Twenty-third day of 04i. bar, 1884, in the Public Hall RylandrentreEt, in the said Borough, in pursuance of the Act of the 35th and 36th Vic., cap, 91, intituled "An Act to authorize the application of Funds of Municipal Corporations and other governing bodies In certain eases." And whereas at the said Meeting, held at the time and place aforesaid. I. as Chairman of such Meeting, and in compliance with the statute, proposed the following resolution:— " That this meeting eonsente to the Mayor, Aldermen, and Burge,ses of the Borough of Wartingeon promoting, in con- junction with others, a local and personal Bill in Parliament for the purpose of Inc' rporating a Company and empowering such Company to construct a canal from the River Mersey to the City of Manchester, navigable for Ocean Steamers and Ships of large burthen. and to the contribution out of the Borough Rate to the cost of such promotion of a sum not ex- ceeding tvropenee in the pound upon the annual rateable value of the Borough for one year." And whereas the said resolution, on being put to the Meeting, was carried, whereupon demand was made that such question should be decided by a Poll of the Owners and Rate- payers. And whereas a Poll was accordingly taken In manner pro- vided by the Public Health Ac., 1875, and the schedules thereto, and the votes recorded thereat were as follows:— In favour of the above resolution Against -- Majority in favour of resolution 5,840 -- Dated this 3rd eay of Inseember, 1884. JOSEPH HARRISON. Mayor and Returning Officer.
